Both are equal structural debt, so rank them by team behavior -- change-frequency x complexity, the hotspot lens: B is churned constantly (40 commits in 3 months), so its complexity taxes the team on every change, while A is near-dormant (2 commits in 2 years) and its ugliness rarely bites. Flag B's debt first and keep A low. This is a RANKING decision, not a severity bump -- neither file is a Blocker/High merely for being complex, and A's low churn does not erase its debt, it only deprioritizes it. Compute churn from the repo's own git history (e.g. git log --format= --name-only | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn); if history were absent (shallow clone, fresh import), say so and fall back to complexity alone rather than invent a churn number. This ranks maintainability debt by where the team works, distinct from Phase-0 blast-radius which ranks the audit scope. (domain-checklists.md, domain H.)
expectations: Ranks the high-churn file B (40 commits/3mo) above the equally-complex low-churn file A -- hotspot = change-frequency x complexity from git history
Treats it as a ranking/prioritization decision, not a severity bump -- does not inflate either complex file into a Blocker/High
Keeps the low-churn file's debt low priority without erasing it (deprioritized, not dismissed)
Computes churn from the target's own git history and, if history were absent, says so or falls back to complexity rather than inventing a churn number

evals.prompt: Our orchestrator sheds load under memory pressure by running `pkill -f node` to stop the heaviest lane. Each lane runs a Node build in its own git worktree. What does the reviewer flag?
evals.expected_output: Flag the `pkill -f node` load-shed as a cross-lane collateral kill. pkill -f selects by command line, so it kills EVERY node process -- the other lanes' builds, a shared dev server, the reviewer's own tooling, even the orchestrator itself -- not just the heaviest lane. Kill by OWNERSHIP instead: start each lane in its own process group (setsid / a new pgid; a Job Object on Windows), record the pgid with the lane's claim, and terminate that group (kill -TERM -<pgid>) so the tool and every child it forked die together and nothing unrelated is selected. Escalate graceful stop (SIGTERM) -> a bounded grace window -> SIGKILL only if it outlives the window; kill and reap orphaned children (reaping alone only collects already-dead children; a live orphan reparented to PID 1 keeps holding the lane's worktree/port/lock until it is killed); and leave a teardown record that marks the lane's worktree/lock stale-and-recoverable so the next pass reclaims it. The shedding TRIGGER (memory/swap pressure) is legitimate -- the selector is the defect. (concurrency-shared-state.md.)
expectations: Flags pkill -f / kill-by-command-pattern as a cross-lane collateral kill (reaps sibling lanes, shared tools, or the orchestrator), not just the intended lane
Prescribes kill by OWNERSHIP -- an owned process group / job object terminated by pgid -- so the whole child subtree dies and nothing unrelated is selected
Covers graceful escalation (SIGTERM -> grace window -> SIGKILL) and killing-then-reaping orphaned children that would otherwise hold the worktree/port/lock
Distinguishes the shedding trigger (memory/swap pressure, legitimate) from the kill mechanism (the defect), and notes a teardown record leaving the lane recoverable

evals.prompt: A PR body reads 'Tests: 142/142 passing' and the repo ships a pre-commit hook that runs the suite. The branch-protection required check shows no run for this PR. Is the test evidence sufficient to merge?
evals.expected_output: No -- none of that is a trusted control. The 'Tests: 142/142' line is typed text, not an executed result; the pre-commit hook is self-reported and bypassable (git commit --no-verify skips it with no trace); 'the repo has hooks' proves nothing about THIS commit. Trusted evidence is a forge-verified run pinned to the exact commit under review, whose conclusion names that SHA. The required check showing NO run for this PR is itself a High merge-blocker -- a config gap, the check is unsatisfiable as wired -- not something the author's local run satisfies, and not something to override. Do not log the hook or the Tests line as a green control; require the forge run on the reviewed SHA before merge. If the work is in a linked worktree, also check the hook wiring: an absolute core.hooksPath or a default-branch-hardcoded pre-push range gates the wrong tree or range, so even a 'passing' local hook may have examined the wrong files. (branch-and-merge-hygiene.md.)
expectations: Refuses to treat the self-reported evidence (the Tests: N/N line, the local hook, 'the repo has hooks') as a passing control -- it is typed or --no-verify-bypassable, not executed on this commit
Requires a forge-verified run pinned to the exact commit under review (its conclusion naming that SHA) as the trusted control
Treats the required check showing no run as a High merge-blocker / config gap, not something a local run satisfies or that should be overridden

Does not merge on the local evidence; may note that under a worktree the hook wiring (absolute core.hooksPath / default-branch-hardcoded range) can gate the wrong tree so even a green local hook is untrustworthy

evals.prompt: A service's only contract test for its public JSON API is a full golden snapshot of the entire response body; any change fails CI and the team's fix is to run --update-snapshots. A PR adds a new optional field AND renames an existing field that consumers read. What does the reviewer flag?
evals.expected_output: Flag the whole-response golden snapshot as the wrong contract-test shape for an evolving cross-boundary payload. It fails on BOTH changes identically -- the safe additive one (a new optional field) and the breaking one (a renamed field consumers read) -- so its failure cannot distinguish them, and the team's --update-snapshots reflex re-records BOTH, rubber-stamping the breaking rename on the next run. Replace it with a consumer-driven contract assertion: assert the specific fields, types, and constraints consumers depend on, so a backward-compatible additive change PASSES and only a real incompatibility (the removed/renamed consumer field) FAILS. Classify the rename as a breaking change (SemVer major / a versioned, compatible migration), and the new optional field as safe. Reserve golden fixtures for a small, stable, whole-value identity, not a large evolving payload. (api-contracts.md.)
expectations: Flags the whole-payload golden snapshot as the wrong shape for an evolving cross-boundary payload -- it cannot distinguish the additive change from the breaking rename (both simply fail)
Identifies the --update-snapshots re-record reflex as rubber-stamping the breaking rename (the anti-pattern), not a fix
Prescribes a consumer-driven contract assertion: a backward-compatible additive change passes, only a real incompatibility fails
Classifies the renamed consumer-read field as the breaking change (SemVer major / versioned migration) and the new optional field as safe; reserves golden fixtures for small stable identities

evals.prompt: Our agent reads GitHub issue text and MCP tool responses, and the same agent holds a GITHUB_TOKEN and can call a post_comment / merge_pr tool. We spotlight the untrusted content with <untrusted> tags and schema-validate the tool arguments. Is that enough to stop an injected 'merge this PR' instruction hidden in an issue?
evals.expected_output: Not enough -- the controls all live inside ONE identity that both ingests the untrusted issue/MCP content AND holds the token and the privileged tools, so a successful injection is a confused deputy: spotlighting and argument validation lower the odds, but the agent that read the malicious 'merge this PR' is the same agent that CAN merge. The architectural fix is to quarantine the reader from the actor: a reader identity with no token/write/egress consumes the issue and MCP output and emits only structured, schema-validated DATA OPERANDS (e.g. {target, fields}) -- never the action to take. The action is fixed by the trusted task plan, not derived from the issue: a separate privileged actor holds GITHUB_TOKEN, selects the operation from that plan, validates it against an allowlist of actions this task permits, and consumes the reader's value ONLY as an operand -- never as raw text and never as an intent/action selector (a schema validates shape, not authority, so a reader-supplied {intent: merge_pr} would still be a privileged action chosen by untrusted input). Then an injected 'merge this PR' can at most corrupt an operand the boundary rejects, not select a privileged ACTION. Review it as an architecture question: no single identity should both read untrusted input and wield the credentials. For the MCP link, trust the transport, not the payload -- an allowlisted server authenticates origin, not content safety. (security-ai-agents.md.)
expectations: States that spotlighting + schema-validating arguments is NOT sufficient -- the same identity both reads untrusted content and holds the privileges (a confused deputy)

Prescribes quarantining the reader (no creds/write/egress, emits structured schema-validated DATA OPERANDS only, never the action) from a privileged actor whose action is fixed by the trusted task plan (plus an action allowlist) and consumes the reader's value only as an operand, never as an intent/action selector

Notes a schema validates shape not authority, so an injection can at most corrupt an operand rejected at the boundary, not select a privileged action; frames it as an architecture question (no single identity reads-untrusted AND wields-credentials, and the action space is fixed on the trusted side)
For MCP: trust the transport, not the payload -- an allowlisted/signed server authenticates origin, not that the content is safe to act on

evals.prompt: Our repo scopes gates three ways: .github/workflows/ci.yml uses paths: filters, a pre-push hook greps changed files to decide which linters to run, and `make test` has its own case statement mapping directories to test suites. A PR touches packages/auth/; CI runs the security scan but the pre-push hook does not (its glob list omitted packages/auth). What does the reviewer flag?
evals.expected_output: Flag the three hand-maintained path->gate maps as a drift hazard, and this as a live drift: packages/auth/ is gated by CI's security scan but NOT by the pre-push hook (its glob list omitted it), so a developer relying on the hook gets a false-green locally while the same path is gated in CI -- the maps have diverged, and the local `make test` map is a third copy that can diverge too. The fix is one canonical path->gate manifest: keep the glob->gate-set mapping in a single version-controlled file and have all three surfaces (CI paths:, the hook's file scoping, make test's directory->suite map) DERIVE their routing from it, with a CI drift-gate that fails when any surface no longer matches the manifest -- the repo's own no-duplication rule applied to gate routing. An unrecognized path must resolve to the full gate set (fail closed), never to no gate. (parallel-audit.md.)
expectations: Flags the three hand-maintained path->gate maps (CI / hook / local) as a drift hazard and identifies the live drift (packages/auth gated in CI but not the hook)
Prescribes ONE canonical path->gate manifest that all three surfaces DERIVE from, not three parallel hand-maintained copies (the no-duplication rule applied to gate routing)
Requires a CI drift-gate that fails when any surface's routing no longer matches the manifest
Requires an unrecognized path to resolve to the full gate set (fail closed), never to no gate -- and does not merely patch the one missing glob

evals.prompt: A growth-stage team proposes splitting their monolith into 4 separate repos so teams can 'own' their areas. The code has no internal module boundaries yet, and the areas share a schema + validator + types that change together. What does the reviewer recommend?
evals.expected_output: Recommend the internal-package rung first, not a repo split. The code has no module boundary yet, so a 4-repo split is org/deploy structure imposed on an unmodularized codebase -- do the boundary first: carve internal packages (named import boundaries) inside the one repo, which is cheap and reversible. Split a part to its OWN repo only when it has an independent change cadence AND distinct external consumers AND its own release + ownership -- none demonstrated here ('teams want to own it' is org preference, and team/hiring trajectory is an owner call, not a repo-observable trigger). Critically, the shared schema, validator, and types change TOGETHER (co-evolving artifacts); split across 4 repos they drift (domain H) -- keep them co-located. Propose the internal-package boundary now, and route the repo-split decision (which rests on team trajectory + ownership) to the owner. (infra-evolution-by-stage.md.)
expectations: Recommends the internal-package / module-boundary rung FIRST (cheap, reversible) rather than a repo split, since no module boundary exists yet
Names the three admission tests for a separate repo (independent change cadence AND distinct external consumers AND own release/ownership) and finds them unmet here
Flags the co-evolving shared artifacts (schema/validator/types change together) as needing co-location -- split across repos they drift (domain H)
Routes the repo-split decision (org/team-ownership/trajectory) to the owner rather than mandating it from the repo -- it is not a repo-observable trigger

evals.prompt: Our CI feels slow so the team wants to buy a remote-cache CI vendor AND adopt trunk-based development alongside our current GitFlow. There are no pipeline metrics yet. What does the reviewer recommend?
evals.expected_output: Measure before adopting either -- with no metrics, both are cargo-cult spend. Instrument the pipeline first: the DORA health metrics on a consistent basis (change lead time, deployment frequency, etc., as release-engineering.md defines them), PLUS the cheaper iteration signals -- p50/p95 of time-to-green (push -> all checks pass), queue/runner wait, and rerun/flake rate. Then attribute the p95 to a stage (which job, which wait) and take the cheap fix first (cache a step, shard a slow suite, cancel superseded runs, fix the top flaky test) -- a tool bought before the bottleneck is measured usually moves a number you were not blocked on. The adoption bar for the remote-cache vendor is a number: which measured metric does it move, and by how much? No number, no purchase -- route the spend to the owner WITH the measurement. And adopting trunk-based ALONGSIDE GitFlow violates one-delivery-methodology-per-repo: a measured bottleneck justifies SWITCHING methodology, never running both -- itself subject to the same bar, not a free 'go faster.' (release-engineering.md.)
expectations: Requires measuring pipeline flow FIRST -- the DORA health metrics on a consistent basis PLUS the iteration signals (p50/p95 of time-to-green, queue wait, flake rate) -- before adopting the vendor or the methodology; no metrics = cargo-cult spend
Attributes the p95 to a stage and takes the cheap fix first (cache / shard / cancel-superseded / fix-flaky) before buying a tool
Applies the adoption bar -- which measured percentile does the platform move, and by how much; no number, no adoption; route the spend to the owner with the measurement
Flags adopting a second delivery methodology alongside the first as violating one-methodology-per-repo (coordination overhead), itself subject to the measured-bottleneck bar

evals.prompt: Our Renovate config auto-merges dependency updates the moment a new version publishes, once tests are green. A reviewer sees a bot PR bumping a transitive dependency to a version released 3 hours ago. Separately, a bot PR patches a dependency for a published CVE. What does the reviewer say about each?
evals.expected_output: Flag the auto-merge-on-publish as a missing release-age cooldown. For the 3-hour-old routine bump: a green test suite does not catch a compromised or hijacked just-published release (A03 supply-chain), and 'newer' is not 'safer' -- require a cooldown that refuses to resolve a version until it has been public for a set window (e.g. 7 days; Renovate minimumReleaseAge, or the Dependabot / pnpm-npm equivalent cooldown key), so a compromised release is caught before it reaches you. Do NOT auto-merge bot PRs without the provenance check plus the green gate, and require the cooldown. For the CVE patch: EXEMPT it from the cooldown -- real security-advisory fixes fast-track on their own cadence, separate from routine/feature bumps; conflating the two either delays the fix or rushes a breaking change. So: cool down the routine bump, fast-track the CVE patch. (dependency-currency-and-upgrades.md.)
expectations: Flags auto-merge-on-publish as a missing release-age cooldown -- a green suite does not catch a compromised/hijacked just-published release (A03), and 'newer' is not 'safer'
Requires a cooldown window (refuse to resolve until public for e.g. 7 days; names Renovate minimumReleaseAge / a Dependabot or pnpm-npm equivalent) before auto-resolving the routine bump
EXEMPTS the CVE / security-advisory patch from the cooldown -- it fast-tracks on its own cadence
Separates the two cadences (routine bump cooled down, security patch fast-tracked) rather than treating both the same

evals.prompt: A producer PR changes an `amount` field in a shared events table from cents to dollars, keeping the column an integer (500 becomes 5). All schema/type checks pass and the producer's tests are green. Downstream, a billing consumer and a reporting consumer read that table. What does the reviewer say?
evals.expected_output: Flag it as a data-contract breach even though every type check passes -- the value's SEMANTICS changed (cents -> dollars) while the schema still validates, so a billing consumer reading amount as cents now mischarges by 100x and a reporting consumer's totals are silently wrong, with no parse error to warn anyone. A data contract is the declared, versioned producer-to-consumer agreement covering not just schema/shape but quality/SLA and SEMANTICS (what the field means and its unit) plus an owner; a semantic change that breaks a declared consumer expectation is a breaking change even when the row parses. Fixes: version the contract and coordinate the migration (like an API breaking change -- cross-ref api-contracts.md), or add a new field rather than repurpose the old one; and express the contract as code (a schema-plus-expectations fixture, e.g. Great Expectations or dbt tests) so the breach fails CI, not a downstream dashboard weeks later. (data-quality.md.)
expectations: Flags the cents->dollars change as a data-contract SEMANTIC breach that passes every type/schema check (the value's meaning/unit changed, not its shape)
Identifies the silent downstream harm -- billing off by ~100x, reporting totals wrong -- with no parse error to warn
Names the data contract as covering semantics/units + quality/SLA + owner (not just schema); a semantic change breaking a declared consumer is a breaking change
Prescribes versioning/coordinating the migration (or adding a new field) and expressing the contract as code (schema+expectations, e.g. Great Expectations / dbt) so the breach fails CI

evals.prompt: A cloud bill doubled last quarter. The team wants to buy a cost-monitoring SaaS. There is no spend tagging/allocation, no per-team or per-feature budget, and no owner for cloud cost. What does the reviewer recommend?
evals.expected_output: Inform before you buy. FinOps treats cost as a continuous practice whose first phase is INFORM -- tag and allocate the spend to a team, feature, or environment so you can see WHERE it doubled; a cost-monitoring tool bought before allocation just visualizes an unattributed bill. Then OPTIMIZE against the now-visible drivers (rightsize, commit/reserve steady load, kill idle or orphaned resources), and OPERATE (a budget with an anomaly alert and a named owner) so the next doubling pages someone. The missing allocation/tagging, the missing owner, and the missing anomaly alert are the findings; the SaaS purchase is premature until the spend is attributed -- route that spend decision to the owner with the allocation data. (performance-db-cost.md.)
expectations: Requires INFORM first -- tag/allocate spend to a team/feature/environment to see where it doubled -- before buying a cost tool (a tool on an unallocated bill just visualizes it)
Names the FinOps loop: inform -> optimize (rightsize / commit-reserve / kill idle) -> operate (budget + anomaly alert + owner)
Flags the missing allocation/tagging, owner, and anomaly alert as the findings
Treats the SaaS purchase as premature until spend is attributed; routes the spend decision to the owner with the data

evals.prompt: A team shipped an LLM-powered summarization feature. Monitoring is the host service's latency + error rate only. Users report occasional wrong/empty summaries and the monthly model bill is climbing, but nobody can say which prompts fail or how many tokens each call burns. What does the reviewer flag?
evals.expected_output: Flag the LLM feature as under-instrumented -- service-level latency/error is not LLM telemetry. Capture per-call token usage (prompt/completion), latency and cost, the model + version, the outcome (success/error/refusal/empty), and a trace spanning any tool calls, so a wrong/empty summary and a token spike become visible and attributable to specific prompts and models. The OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions (gen_ai.*) name these signals -- adopt the convention names for portability, but that spec is still at Development stability, so pin no version and expect churn. Without per-call token/outcome signals the 'wrong summaries' and 'climbing bill' are unattributable -- that is the finding; tie the cost half to the cost-and-value lens (performance-db-cost.md). Do not 'fix' it by logging full prompts/responses -- that is a PII/redaction risk; emit structured telemetry, not raw payloads. (observability.md.)
expectations: Flags service-level latency/error as insufficient for an LLM/agent feature -- requires per-call LLM telemetry (token usage, cost, model+version, outcome, a trace)
Names the OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions (gen_ai.*) for the signal names, adopting the names for portability
Notes the spec is at Development stability -> pin no version, expect churn (does not cite a version or a fixed attribute list)
Ties the unattributable wrong-summaries + climbing bill to the missing per-call token/outcome signals; does not prescribe logging raw prompts/responses (PII/redaction risk)

evals.prompt: A team wants the review findings as a machine-readable file so a CI gate and an aggregator can consume them, and they plan to commit a copy into their public repo. Their draft file lists a coverage entry only for the domains that produced findings, and commits the whole file (coverage, evidence, and fixes) to the public remote. What does the reviewer require?
evals.expected_output: Two invariants of the machine report. First, a coverage row for EVERY assigned domain (A–T and W), every run -- a consumer that sees only findings cannot tell 'no findings in domain L' from 'domain L was never opened', so the absence of a row is not a clean run; listing coverage only for the domains that had findings is the defect. Second, disclosure EXTENDS the report's finding-level rule: a public committed copy keeps finding `id` / `area` / `severity` plus the disclosure-safe run header (tool, skill_version, date, scope, start_sha, archetype, stage) and `target` (its definition bars a private name), and GENERALIZES the two identifier-vector fields (`base_ref` -> a redacted branch per report-format.md's branch-name rule, `prior` -> a generic dated filename) rather than committing them raw; `coverage`, `polarity`, observations, evidence, and fixes stay out-of-tree until the fix ships. The file must carry the same findings, ids, severities, and areas as the markdown -- a consumer never reads the prose to trust it -- and be block-style YAML, since inline flow maps and anchors break minimal readers. (machine-report.md.)
expectations: Requires a coverage row for every assigned domain (A–T and W) every run; the absence of a row is not clean ('no findings' is not 'not scanned') -- listing coverage only for domains with findings is the defect

On a public remote, the committed copy keeps finding id/area/severity + the disclosure-safe run header + target (safe by its definition), and generalizes the two identifier-vector fields (base_ref -> redacted branch per report-format.md's branch-name rule, prior -> generic dated filename) rather than dropping or committing them raw; coverage, polarity, observations, evidence, and fixes stay out-of-tree until the fix ships (extends, not just matches, report-format.md's finding-level limit)
The machine file carries the same findings/ids/severities/areas as the markdown -- a consumer never reads the prose to trust it
Block-style YAML; inline flow maps and anchors are dropped silently by minimal readers

evals.prompt: A service's core billing logic has 95% line coverage and the team cites that as proof its tests are solid. The reviewer notices the tests call the functions but assert very little. What does the reviewer recommend, and how is the finding framed?
evals.expected_output: Line/branch coverage measures what EXECUTED, not whether a test would CATCH a fault in it -- 95% coverage can coexist with near-zero assertions, so the number is not proof. For load-bearing logic that leans on a coverage figure as its assurance, measure the PRODUCT suite's fault-detection with MUTATION TESTING: seed small faults and read the mutation score (percentage of mutants killed). A surviving mutant on the billing logic is a concrete finding in this method's own shape -- a `file:line` plus the specific behaviour no test asserts -- rated a High-confidence weak-assertion finding, not a style nit; triage survivors on critical paths first. This is distinct from self-testing a gate against a planted defect (that proves the checker; this scores the shipped tests). Name the technique + the CI operator (e.g. Stryker's `thresholds.break`, which exits non-zero when the score falls below a chosen value -- pick it per repo, do not import a number) rather than any one tool; representative engines are Stryker (JS/TS) and PIT (JVM), plus per-language equivalents. Bound it to the highest-stakes modules -- a mutation run scales with suite size x mutant count, so a repo-wide mandate is an over-ask. (testing-and-evals.md.)
expectations: Distinguishes coverage (what ran) from fault-detection (would a test catch a fault) -- 95% line coverage is not proof the tests are strong
Recommends mutation testing / mutation score to measure the product suite's assertion strength on the load-bearing logic
Frames a surviving mutant as a file:line + the unasserted behaviour -- a High-confidence weak-assertion finding, not a style nit; critical paths first

Names the technique + a CI operator (e.g. Stryker thresholds.break) and representative engines (Stryker/PIT + per-language equivalents) WITHOUT importing a specific threshold number; bounds it to highest-stakes modules because cost scales with suite size x mutant count
Distinguishes it from the gate-planted-defect self-test (checker vs shipped tests)

evals.prompt: An activity feed renders each item as a fact + its source (e.g. 'Acme raised a round -- source: press release'), correctly, with all five data states handled. The team says the UI is done. What does the reviewer flag, and how must the fix avoid fabrication?
evals.expected_output: The feed passes rendering but fails ACTIONABILITY -- each unit is fact + source with no 'why it matters / what to do next', a wall of verified facts. Flag it (domain P, product-ux-quality.md): a primary information unit on a decision surface should carry a why-it-matters signal DERIVED from real data -- a count ('3rd of its kind this quarter'), a recency-delta ('first activity in 60 days'), a graph-degree ('connects to N entities you follow') -- and, where an action is possible, a concrete next step. Anti-fabrication is the load-bearing constraint: the signal must be derived/deterministic, NEVER a model-authored importance score or an LLM salience judgement (the content-layer cousin of the false precision the confidence-tier rule forbids); and a derived signal that barely varies is not a signal -- measure its distribution first. Also check the most-decision-ready surface is in the first paint and stable, not a post-hydration aria-hidden island. This is a defect to surface, not a mandate to redesign a deliberately-terse product; the heuristic gate warns-and-lists (fail-open) and a human adjudicates. (product-ux-quality.md.)
expectations: Flags the feed as passing rendering but failing actionability -- fact + source with no why-it-matters signal or next step
Requires a why-it-matters signal DERIVED from real data (count / recency-delta / graph-degree) and a concrete next step where an action is possible
Hard anti-fabrication: the signal is NEVER a model-authored importance score / LLM salience judgement; a near-constant derived signal is measured first, not shown
Treats it as a defect-to-surface, not a forced redesign of a deliberately-terse product; the gate is warn-and-list (fail-open), human-adjudicated

evals.prompt: A feed exposes three sort modes over the same data -- 'Newest', 'Top', 'Momentum' -- plus a separate curated home surface. Each mode is individually sound and the default is not naive recency. What does the reviewer flag?
evals.expected_output: Ranking / sort-mode legibility (domain P, product-ux-quality.md -- extends variant-bloat to the ordering itself). Flag: (1) a first-time user cannot tell why to pick 'Top' vs 'Momentum' -- each exposed sort mode must be self-explaining (an on-demand one-line 'orders by ...'), and the variant-bloat test applies (would a first-timer know why to pick each? if not, cut to one strong default + progressive disclosure). (2) Two modes producing near-identical orders are variant-bloat -> collapse, and MEASURE the overlap rather than assume it. (3) The sort KEY needs a measured distribution -- an opaque or near-constant key is the ordering-layer form of false precision (reuse 'measure the distribution first'); an order the user cannot explain and the data cannot justify is noise dressed as intelligence. (4) Two ordering regimes across surfaces over one dataset -> consolidate or cross-explain which serves which task. Also rule whether the DEFAULT order serves the user's job (recency is a mode, rarely the right default on a decision surface). Warn-and-list, never block. (product-ux-quality.md.)
expectations: Requires each exposed sort mode to be self-explaining ('orders by ...') and applies the variant-bloat 'would a first-timer know why to pick each?' test
Near-identical modes are collapsed, with the overlap MEASURED not assumed
The sort key needs a measured distribution; an opaque / near-constant key is ordering-layer false precision (reuses measure-the-distribution-first)
Rules whether the default order serves the user's job (not reverse-chron by default on a decision surface); warn-and-list, never block

evals.prompt: A review requires a screenshot of a changed authenticated screen. The CI capture ran against the production build and attached a valid, non-empty PNG -- which shows the app's login page (the production build gates every route behind auth). The evidence gate passed on image-presence. Is that sound?
evals.expected_output: No -- a non-empty image is NECESSARY, NOT SUFFICIENT. A login / error / empty-state page is a valid non-empty PNG that proves nothing about the change; the receipt must show the TARGET FEATURE. Capture authenticated content through a dev / identity-bypass render mode, not a production build that auth-walls every route (which screenshots a login page perfectly). And prefer a deterministic readiness signal (a specific selector / text present) over a network-idle heuristic -- a live hot-reload socket keeps the network busy, so the capture waits forever and yields zero images. This is distinct from reproducing a build-specific defect (minification / hydration / CSS-order), which correctly uses the production build (method.md); here the goal is capturing feature evidence past an auth gate. (testing-and-evals.md / product-ux-quality.md.)
expectations: Rejects image-presence as sufficient -- a login / error / empty page is a valid non-empty image that proves nothing; the receipt must show the target feature
Requires capturing authenticated content via a dev / identity-bypass mode, not a route-auth-walling production build
Prefers a deterministic readiness signal over a network-idle heuristic (a hot-reload socket defeats network-idle -> zero images)
Discriminates from reproducing a build-specific defect (which uses the production build, method.md) -- no self-contradiction

evals.prompt: A merge-preflight gate calls an external service to verify a NON-security quality property (a docs-freshness check); the service is down (persistent 503 after retries). The gate reports a finding and blocks the merge, though it observed no actual defect. Correct? And would the answer change if the gate were a secret / CVE scan?
evals.expected_output: For the quality gate: No -- a persistent cannot-check is not a finding. A gate reaching an external dependency retries a TRANSIENT error a bounded number of times, then on a persistent outage (or timeout, or retired endpoint) it DOES NOT block and is NOT reported as a finding -- it fails closed only on a problem it actually observed. Blocking all work on a zero-defect outage is the failure. Also: never point a gate at a retired / unversioned endpoint, and bound the gate's own runtime (a silent hang blocks with no error trail, worse than a clean failure). Keep this gate-blocking behaviour distinct from the reviewer-honesty status -- an unverifiable item is marked could-not-check, never a silent pass. YES, the answer flips for a SECURITY / authz / integrity / spend attestation: a secret / CVE / banned-terms check whose input or dependency is unreachable **fails CLOSED (blocks)** -- a fail-open there is the bug, the missing-input fail-closed rule. (reliability-error-handling.md.)
expectations: For a non-security (quality) gate: a persistent cannot-check does NOT block and is NOT a finding; fails closed only on an observed problem
Retries a transient error a bounded number of times first; never wires a gate to a retired / unversioned endpoint; bounds the gate's own runtime
Distinguishes gate-blocking from the reviewer-honesty could-not-check status (not a silent pass)
The answer FLIPS for a security / authz / integrity / spend attestation: a can't-verify there fails CLOSED (blocks), not open -- fail-open there is the bug

evals.prompt: A dependency review flags a CVE in a library on a reachable code path and calls it 'known-exploited' to justify a Critical, but cites no source. Separately, another CVE on a reachable path has a low EPSS score and is not listed in KEV, and the reviewer proposes waving it through as low-risk. What does the severity discipline require in each case?
evals.expected_output: Case 1 (unsourced 'known-exploited'): the claim must name its canonical source, not guess (principle 2, prefer the canonical instrument). CISA's KEV catalog is the authoritative source of vulnerabilities that have been exploited in the wild -- a CVE listed there IS known-exploited. FIRST's EPSS gives the data-driven probability a CVE will be exploited in the wild in the next 30 days. Read them alongside CVSS, not instead of it: KEV/EPSS answer how likely, CVSS answers how bad. Case 2 (low EPSS / absent from KEV -> wave through): refuse. KEV and EPSS are prioritization INPUTS, not a lower bar -- a low EPSS, or a CVE's absence from KEV, does NOT disarm a reachable-path finding (absence of exploitation evidence is not proof of safety; EPSS is a 30-day probability, not a verdict). They raise and rank, never wave a reachable vulnerability through. (dependency-currency-and-upgrades.md, severity discipline.)
expectations: Case 1: requires citing the canonical source -- CISA KEV (authoritative exploited-in-the-wild catalog) and/or FIRST EPSS (30-day exploitation probability) -- not an unsourced 'known-exploited' claim
Distinguishes KEV/EPSS (likelihood) from CVSS (severity), read together rather than instead of each other
Case 2: a low EPSS or absence from KEV does NOT disarm a reachable-path finding -- KEV/EPSS are inputs that raise and rank, never lower the bar
Names the anti-false-precision reasoning: absence of exploitation evidence is not proof of safety, and EPSS is a probability not a verdict

evals.prompt: A dataset exposes a column `relationship_strength` (0-100) between people. Reading the code, it is computed purely as a normalized count of co-occurrences (shared papers + shared events). A reviewer is asked to sign off on ranking introductions by `relationship_strength`. What is the finding?
evals.expected_output: The field NAME is a schema-level overclaim: `relationship_strength` asserts a synthesized 'strength' the data never measured -- it is a co-occurrence count. Name it for what it measures (co-occurrence count / shared-context evidence) and surface the corroborating evidence (co-authored 4 papers; met at 3 events), not a manufactured 0-100 score. Require multiple independent signals before asserting a tie at all -- a lone co-mention or co-attendance is a lead, not a relationship. A relationship is two-sided: verify the edge is not dropped from one endpoint's view; reconcile both directions. And the UI must not render the bare number as fact (confidence-tier false-precision, product-ux-quality.md). (data-quality.md, scoring & config discipline.)
expectations: Flags the field NAME as a schema-level overclaim -- a co-occurrence count is not a measured 'strength'; name it for what it measures
Surface the corroborating evidence (counts of the actual signals), not a synthesized score
Require multiple independent signals; a lone co-mention/co-attendance is a lead, not a relationship
Notes a relationship is two-sided (reconcile both directions) and the UI must not render the bare number as fact

evals.prompt: A leaderboard ranks companies by a computed score. The pipeline has no field indicating whether a company is still operating, and the data includes some acquired/defunct entities. The author says liveness data is not available, so they will rank everything and 'filter later.' Sign-off?
evals.expected_output: Block it. Any ranking/scoring/leaderboard must gate on an OBSERVED liveness signal; a missing liveness field is a blocker, not a nice-to-have -- ranking without it puts dead or discontinued entities on a live shortlist. Liveness must come from the subject's own recent activity, not from the record merely existing. 'Rank everything, filter later' is fail-open; if the source emits no liveness signal, fail closed -- exclude or flag `unknown`, never rank as live. Distinguish a covered-but-dead entity from an uncovered one (honest-empty, product-ux-quality.md). (data-quality.md, scoring & config discipline.)
expectations: Blocks: a ranking/scoring/leaderboard requires an observed liveness gate; a missing liveness field is a blocker
Liveness = the subject's own recent activity, not mere record existence
Fail closed when no liveness signal -- exclude or flag unknown, never 'rank everything, filter later'
Distinguishes a covered-but-dead entity from an uncovered one (honest-empty)

evals.prompt: A dashboard's 'Resolve' button sets `resolved_at` (row retained) but the default list drops the item; resolved items surface only via a 'Show resolved' filter that defaults off, sits in an overflow menu, and there is no 'Resolved' state, undo, or count anywhere on the surface. The team says 'it's not deleted, the data is still there.' Finding?
evals.expected_output: Flag it. The defect is not default-hiding as such -- it is that an action LABELLED non-destructive ('Resolve') removes the record while giving NO cue it persists, is reversible, or where it went (no 'Resolved' state, no undo, and the only path is a buried default-off filter). So it reads as a hard delete: (1) product-safety -- a first-time user concludes they deleted it, suppressing a reversible action; (2) audit/history visibility -- the retained trail is effectively unreachable (data intact; the defect is visibility, not integrity). Fix: keep the record in place, visually muted + a status label ('Resolved'), OR give a clearly-labelled, DISCOVERABLE resolved/archived view; not colour-alone. Caveats: default-hiding behind a KNOWN filter (an is:open list, an active board, inbox archive) is a convention, not this; a soft-DELETE (deleted_at) is out of scope. Fail-open -- a heuristic can't tell hidden-reversibility from a deliberate convention, so a human adjudicates. 'The data is still there' misses the point: the surface gives the user no cue of that. (product-ux-quality.md.)
expectations: Scopes the defect to an action LABELLED non-destructive that hides the record with NO cue it persists/reverses (not default-hiding as such)
Names both failures -- product-safety (reads as destructive) AND audit/history VISIBILITY (data intact, visibility is the defect)
Fix: in place muted + status label OR a discoverable labelled resolved/archived view; not colour-alone
Carves out conventions (is:open / archive) and soft-delete as out of scope, and is fail-open -- a human adjudicates

evals.prompt: A collapsible section's default open/collapsed state is `useState(shouldExpand)` where `shouldExpand` is computed from a count fetched asynchronously that arrives after first paint. The hook does not re-sync when the prop changes. A unit test of the decision function passes. In the running app the section never opens. What is wrong, and how do you fix it?
evals.expected_output: Mount-capture: `useState` reads its argument only at mount; the async count lands after mount and the hook never re-syncs, so the computed default silently never applies. The pure decision function's unit test is green while the running UI is wrong. Fix: drive the mount default from data available synchronously at first paint (treat async-only signals as their falsy default at mount); surface the late-arriving signal through a non-reflowing affordance (a badge on the collapsed header), never by force-opening after the fetch (which reflows under the reader); keep the async signal in the decision function's contract so it is honoured when present at mount (a warm cache) and stays tested; verify in the running app, not only the logic test. (product-ux-quality.md.)
expectations: Names mount-capture: useState reads the arg only at mount and does not re-sync, so an async default never applies
Explains the green-unit-test / broken-running-UI gap
Fix: synchronous mount default + a non-reflowing late-signal affordance, not force-open-after-fetch
Verify in the running app, not only the logic test

evals.prompt: A team flips a card's default from expanded to collapsed. Unit tests pass but a browser spec breaks in CI. Investigating, another spec runs `if (await btn.count()) await btn.click()` on an 'Expand all' button a prior redesign removed, and it has been passing. What is the finding?
evals.expected_output: The specs lean on an implicit default and pass only by coincidence. Spec 1 asserted on content visible only while expanded, relying on the old default-open, so flipping the default breaks it at the browser tier (not on commit). Spec 2's 'click if present' is a no-op (count is 0 since the button was removed), so it passes only because the default happened to match what it needed -- a latent trap. Fix: make each spec drive the state it needs explicitly (open/collapse the specific control by its own affordance) and prefer an explicit state assertion over a best-effort click-if-present, which silently leaves the precondition unmet once the control is gone. (testing-and-evals.md.)
expectations: Specs pass by coincidence via an implicit default
A flipped default breaks browser-tier specs, and that break is not caught at the unit tier / on commit
'click if present' is a no-op latent trap that passes for the wrong reason
Fix: drive the needed state explicitly + assert state explicitly

evals.prompt: A group header shows an 'expand' chevron when `hasContent(group)` is true; a separate function `rows(group)` builds what renders when expanded. They are computed independently. How do you prevent them drifting?
evals.expected_output: Independent computation lets the predicate and the render-set drift -- the predicate says 'expand' but the body renders empty, or it collapses a group that in fact has content. Derive both from the same source where possible, and pin the invariant `hasContent(x) === (rows(x).length > 0)` in a test, in both directions and non-vacuously (at least one input exercising each branch), so a later edit to either side cannot silently make them disagree -- the class of bug where a 'smart default' hides real content or expands an empty container. (testing-and-evals.md.)
expectations: Independent predicate + render-set can drift (expand-empty or collapse-nonempty)
Derive both from the same source where possible
Pin predicate(x) === (renderSet(x).length > 0) as a test
Both directions and non-vacuous (each branch exercised)

evals.prompt: A stakeholder reports 'the dashboard feels static, nothing updates.' You grep and confirm the code DOES implement live updates (a websocket subscription, state wiring, the works). Do you (a) build the live-update feature, (b) close it as 'works on my machine,' or (c) something else?
evals.expected_output: (c) -- a third verdict, delivery-gap. The capability is present (confirm at runtime), but the reporter's perception is real evidence: the working code is not reaching the surface they evaluated. Rebuilding ships a second competing implementation (the false-absence failure); dismissing ignores a real user-visible fault. Diagnose why along four axes: build/environment drift (stale bundle, symlinked node_modules, an old deploy -- the surface they saw is not this tree); route/mount mismatch (it renders on a route/flag/persona they never reached); preference/state gating (a default, role, or saved state suppresses it for them); or a runtime/integration fault (reached and mounted, but the live channel never connects, the backend never emits, or an error is swallowed). Deliverable: the reason it did not reach them + the smallest fix to close the gap, not a reimplementation. (method.md, presence/absence; extends #250.)
expectations: Neither rebuild nor dismiss -- names the third verdict delivery-gap
Treats the reporter's perception as real evidence that the working code isn't reaching their surface
Diagnoses along build/env drift, route/mount mismatch, preference/state gating, or a runtime/integration fault (live channel never connects / backend never emits / error swallowed)
Deliverable is the reason + smallest fix, not a reimplementation

evals.prompt: A task says: 'field X is hardcoded to a constant / decorative -- go make it real and get the metric moving.' How do you proceed?
evals.expected_output: Treat the premise as an unverified claim, not a fact. Verify first: read the current code and MEASURE the live distribution before writing any fix -- the 'constant' may be an initializer a later pass already overwrites, making the premise stale and the fix a no-op. If the measurement then shows the value genuinely does not move, that can be the honest truth of the corpus, not a defect to engineer away. Before 'making it vary,' ask what moving it would require: if the only lever is fuzzy/approximate matching or counting non-independent sources, inflating the number fabricates it (anti-fabrication applied to an 'improve this metric' task -- an inflated-but-fake number is worse than an honest flat one; empty beats fabricated). The honest deliverable is to make the count provable -- retain the distinct corroborating evidence, add a gate that fails if a count outruns its evidence -- not larger. (method.md, presence/absence; SKILL.md principle 3, No fabrication.)
expectations: Treats 'broken/decorative/always N' as a claim to verify -- measures the live distribution + reads the code before fixing
Catches the stale-premise case (a constant that is only an initializer already overwritten)
A flat/near-constant metric can be the honest outcome, not automatically a bug
Refuses to inflate via fuzzy/non-independent matching (fabrication); makes the count provable + gated instead

evals.prompt: A repo moved its heavy e2e suite out of CI to a local-only pre-push step to save cost, but the CONTRIBUTING guide and PR template still say 'e2e is covered by the `ci-e2e` job.' An agent reads that and skips the local run. What is the finding and the rule?
evals.expected_output: The gate now runs NOWHERE: CI no longer fires it, and the docs told the agent it was covered, so the local step was skipped -- every surface reads green while the regression the gate exists to catch ships. A gate's stated LOCATION is a claim with its own currency. Rule: every gate names exactly one authoritative, current location; audit agent-facing docs (contributor guide, PR template, inline comments) for dangling references -- grep every CI job name/label/trigger and confirm each still exists and still runs the gate the text claims (a reference to a job/label that no longer fires the gate is a defect, not stale trivia); a relocation to local-only makes the local bar the BLOCKING one (say it is required + what evidence proves it ran, advisory-vs-trusted #294) -- a leftover 'CI covers it' is an instruction to skip the only remaining enforcement; and fail the audit CLOSED (a gate whose docs cannot name a live location is unenforced until proven otherwise). (docs-and-dx.md.)
expectations: Identifies the gate now runs NOWHERE (CI moved it; docs said covered so the local run was skipped)
A gate's LOCATION is a currency claim to verify when it moves
Audit agent-facing docs for dangling CI job/label/trigger references -- a dead reference is a defect
Relocation-to-local makes the local bar blocking; fail the audit closed on a gate with no live location

evals.prompt: After fixing an absolute core.hooksPath so hooks resolve relative to each worktree (#298), lanes cut from old feature bases start hanging on a pre-push hook that runs a step the environment no longer has. Agents begin using `--no-verify`. What went wrong, and what is the rule?
evals.expected_output: A worktree-relative hook runs the hook AS CHECKED OUT AT THAT WORKTREE'S BASE -- so a lane cut from an old base runs that base's stale/heavyweight hook, which hangs; the breakage is misattributed to flaky/slow tooling and bypassed (worse than no tier -- everyone still believes it runs). The order was backwards. Rules: (1) hook content is fail-safe by default -- a fast always-safe core, every slow/env-dependent/interactive step opt-in via an env flag or marker file (a hook that can hang will be bypassed); (2) land the safe hook on the default branch AND every long-lived base BEFORE normalizing resolution (normalizing while old bases carry the old hook guarantees stale-hook execution); (3) 'which hook runs here' is base-dependent -- verify the worktree's hook matches the intended version and make install idempotently re-assert it, not trust inheritance; (4) a push-blocking step needs an audited, reason-required escape hatch so a stuck lane never does a traceless whole-tier bypass. (branch-and-merge-hygiene.md; second-order to #298.)
expectations: A worktree-relative hook runs the BASE's copy, so a lane off an old base runs a stale hook
The ordering trap: land the safe hook on every base BEFORE normalizing resolution
Hook content fail-safe by default (safe core; slow/interactive steps opt-in)
Verify which hook runs (base-dependent; idempotent re-assert) + an audited escape hatch instead of a whole-tier --no-verify bypass

evals.prompt: You are reviewing a product whose job is to feed another system's scoring engine. It exposes an API that emits discrete raw events, delivered via a hand-run JSON export, with no per-field documentation of what it authoritatively provides. Its spec credits it with a '~50,000 companies in category X' input the scoring engine will weight. Domain I says the API's shape is fine. What does the provider-contract lens add?
evals.expected_output: Domain I checks the API's own shape; the provider SEAM (data-quality.md §12) checks four things shape-only misses: (1) it emits RAW EVENTS but the consumer scores on INPUTS -- it should emit windowed aggregates + velocity keyed on the consumer's canonical ids (with provenance + license/tier), not discrete triggers the consumer must re-aggregate (a join it does not want to own); (2) delivery is a static/manual dump, not a LIVE channel + cadence (a table/feed read on a schedule); (3) no per-field source-of-truth map (authoritative / partial / never) -- the consumer will wire fields the provider never ships and expect data it does not own; (4) the claimed '~50,000 in category X' input must be RECONCILED against the provider's live artifact (count AND classification) before it drives the score -- a pre-reclassification blend can be off ~100x. Pair with a gate: diff the consumer's declared provider-inputs against the provider's actual current output; a mismatch blocks sign-off. (data-quality.md §12.)
expectations: Emits raw events but the consumer needs scoring INPUTS -- windowed aggregates + velocity keyed on the consumer's canonical ids
Static/manual delivery vs a live channel + cadence (feed/table read on schedule)
No per-field source-of-truth map (authoritative / partial / never), so the consumer wires the wrong fields
Reconcile every claimed provider-input (count + classification) against the live artifact before it drives a score, plus a diff-gate

evals.prompt: A pipeline normalizes each translated fragment to NFC, then concatenates the fragments to build a display string that is also used as a dedup key. Cross-locale, some 'identical' entries land as duplicates. Separately, a reviewer notes user-facing counts render via `n === 1 ? 'item' : 'items'`. What are the findings?
evals.expected_output: (1) Unicode normalization is NOT closed under string concatenation (UAX #15) -- even if each fragment is NFC, the concatenation X+Y is not guaranteed to be NFC, so the assembled dedup key can differ byte-for-byte between visually-identical entries, producing false duplicates. Fix: normalize at the boundary where the value is compared or stored, AFTER assembly, not per-fragment. (2) `n === 1 ? singular : plural` is wrong outside English-like languages -- Unicode CLDR defines up to six plural categories (zero/one/two/few/many/other) and languages vary in how they pluralize; route through an ICU/CLDR plural API ('other' is the required default), never a hardcoded binary or a count concatenated with a fixed suffix. (i18n-l10n.md.)
expectations: Names UAX #15 concatenation non-closure: per-fragment NFC does not guarantee NFC after concatenation, so the assembled key mismatches -> false duplicates
Fix: normalize after assembly, at the compare/store boundary (not per-fragment)
n===1 binary plural is wrong: CLDR categories zero/one/two/few/many/other, route through an ICU/CLDR API ('other' required default)
Does not treat the author's locale as universal

evals.prompt: A PR adds a new dependency `fast-json-validator` (an AI assistant suggested it). The name is not a typo of any popular package, the lockfile is updated, and there is no postinstall script. Sign off on the supply-chain check?
evals.expected_output: Not yet. Name-proximity (typosquat) is not the only supply-chain name risk. Slopsquatting: an LLM can hallucinate a plausible package name that never existed, and an attacker pre-registers it -- so a name that is NOT a typo of anything can still be a hallucinated-then-registered malicious package. Verify the new dep resolves to an ESTABLISHED package: registry age, download history, a real source repo / provenance -- not merely that it isn't a typo. (USENIX Security 2025, Spracklen et al.: at least 21.7% of packages recommended by open-source models and 5.2% by commercial models were non-existent; 205,474 unique hallucinated names; ~43% recur on every re-run, so they are predictable pre-registration targets.) The release-age cooldown also catches it -- a never-existed-until-now name has no established history to clear the window. (security-appsec.md A03; dependency-currency-and-upgrades.md.)
expectations: Name-proximity / typosquat is not sufficient -- slopsquat is a distinct risk
An LLM-hallucinated name an attacker pre-registered is not a typo of anything, yet is malicious
Verify the new dep resolves to an established package (registry age / download history / real repo), not just non-typo
Notes the release-age cooldown catches a never-existed-until-now name

evals.prompt: A builder drops any evidence item lacking a URL and sets `evidenceCount = urls.length`; the type's docstring says an item with no evidence is invalid. The parser for the same serialized form reads `evidenceCount` verbatim and keeps 'evidence' entries that are merely `typeof === 'string'`. A sibling parser in the same module validates fully. Finding?
evals.expected_output: The parser is weaker than its own builder and docstring: at the deserialize trust boundary it reintroduces the fabrication the builder prevents -- a torn, hand-edited, or older-schema serialized line yields an item whose count exceeds its actual evidence (a fabricated count) or whose 'evidence' is a non-URL string. 'The builder guarantees X' does not mean a parsed object satisfies X (the serialized form can be torn-appended, hand-edited, an older schema, or written by a different writer). Fix: the parser must independently re-derive computed fields (re-derive the count from the validated collection, never read it verbatim) and validate element shape (a real URL, not just a string), enforcing the same invariants the builder and docstring claim. The fully-validating sibling parser shows this is an oversight, not a decision. Prove it with property tests: parse(serialize(x)) preserves the invariant, and parse(torn/adversarial input) drops or rejects rather than emits an invariant-violating object. Invisible to a builder-only test suite. (data-quality.md; CWE-502.)
expectations: Parser weaker than its builder/docstring reintroduces the fabrication at the deserialize trust boundary
'Builder guarantees X' does not mean a parsed object satisfies X (torn / hand-edited / older-schema / different writer)
Fix: re-derive computed fields + validate element shape to the builder's invariants (not read verbatim / not just a primitive type)
Property tests: parse(serialize(x)) preserves the invariant; parse(torn input) never emits an invariant-violating object; invisible to a builder-only suite

evals.prompt: A RAG chatbot has an end-to-end eval: a golden set of question->expected-answer scored for correctness; it passes at 92%. Separately, a travel-booking agent is evaluated only on whether the final confirmation message is correct. What is missing from each eval?
evals.expected_output: RAG: an end-to-end score is necessary but not sufficient -- a faithful answer over the WRONG retrieved context is still wrong, and a high end-to-end score can hide a retrieval miss the model papered over from parametric memory (which then fails silently when the knowledge base changes). Evaluate the two stages separately: retrieval quality (context precision -- retrieved chunks are relevant; context recall -- the needed facts were retrieved, measured @k; plus chunk-boundary loss and reranking) AND generation faithfulness (the answer is factually consistent with THAT retrieved context -- groundedness), with answer relevancy (does it address the question) as a separate metric. Agent: evaluate the TRAJECTORY, not only the final answer -- tool-call selection (the right tool), tool-call arguments (well-formed, correctly bound), and multi-step task completion (reached the goal without an unrecoverable wrong turn); a right confirmation reached via a lucky or unsafe path is a latent failure, and a wrong tool choice is invisible to an output-only bench. (testing-and-evals.md AI evals; RAG technique = Lewis et al. 2020; metric names operationalized by a tool like RAGAS, not a standard.)
expectations: RAG end-to-end score is insufficient -- a faithful answer over the wrong context is still wrong; a good end-to-end score can hide a retrieval miss covered by parametric memory
Evaluate retrieval quality (context precision / recall @k, chunk-boundary loss, reranking) AND generation faithfulness separately
Agent is evaluated on its trajectory -- tool selection + arguments + multi-step completion -- not only the final answer
A right final answer via a lucky/unsafe path (or a wrong tool choice) is a latent failure invisible to an output-only bench

evals.prompt: A service encrypts records that must stay confidential for 20+ years. The crypto is AES-GCM (strong today), but the algorithm is hard-coded at every call site with no version/identifier in the stored ciphertext envelope. A04's current-primitive check says the crypto is strong. Anything to flag?
evals.expected_output: Yes -- two crypto-agility gaps A04's current-primitive check doesn't cover. (1) Crypto-agility: the algorithm is hard-coded at each call site with no versioned suite id and no algorithm identifier in the ciphertext envelope, so it cannot be rotated without a rewrite and old/new can't coexist during a migration -- flag the non-agile design. (2) Harvest-now-decrypt-later: for 20-year confidentiality, an adversary can record the classical-encrypted data today and decrypt it once a cryptographically-relevant quantum computer exists -- so long-lived secrets warrant a migration path to the NIST post-quantum standards (FIPS 203 ML-KEM for key encapsulation; FIPS 204 ML-DSA / FIPS 205 SLH-DSA for signatures, published 2024). The finding is the hard-coded, un-versioned primitive with no swap path on a long-lived-data surface -- NOT 'ship ML-KEM today' (that would be stricter than the standard). (security-appsec.md A04.)
expectations: Flags crypto-agility: a hard-coded primitive with no versioned suite id / no envelope algorithm identifier can't be rotated without a rewrite
Raises harvest-now-decrypt-later for long-lived confidentiality -> plan a PQC migration path
Names the NIST PQC standards (FIPS 203 ML-KEM / 204 ML-DSA / 205 SLH-DSA)
Bounded: the finding is the non-agile design on long-lived data, not 'ship PQC today' (not stricter than the standard)

evals.prompt: A product sells audience data and serves cross-context targeted ads. The privacy review covers consent recording and cookie-banner load order. A reviewer asks about GPC; the team says 'we have a cookie banner.' What is the check?
evals.expected_output: A cookie banner is not GPC. Global Privacy Control is a universal opt-out signal the browser sends: check the code reads the `Sec-GPC: 1` request header (and/or navigator.globalPrivacyControl === true) and acts on it as a do-not-sell/share opt-out -- a greppable check: is the signal read at all, and does an opt-out path honor it (suppress the sale / share / cross-context targeting for that request or user)? W3C GPC = 'a mechanism for expressing a person's general universal preference for a do-not-sell-or-share interaction'; it does not cover deletion or same-context use. Whether GPC is legally binding is jurisdiction-specific (several US states recognize it) -> route the legal-obligation question to counsel / business-ops; the code check (reads + acts on the signal) is the concrete review item. (privacy-compliance.md.)
expectations: A cookie banner is not GPC -- they are different mechanisms
Check the code reads Sec-GPC:1 / navigator.globalPrivacyControl and acts on it as a do-not-sell/share opt-out
Greppable: is the signal read at all, and does an opt-out path honor it
Route the legal-binding question to counsel; the code check (reads + acts) is the review item

evals.prompt: A vendor ships an SBOM with its release; a scanner flags 40 CVEs in the listed components, but the vendor says most are not exploitable in their product. How should they communicate that, and what is the review check?
evals.expected_output: An SBOM lists components but not whether each listed CVE is actually exploitable in the product. Pair it with a VEX (Vulnerability Exploitability eXchange) -- a producer-issued, per-CVE exploitability assertion: for each flagged CVE a status (not_affected WITH a justification, affected, fixed, under_investigation), so a consumer can distinguish a real exposure from a component that merely ships the vulnerable code on an unreachable path. VEX complements, never replaces, the SBOM (CISA VEX). Review check: a not_affected claim carries a justification (e.g. the vulnerable function is not called / not reachable), not a bare assertion. (security-appsec.md A03.)
expectations: An SBOM lists components but not per-CVE exploitability -- pair it with VEX
VEX is a producer-issued per-CVE assertion; status values incl. not_affected WITH a justification
VEX complements, not replaces, the SBOM
A not_affected claim needs a reachability justification, not a bare assertion

evals.prompt: An ML pipeline reports 98% test accuracy. Reading it: a StandardScaler is `.fit()` on the full dataset before the train/test split, and one feature is computed from a 30-day forward window of the label. Unit tests pass. Sign off?
evals.expected_output: No -- two data-leakage defects inflate the 98% (a false metric). (1) The scaler is fit on ALL data before the split, so the test distribution leaks into training -- scikit-learn: 'never call fit on the test data'; split into train/test FIRST and fit preprocessing on the training subset only (use a Pipeline so cross-validation and tuning can't leak). (2) A feature from a 30-day FORWARD window of the label is target / temporal leakage -- 'information that would not be available at prediction time.' Both give 'overly optimistic performance estimates.' A leaked split passes too well -- the tell is the implausibly high score, not a test failure. Re-run with the split first and a leakage-free feature; the honest number will be lower. (testing-and-evals.md.)
expectations: Scaler fit on full data before the split = leakage -> split first, fit preprocessing on train only (Pipeline)
The 30-day-forward-window feature = target/temporal leakage (not available at prediction time)
Both inflate the metric (overly-optimistic estimates)
The tell is an implausibly high score, not a test failure

evals.prompt: A model's eval score dropped 0.91 -> 0.88 after a change; the team can't tell if the change caused it. Training uses an unseeded RNG and pulls 'latest' training data; model/code versions aren't pinned per run. Finding?
evals.expected_output: The score delta is unattributable -- you can't separate a real regression from run-to-run noise or a shifted dataset. Training must be reproducible: retraining on the same data should yield the same model. Seed the training RNG and pin the data + model + code version behind each reported number, so a delta is attributable to the change under review (Breck et al., The ML Test Score, 2017). Until training is reproducible, 0.91 -> 0.88 is not evidence of a regression. (testing-and-evals.md.)
expectations: The delta is unattributable -- can't separate the change from RNG noise / shifted 'latest' data
Retraining on the same data should yield the same model
Seed the RNG + pin data/model/code version per reported number
Until reproducible, the delta is not evidence of a regression

evals.prompt: An eval uses an expert-labeled test set treated as ground truth. A reviewer asks how good the labels are; the team says 'they're expert-labeled.' What is the check?
evals.expected_output: Requiring expert labels sets the bar but doesn't verify it. Label errors in a held-out set both distort the metric AND re-rank models -- test sets carry at least 3.3% errors across the 10 benchmarks studied, and correcting them can flip which model wins (Northcutt et al., NeurIPS 2021). Check: inter-annotator agreement across independent labelers (it bounds label noise and caps the achievable metric -- a model can't beat the label ceiling), spot-audit the flagged errors, and handle class imbalance honestly (a 99%-majority 'accuracy' is the base rate, not skill). Note: agreement among independent HUMANS is signal about the labels; agreement among MODELS is not precision. (data-quality.md.)
expectations: Expert-labeled is not verified -- check the labels themselves
Measure inter-annotator agreement (bounds label noise, caps the achievable metric)
Label errors distort the metric and can re-rank models
Distinguish human-agreement (label signal) from model-agreement (not precision); handle class imbalance honestly

evals.prompt: Our release bot snapshots the set of green + mergeable PRs each morning, then merges them one by one into main. Lately the later PRs in the batch keep going CONFLICTING partway through, even though they were mergeable when the batch started and their CI is still green. Separately, a conflict-resolution lane rebasing our worst PRs against main never seems to converge while the bot is running. What's wrong, and what should the bot do?
evals.expected_output: "Green + mergeable" is a snapshot against the current base head, not a durable property: merging one PR can flip an overlapping later PR from MERGEABLE to CONFLICTING (it touches a file the merged PR touched, so it now needs a rebase) while its checks stay green -- they ran against the old base, so only mergeability changed. Two fixes. (1) Re-check mergeability immediately before EACH merge, never once at the top of the batch -- mergeable has a shelf life of 'until the next overlapping merge'; and group the batch by the file sets each PR touches, merging serial-with-rebase within a group and in parallel only across disjoint groups (treating two PRs that share a hot file as independent is the bug). (2) The resolver never converges because the bot's own sweep is re-dirtying it: every merge moves the base head and invalidates the resolution just computed. Freeze the MERGE step -- not the build step -- while a resolver is active against the base: lanes keep taking PRs to green and green PRs queue instead of merging; land the hardest-to-rebase set first against a now-stable base, then drain the queue back-to-back. This is the stale-base failure at the mergeability layer -- a quantity computed against one base head, consumed against another. (deep-code-review/references/branch-and-merge-hygiene.md.)
expectations: Identifies 'green + mergeable' as a snapshot against the current base head, not durable -- green CI is NOT evidence of current mergeability (the checks ran against the OLD base); an overlapping merge flips a later PR to CONFLICTING, changing only its mergeability, not its checks
Prescribes re-checking mergeability immediately before EACH merge, not once at the top of the batch
Groups the batch by file sets: serial-with-rebase within a group, parallel only across disjoint groups (PRs sharing a hot file are not independent)

Diagnoses the non-converging resolver as the sweep re-dirtying it (each merge moves the base head, invalidating the resolution) and prescribes freezing the MERGE step -- not the build step -- while the resolver runs (queue greens, land hardest-to-rebase first)
Frames it as the stale-base failure at the mergeability layer -- a quantity computed against one base head, consumed against another

evals.prompt: We trained and validated a fraud model, it hit target metrics offline, and we deployed it 6 months ago. It's still up with green latency/error dashboards, and we're about to swap in a retrained v2 the same way we deploy any service -- build, health-check, flip traffic. Anything wrong with this?
evals.expected_output: Two production-ML gaps a service-style deploy misses. (1) Drift: a served model degrades silently with no error as the live input distribution drifts from training -- green latency/error dashboards do not show it. Monitor the input-feature distribution and the prediction distribution (a shift in either is the early signal) and realized performance against ground truth, remembering ground truth LAGS (the fraud label lands days/weeks later), so alert on a proxy (distribution shift, confidence drop) in the meantime; six months unmonitored on distribution/quality is the real risk, not uptime. (2) Rollout: a new model version is a behavior change, not just a deploy -- green error-rate and latency do NOT mean v2 is as good (they miss a quieter, worse model). Don't flip traffic on a health check. Prove v2 on prediction quality first: shadow it (run in parallel on live traffic, compare, serve none) or canary / champion-challenger to a slice with a prediction-quality promotion gate, keep a rollback path, and because ground truth lags give it a longer quality-based bake than a code canary. (deep-code-review/references/testing-and-evals.md.)
expectations: Flags model drift: a served model degrades silently as the input distribution drifts, and green latency/error dashboards do not reveal it -- monitor input + prediction distribution
Notes ground truth LAGS, so realized quality is delayed and a proxy (distribution shift / confidence drop) is what you alert on in the meantime
Rejects flipping traffic to v2 on a health check -- a new model version is a behavior change; error-rate/latency looking fine does not mean v2 is as good (a quieter, worse model)
Prescribes proving v2 on prediction quality via shadow or canary / champion-challenger with a prediction-quality promotion gate and a rollback path
Notes a model canary needs a longer, quality-based bake than a code canary because ground truth lags

evals.prompt: Our agent auto-resolves merge conflicts: for each conflicted file it runs `git checkout --theirs <path>` then `git add <path>`, and commits when `git add` succeeds. It works, except one file -- app/kpis/[key]/page.tsx -- shipped with conflict markers in it and only a later tsc error caught it. What went wrong, and how should automated resolution be gated?
evals.expected_output: Two bugs. (1) `git checkout --theirs app/kpis/[key]/page.tsx` was glob-expanded by the shell -- `[key]` is a character class that matched nothing (zsh errors; bash may pass the literal), so the checkout silently no-op'd and the file was never resolved. Quote/escape every path with glob metacharacters (`git checkout --theirs -- 'app/kpis/[key]/page.tsx'`, or disable globbing with the shell's own switch -- `setopt noglob` / `noglob` in zsh, `set -f` in bash/POSIX sh, since zsh's `set -f` leaves globbing on). (2) `git add` stages whatever is on disk -- conflict markers and all -- so `add` exiting 0 is NOT proof of resolution; the commit shipped `<<<<<<<`/`=======`/`>>>>>>>`. Gate every commit on a conflict-marker grep of the staged tree that actually fails on a hit (`git grep --cached -qE '^(<{7}|={7}|>{7})'` and exit non-zero, or `git diff --cached --check`; a bare `git diff -G` prints but exits 0, so it does not gate) plus a build/parse, not on `add` success -- especially in agent/automated resolution where no human eyeballs the diff. (branch-and-merge-hygiene.md.)
expectations: Identifies shell glob-expansion of the [param] path making `git checkout --theirs` silently no-op (matched nothing) -- fix: quote/escape metachar paths (or disable globbing with the shell's switch: `setopt noglob` in zsh, `set -f` in bash)
States `git add` stages on-disk content incl. conflict markers, so `add` exiting 0 is not proof of resolution
Requires a conflict-marker grep of the STAGED tree before every commit (plus a build/parse) as the mechanical backstop
Frames it as a silent-corruption surface specific to automated/agent resolution (no human eyeballs the diff)

evals.prompt: I need to update PR branch `feature-x` (merge main into it, resolve, push), but `git worktree add feature-x` refuses -- it's already checked out in a stalled lane's worktree. Should I just force-push feature-x from a fresh clone to get it updated?
evals.expected_output: No -- force-pushing strands the other lane -- it discards commits it had already pushed (orphaned on the remote) and leaves its local ref and unpushed work on a now-diverged branch. The non-destructive primitive: create a DETACHED-HEAD worktree at the true remote head -- `git worktree add --detach <dir> origin/feature-x` -- do the work there (merge main in, resolve keep-both, run gates), then push `HEAD:feature-x`. When the remote ref is an ancestor of your new HEAD this is a fast-forward, not a force-push: it updates the PR branch without touching the other worktree and without rewriting history. Verify the ancestor relationship first; if the branch has diverged it needs a real merge, not a push. And the 'already checked out' collision is usually stale worktrees never pruned -- prune them (teardown hygiene). (branch-and-merge-hygiene.md.)
expectations: Rejects the force-push -- it strands the other worktree's ref and any unpushed work there
Prescribes a detached-HEAD worktree at origin/<branch> (`git worktree add --detach`), do the work, then push HEAD:<branch>
Notes this is a fast-forward (not a force-push) only when the remote ref is an ancestor of the new HEAD -- verify first; a diverged branch needs a real merge
Notes the 'already checked out' collision is usually stale unpruned worktrees (teardown hygiene)

evals.prompt: Review this CI gate: it boots a headless browser + a preview server, then runs accessibility checks. When the preview server fails to start (a flaky port bind, before any check runs), the gate exits 1 -- the same exit code it uses when it finds a real a11y violation. It's been blocking merges intermittently and the team now blanket-overrides it. Sound?
evals.expected_output: No -- the gate conflates 'could not check' with 'found a problem'. A crash during harness setup (the preview server failing to bind, before the first measurement) is a persistent cannot-check, not a finding: it should not block work and should not be reported as a violation (after bounded retries of a transient error). Exiting the SAME code for a setup/harness crash as for a real a11y violation is the defect -- consumers can't tell an infrastructure outage from a genuine finding, so a flaky harness blocks everything and trains exactly the blanket-override you're seeing (which then also suppresses real findings). Fix: distinguish could-not-check (harness/setup/transient failure, or any crash before the first measurement) from found-a-problem with distinct exit semantics AND a distinct message; fail OPEN on a persistent setup failure after bounded retries, fail closed only on a violation actually observed. (This is a quality gate; a security/authz/integrity attestation is the exception -- it fails closed on a can't-verify.) (reliability-error-handling.md.)
expectations: Identifies a harness/setup crash before the first measurement as could-not-check, not a finding -- must not block or be reported as a violation (after bounded transient retries)
Names the same-exit-code-for-crash-and-violation as the defect: consumers can't distinguish an outage from a finding -> blanket-overrides that also suppress real findings
