The per-request token cap doesn't help — it bounds each call's size before dispatch; this is wasted spend on a call already in flight, orthogonal to the cap. Wire the consumer's abort/close (req.on('close') / AbortController / context cancellation) through to the model API call so a disconnect aborts the upstream generation. Red flag: a streaming model call with no abort path from the consumer. (Unbounded Consumption — LLM06 — via non-cancelled generation.)
expectations: Identifies that the client disconnect isn't propagated upstream, so generation continues server-side and bills for unread tokens (not a fault of request size)
Explains why the enforced per-request token cap doesn't address it — the cap bounds a call before dispatch; this is wasted spend on a call already in flight (cancellation, not a ceiling)
Requires wiring the consumer abort/close (req.on('close')/AbortController/context) through to the model call

evals.prompt: A web app embeds a payment widget in an iframe and listens for results: `window.addEventListener('message', e => applyDiscount(e.data.code))`. It works in testing. Security concern?
evals.expected_output: Yes — the handler trusts `e.data` with no check on `e.origin`. Any origin (including an attacker's page that frames or opens the app) can `postMessage` to the window, so a malicious sender can call `applyDiscount` with a forged payload — an origin-validation flaw (CWE-346). Verify `event.origin` against an allow-list of expected sender origins before using `event.data`, and validate the message shape too (a trusted sender can still relay malformed data). MDN: 'always verify the sender's identity using the origin and possibly source properties.'
expectations: Identifies that the handler trusts event.data with no event.origin check — any origin can postMessage (CWE-346 origin-validation)
Requires validating event.origin against an allow-list of expected origins before using the data
Also requires validating the message shape/syntax (a trusted sender can relay a malformed payload)

evals.prompt: An app loads a charting library and a font-loader from public CDNs via plain `<script src="https://cdn.example.com/…">` tags. Security review of the frontend — anything missing?
evals.expected_output: Yes — no Subresource Integrity. If the CDN (or its account) is compromised and the file is altered, every user's browser executes the attacker's code — a supply-chain vector. Add an `integrity="sha384-…"` hash (sha256/384/512) and `crossorigin` to each third-party `<script>`/`<link>` so the browser refuses a resource whose hash doesn't match; regenerate the hash on legitimate version bumps (or pin+vendor the dependency). Cross-origin SRI needs the `crossorigin` attribute + CORS headers.
expectations: Identifies the missing Subresource Integrity on third-party/CDN scripts — a CDN compromise runs arbitrary code in every user's browser
Requires an integrity hash (sha256/384/512) + crossorigin on the third-party script/link tags
Notes the hash must be regenerated on version bumps (or the dep pinned/vendored)

evals.prompt: A banking app's 'transfer funds' confirmation page sets no `frame-ancestors` and no `X-Frame-Options`. Output encoding and CSP script-src are otherwise solid. Is the page safe?
evals.expected_output: No — with no framing policy the page can be loaded in a transparent iframe on an attacker's site and overlaid so a user's click lands on the real 'confirm transfer' button (clickjacking / UI redress). Output encoding and script-src stop XSS, not framing. Every page rendering an authenticated or state-changing action must restrict who may frame it: `Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'self'` (or an explicit allow-list), with legacy `X-Frame-Options: DENY/SAMEORIGIN` as a fallback for old browsers. Clickjacking is its own threat class, independent of XSS defenses.
expectations: Identifies clickjacking/UI-redress: with no framing policy the state-changing page can be framed and overlaid to hijack a click
Notes XSS defenses (output encoding, script-src) don't address framing — it's a distinct threat
Requires frame-ancestors (CSP) on authenticated/state-changing pages, with X-Frame-Options as legacy fallback

evals.prompt: A migration runs an ALTER TABLE the team knows is instant (metadata-only). In staging it's fine; in production, running it during business hours briefly freezes ALL queries to that table for minutes. The DDL itself is fast. What happened?
evals.expected_output: Lock ACQUISITION, not DDL duration, is the hazard. The ALTER TABLE needs an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock (PostgreSQL), which conflicts with every other mode. A long-running transaction held a conflicting lock, so the fast DDL had to wait — and because PostgreSQL's lock manager grants a request only if it conflicts with no existing OR already-waiting lock, the pending ACCESS EXCLUSIVE then made every later query queue behind it, freezing the table until the long transaction finished. Fix: run DDL with a bounded lock_timeout (+ retry/backoff) so it gives up rather than holding the queue, and confirm no long-running transaction is open against the target before running it. 'Instant' says nothing about how long the DDL waits to acquire its lock.
expectations: Identifies lock ACQUISITION (not DDL duration) as the cause — ACCESS EXCLUSIVE waits behind a long transaction, then (via the wait-queue rule) blocks all later queries on the table
Notes a long-running transaction holding a conflicting lock is the trigger
Requires a bounded lock_timeout + retry and checking for open long transactions before running DDL

evals.prompt: A migration adds a FOREIGN KEY, a UNIQUE constraint, and widens a varchar column, all on a large live table with plain DDL. Reviewers approved it because 'none of these is a NOT NULL, so it's fine.' Correct?
evals.expected_output: No — UNIQUE/FOREIGN KEY/CHECK and a column type change trigger the same full-table validation-scan-under-lock that NOT NULL does; the 'only NOT NULL is risky' heuristic misses the family. A plain ADD CONSTRAINT scans the whole table under a lock that blocks writes for the duration — ACCESS EXCLUSIVE for UNIQUE/CHECK/PRIMARY KEY, though ADD FOREIGN KEY itself takes the weaker SHARE ROW EXCLUSIVE (still blocking writes, not reads). Use the two-phase form: ADD CONSTRAINT ... NOT VALID (commits immediately, no scan) then a separate VALIDATE CONSTRAINT (weaker SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE lock, existing rows only) for FK/CHECK; for the UNIQUE, CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY then ADD CONSTRAINT ... USING INDEX. Treat the varchar widening as a rewrite hazard on the same expand-contract path.
expectations: Identifies that UNIQUE/FK/CHECK/type-change trigger the same full-table-scan-under-lock as NOT NULL — the 'only NOT NULL' heuristic misses the family

Requires the two-phase ADD CONSTRAINT NOT VALID + VALIDATE CONSTRAINT (and CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY + USING INDEX for uniqueness); notes ADD FOREIGN KEY's lock (SHARE ROW EXCLUSIVE) is weaker than ACCESS EXCLUSIVE but still blocks writes
Treats the column type change as a rewrite hazard on the same expand-contract path

evals.prompt: A 'decrement inventory if in stock' does SELECT qty; if qty>0 UPDATE qty=qty-1, wrapped in BEGIN/COMMIT. Under load, stock goes negative. The dev says 'it's in a transaction, so it's atomic.' What's the misconception and the fix?
evals.expected_output: A transaction boundary is not a concurrency guard. At the default isolation level (Read Committed in PostgreSQL, REPEATABLE READ in MySQL/InnoDB), two concurrent transactions can both read qty=1 on the plain SELECT and both UPDATE — a lost update; BEGIN/COMMIT gives atomicity+durability, not isolation from a concurrent read-modify-write. Fix: take a row lock (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE), use a conditional/CAS update (UPDATE ... WHERE qty>0 and check rows-affected), a UNIQUE/CHECK constraint, or elevate to SERIALIZABLE. Any approach that can abort under contention — a serialization failure at SERIALIZABLE, or a deadlock with FOR UPDATE — must retry the WHOLE transaction with fresh reads (SQLSTATE 40001 / an InnoDB deadlock rollback), not just the failed statement, which would reintroduce the bug.
expectations: Identifies that at the default isolation (Read Committed / InnoDB REPEATABLE READ) BEGIN/COMMIT does not prevent a lost update on a plain read-modify-write — atomicity is not isolation
Requires FOR UPDATE / a conditional-CAS update / UNIQUE / SERIALIZABLE, not the transaction boundary alone

Notes any approach that can abort under contention (serialization failure at SERIALIZABLE, or a deadlock with FOR UPDATE; 40001 / InnoDB rollback) must retry the WHOLE transaction with fresh reads, not the single statement

evals.prompt: A coordinator merges a batch of green+mergeable PRs back-to-back. After the first merges, it reads the next PR's mergeable field, sees it's not MERGEABLE, treats it as CONFLICTING, and skips it — ending up landing only the first PR each run even though the others were fine. What's wrong?
evals.expected_output: GitHub computes mergeability asynchronously: right after a base-changing merge, an overlapping PR's mergeable field is briefly null/UNKNOWN while the forge recomputes — that is 'not yet known,' not CONFLICTING. The coordinator reads that transient UNKNOWN as CONFLICTING and skips a PR that is actually mergeable, so it lands only the first of the batch. Fix: poll until mergeability settles to a definite state (a bounded 2-4 tries with short backoff), retry only UNKNOWN, and never auto-retry a definite CONFLICTING as if transient. (Distinct from a real MERGEABLE->CONFLICTING flip when an earlier merge touches a shared file — that's a genuine rebase need, not a recompute race.)
expectations: Identifies GitHub's async mergeability recompute → a transient null/UNKNOWN state after a base-changing merge, distinct from CONFLICTING
Explains the bug: treating UNKNOWN as CONFLICTING skips a mergeable PR (lands only the first of the batch)
Requires polling until settled (bounded retries), retrying only UNKNOWN, never auto-retrying a definite CONFLICTING

evals.prompt: A merge preflight blocks if the PR body contains a 'DO NOT MERGE' line and allows the merge if it's absent. A bot that reformats PR bodies edits the line out; the preflight then sees no marker and merges — with no human approval. What's the design flaw?
evals.expected_output: The hold lives in a MUTABLE, self-reported surface (the PR body), so its absence is not authorization — anyone or any automated edit can clear it with no approving review and no trace (deletion-by-edit). 'No marker present → clear to merge' is fooled exactly as here. Fix: back the hold out of band — a branch-protection rule, a required review, or a status check the author can't toggle — never mutable body text alone; make body-editing automation append/insert-only with a before/after diff; and treat a hold-marker disappearance with no corresponding approving review as STILL HELD (fail closed). It's the mirror of 'a self-reported Tests: N/N line is not a passing control.'
expectations: Identifies that the hold is in a mutable self-reported surface, so its absence/removal is not authorization (deletion-by-edit, no trace)
Requires backing the hold out-of-band (branch protection / required review / status check), not mutable body text
Requires fail-closed on a marker disappearance with no approving review, and append/insert-only body automation with a diff

evals.prompt: A merge-train coordinator waits on the union gate before landing a batch. One run, the union job hangs (a wedged runner) instead of failing; the coordinator waits indefinitely and the whole queue stalls with no red status. How should it detect and handle this?
evals.expected_output: A hang produces no failure to react to, so waiting-for-red never fires. Detect it by LIVENESS, not elapsed time alone: during the gate RUN the base head is stationary by design (nothing lands until the gate concludes), so the live signal is the gate job's own OUTPUT — no new log output past ~2x its normal window is a hang (the long in_progress shard rule, applied to the conductor); cancel and root-cause. (Base-head movement is the hang signal only in the merge DRAIN phase, where members are landing.) Then don't block forever: treat a hung heavy gate as a can't-check / UNVERIFIED (never a pass), timebox it, and fall back to the deterministic runnable subset (lint/unit/type) as a proof-of-record, escalating the heavy gate's absence — but never merge a member the union never validated. Emit progress so a stall is visible; and keep flaky heavy gates in per-change pre-merge checks, not as a blocking union term.
expectations: Identifies that a HANG (vs a failure) produces no red, so a waiting coordinator stalls the whole queue silently

Detects the hang by the gate job's OUTPUT liveness (no new output past ~2x normal), not elapsed time alone — noting the base head is stationary during the gate run by design (base-head movement is the drain-phase signal); cancels+root-causes
Treats a hung gate as can't-check/UNVERIFIED — timebox + fall back to the runnable subset as proof-of-record (never merge on it), emit progress, keep heavy gates in per-change checks

evals.prompt: A service's SIGTERM handler immediately closes the HTTP listener, then waits for in-flight requests, then exits. On every rolling deploy, clients see a burst of connection-refused/reset errors. What's the ordering bug?
evals.expected_output: The listener is closed BEFORE the load balancer stops routing to the instance. On SIGTERM the readiness probe must flip to unready FIRST so the LB takes the instance out of rotation; only then stop accepting. Because it closes the listener first while the LB still considers it in rotation, new requests keep arriving at a closed socket → connection-refused/reset. Correct order (12-Factor's finish-in-flight goal, extended for a load balancer): fail readiness → LB deregisters → stop accepting new connections → drain in-flight requests (bounded) → exit. The reverse order is the bug.
expectations: Identifies the reverse ordering: the listener closes before readiness fails / the LB deregisters, so new requests hit a closed socket (connection-refused/reset)
Requires failing readiness FIRST (LB takes it out of rotation), THEN stop accepting, THEN drain
Names the correct SIGTERM sequence: unready → stop accepting → bounded drain → exit

evals.prompt: A service drains in-flight requests on shutdown by waiting for all of them to finish, with no timeout, relying on the platform's default kill-after grace period. Deploys sometimes hang; other times requests get cut off. What's wrong?
evals.expected_output: Two problems. (1) Unbounded drain: waiting for ALL in-flight requests with no timeout lets one slow/stuck request hang the whole deploy — bound the drain to a timeout >= the slowest legitimate request (e.g. p99), force-close survivors and log the count; zero drain isn't graceful either. (2) The platform grace period (and the LB's deregistration-propagation delay) is a SEPARATE, additive clock the app doesn't control — sizing the drain against the platform default rather than real in-flight duration reproduces the race: the platform hard-kills mid-drain (cut-off requests) or the LB still routes during the window. Size the app's own drain against real request duration, and ensure the platform grace window exceeds it.
expectations: Identifies unbounded drain (no timeout) as hanging the deploy — requires a bounded drain (timeout >= p99, force-close + log survivors)
Identifies that the platform grace period / LB deregistration delay is a separate additive clock, not the app's drain budget
Requires sizing the drain against real in-flight duration and the platform window exceeding it

evals.prompt: A queue worker on an at-least-once queue processes a message; on SIGTERM (deploy) it just exits. Occasionally a message in flight at deploy time is neither completed nor retried — work silently disappears. Cause and fix?
evals.expected_output: The worker exits without returning (nacking) its in-flight message, so whatever was mid-processing is lost. On an at-least-once queue, graceful shutdown means nack/return the current job (or finish it if short and safely resumable) so it's redelivered — per 12-Factor disposability ('returning the current job to the work queue'). 'Exit after whatever was in memory' silently drops (or, once the broker's visibility timeout redelivers a partially-applied job, double-processes) work on every deploy. Fix: on SIGTERM stop pulling new messages, nack/return the in-flight one, and make processing idempotent so redelivery is safe.
expectations: Identifies the worker exits without nacking/returning its in-flight job, so it's dropped (or later double-processed) on an at-least-once queue
Requires nacking/returning the current job on shutdown (or finishing if short/safely resumable) so it's redelivered
Requires idempotent processing so redelivery is safe, and stopping new-message pull first

evals.prompt: A service calls a slow third-party enrichment API and its own critical primary database through one shared connection/HTTP pool. When the enrichment API degrades (slow, not down), the whole service's latency spikes and even pure-DB requests start timing out. Why, and what's the fix?
evals.expected_output: No bulkhead: one shared pool couples the two dependencies. When the slow enrichment API holds pool slots waiting on its own timeouts, there are no slots left for the healthy critical DB path — every caller starves behind the saturated one, a cascading failure (Release It!, Bulkheads). Fix: partition the pool by dependency/traffic class — give the risky/optional enrichment call its own bounded pool (and its own timeout + circuit breaker) so its saturation can't consume the critical path's capacity; and fail fast (admission check) rather than queueing new work when that pool/breaker is exhausted. Distinct from tenant-vs-tenant noisy-neighbour isolation (that's a different axis).
expectations: Identifies the shared pool coupling: the slow dependency exhausts shared slots so the healthy/critical path starves (cascading failure)
Requires partitioning the pool per dependency/traffic class (separate bounded pool for the risky/optional call) + its own timeout/breaker
Adds fail-fast/admission-check when the pool or breaker is exhausted, rather than queueing

evals.prompt: A worker holds a connection pool of 20 to a database that accepts at most 100 connections. It works at 3 replicas. Ops scales it to 8 replicas under load and the database starts refusing connections. What was missed?
evals.expected_output: A fixed downstream capacity (the DB's 100-connection limit) is a shared budget that divides across replicas — 8 replicas × 20 = 160 > 100, so the pool sizing that was safe at 3 replicas (60) oversubscribes the DB at 8. The per-instance pool size must be derived from the downstream's total capacity divided by the replica count (with headroom/a floor), not treated as a fixed per-instance constant that survives fan-out. Fix: size per-replica against the shared downstream budget (e.g. a global limit enforced centrally, or per-instance = capacity/replicas with margin), and alert when replica-count × per-instance-pool approaches the downstream ceiling. (A bulkhead concern: unbalanced capacity under scale-out.)
expectations: Identifies that the fixed downstream capacity is shared and divides across replicas — per-instance pool × replica count oversubscribes it on scale-out
Requires sizing the per-instance pool against the downstream's total capacity / replica count (with a floor/headroom), not a fixed per-instance constant
Notes monitoring replica-count × per-instance-pool vs the downstream ceiling

evals.prompt: A pipeline: step A writes data.json, step B reads data.json. Someone adds a timeout-abort to step A (it used to hang). Now step A sometimes aborts mid-write, leaving a truncated data.json; step B reads it as if valid and ships garbage. What are the two defects?
evals.expected_output: (1) Adding the abort to step A is a WRITE-PATH change: an abort mid-write leaves a truncated/half-written artifact — the abort must preserve last-good (skip/atomic-rename) and signal failure, never write-then-throw (leave a partial file). (2) Step B gates on the artifact's EXISTENCE, not step A's SUCCESS: existence ≠ freshness ≠ success, so a present-but-invalid file from a crashed/aborted producer is consumed as valid. Fix: A writes atomically (temp + rename) or preserves last-good on abort and reports failure; B gates on A's success signal (exit status / a completion marker / a checksum), not merely that the file is there. Present ≠ valid.
expectations: Identifies the abort-added-to-a-formerly-hanging-step as a write-path change that can leave a truncated artifact — must preserve last-good / write atomically, not write-then-throw
Identifies that the consumer gates on artifact EXISTENCE not producer SUCCESS (existence != freshness != success)
Requires gating on a success signal (exit/marker/checksum) + atomic write or last-good preservation

evals.prompt: An alerting system fires a Slack message every time its 1-minute poll sees CPU > 90%. It already dedups by message id so a redelivered queue message won't double-send. During a 2-hour incident it sent 120 identical alerts. The dedup 'works' — why the flood, and what's the fix?
evals.expected_output: Delivery-idempotency (dedup by message id) stops the SAME message firing twice; it does nothing about REPEATED REAL firings of the same underlying condition — each poll while CPU stays >90% is a genuinely new firing, so 120 polls = 120 alerts. Fix: firing-suppression — a cooldown window per (entity, signal type): after firing for host X's high-CPU, suppress re-fires for N minutes — with suppression-with-audit (increment a counter + record last-suppressed timestamp, never a silent drop) so a real re-fire after the cooldown still gets through and an over-suppression bug is visible. A distinct mechanism from delivery-idempotency.
expectations: Distinguishes delivery-idempotency (same message twice) from repeated REAL firings of the same condition — dedup can't stop the latter
Requires a cooldown window per (entity, signal type) to suppress re-fires of the same condition
Requires suppression-WITH-AUDIT (counter + last-suppressed timestamp, not a silent drop) so real re-fires and over-firing stay visible

evals.prompt: An overnight job processes 5000 records. Its upstream API is down, so every record fails, but the job catches each error and continues; a process heartbeat keeps pinging so the liveness check stays green, and it 'completes' at dawn having done nothing. The team says 'add a dead-man switch.' Is that enough, and what's actually missing?
evals.expected_output: A process heartbeat only proves the process is alive, not that work is succeeding — so it stays green through a total grind; a dead-man switch is better but not enough. A dead-man on LAST-SUCCESS would eventually fire here (zero items succeeded, so last-success goes stale) — but only AFTER its staleness window closes, which on an overnight run can be the whole run; and it never fires for a PARTIAL grind, where some items still succeed and keep last-success fresh. What's missing is IN-FLIGHT visibility: progress emission — processed/total + a running FAULT count and a fault-rate alert — so a stalled-but-alive run is caught while the window is still burning, early enough to abort. Bounding the lane (abort on a high consecutive-fault fraction) is the complementary fix. A green heartbeat is not evidence of progress.
expectations: Distinguishes a process heartbeat (proves alive, not succeeding) from a last-success dead-man, and notes the dead-man catches a zero-success grind only AFTER its staleness window — and not at all for a partial grind that keeps last-success fresh
Requires in-flight progress emission — processed/total + a running fault count (+ fault-rate alert) — so a silent grind is visible while the window is still burning

evals.prompt: A batch lane processes 1400 items; each has a retry cap of 3 with backoff, so no single item retries forever. The upstream is down for hours; the lane dutifully retries all 1400 items × 3 = thousands of failing calls, consuming the whole run window. The per-item cap was respected. What's the design gap?
evals.expected_output: A per-item retry cap bounds EACH item's own retries, not the LANE as a whole — so 1400 individually-bounded-but-failing items still burn the entire run when the upstream is down. The gap is a lane-level budget: when a large fraction of CONSECUTIVE items fault (signaling the upstream itself is down, not one poison item), abort the remaining lane fast — a wall-clock cap and/or a consecutive-fault threshold — rather than exhausting every item's retries against a dead dependency. Distinct from the per-item circuit-break/retry-cap and from the dead-letter path for a single poison item.
expectations: Identifies that a per-item retry cap bounds each item, not the lane — many bounded-but-failing items still consume the whole run
Requires a lane-level budget: abort the remaining batch on a high consecutive-fault fraction (wall-clock and/or consecutive-fault threshold)
Distinguishes it from per-item retry-cap/circuit-break and from the single-poison-item dead-letter path

evals.prompt: A payout system requires an 'approve' step before a payout executes. The IDOR/authorization review passed: a user can only see and act on their own team's payouts. But one finance user can both create a payout AND click approve on it. Is the authz complete — and if the team asks whether they're legally required to have this control, what do you tell them?
evals.expected_output: No — that's a segregation-of-duties gap, orthogonal to the IDOR/cross-principal check that passed. IDOR ensures principal A can't touch principal B's object; SoD ensures the SAME principal can't both initiate and approve a consequential action. Here one user completes the whole payout chain alone, so a single compromised or malicious account moves money unchecked. Fix: enforce approver != requester server-side on a stable principal id (not a client flag or display name) for consequential actions (payout, credential issue, privilege grant, protected-surface merge); ensure a user can't self-grant the approver role to satisfy it. Whether the target is legally required to (SOX/PCI/NIST AC-5) routes to counsel, not this gate.
expectations: Identifies SoD as distinct from the IDOR/cross-principal access check — the same principal must not both initiate and approve a consequential action
Requires approver != requester enforced server-side on a stable principal id (not a client field/display name), scoped to consequential actions
Notes a user must not be able to self-grant the approver role; routes the compliance-mandate question to counsel/business-ops

evals.prompt: A workflow blocks self-approval by checking `request.body.approved_by != request.body.requester`. Separately, users with the 'admin' role can edit their own role assignments. The same team also proposes requiring a second approver before anyone can change their own profile avatar. Review the SoD design.
evals.expected_output: Two real defects plus one over-reach. (1) approved_by is read from a CLIENT field (request body) — trivially forgeable, so the check proves nothing; SoD must compare the authenticated approver's stable principal id (from the session/token, server-side) against the requester's, never a client-supplied name/flag. (2) An admin who can edit their own role assignments can self-grant the approver role, collapsing 'two distinct principals' back to one — the role grant must be outside the requester's control (a separate admin / an out-of-band process). (3) But requiring dual approval to change an avatar is scope over-reach: SoD guards genuinely consequential actions (moving money, issuing credentials, granting access), and gating a trivial write is friction that trains users to rubber-stamp, not control. Fix: derive both identities server-side from authenticated context, put the approver-role grant behind a distinct principal, and scope the control to consequential actions only.
expectations: Identifies the client-supplied approved_by field as forgeable — SoD must compare server-side authenticated principal ids, not a client field/name
Identifies that an admin editing their own role assignments can self-grant the approver role, collapsing two principals to one — the role grant must be outside the requester's control
Flags dual-approval on a trivial action (avatar change) as scope over-reach — SoD is scoped to consequential actions; gating trivial writes is friction, not control

evals.prompt: A data collector upgrades its flat source registry into a pivot engine: an identifier feeds a transform that emits new entities, which feed the next transform, several hops deep (the Maltego/SpiderFoot pattern). The team runs the identity/fanout gate once, on the final output. What's the design flaw?
evals.expected_output: Gating only the final output is wrong on two axes a single-source lane doesn't have. (1) Attribution risk multiplies per hop: a wrong entity at hop 2 poisons every entity derived at hops 3+, so a single end-of-chain gate attributes a whole poisoned subtree — each transform's OUTPUT entities must re-pass the identity/fanout gate (and false-merge check) BEFORE they're attributed and fed onward, not just once at the end. (2) Identity-disclosure risk multiplies per hop: each hop contacts a new host directly, so a pivot toward a gated host must route through a contracted broker under a declared collection-identity policy (anonymous/identified/brokered), never spoof, and the pivot must not become a rate-limit-evasion fan-out. Fix: per-hop guards — a fanout/identity gate on every transform's output, an identity-policy check on every transform's fetch. A pivot graph without per-hop gates is both a fanout amplifier and an identity-exposure amplifier.
expectations: Identifies that attribution risk compounds per hop — a wrong entity mid-chain poisons downstream hops, so each transform's output must re-pass the identity/fanout gate before attribution, not only at the chain end

Identifies that identity-disclosure risk compounds per hop — each hop is a new host contacted directly, requiring a per-hop identity-policy check (broker for gated hosts, never spoof) and no rate-limit-evasion fan-out
Requires per-hop guards on both the transform output (fanout) and the transform fetch (identity), not a single end-of-chain gate

evals.prompt: A talent-intelligence product ranks people by public activity (open-source commits, conference talks, papers). It already corrects demographic bias. An operator and an investor both come back with near-empty profiles and rank at the bottom as 'inactive.' Is the ranking sound?
evals.expected_output: No — this is observability bias, distinct from demographic bias (which the product already corrects) and from a temporal coverage gap. Whole CLASSES of person are structurally less observable on public signal: engineers/researchers/OSS contributors work in public and over-represent; operators and investors work privately and under-represent — regardless of time window. So an empty profile here means NOT PUBLICLY OBSERVABLE, not inactive, and ranking it at the bottom as 'low-activity' systematically penalizes exactly the people the public surface can't see. Fix: label each person's public-footprint class (high vs low observability) and carry it into the ranking — an empty/low profile in a low-observability class renders as 'not observed,' never 'inactive,' and the ranker must not treat unobserved as low-activity. Empty-beats-fabricated at the coverage layer.
expectations: Identifies observability bias as distinct from demographic bias and from a temporal coverage gap — whole entity CLASSES are structurally less publicly observable
States that an empty profile in a low-observability class means 'not observed,' not 'inactive'
Requires labeling a public-footprint class and not letting a ranking read unobserved as low-activity (penalizing the unseen)

evals.prompt: A reviewer opens a PR that adds a new TypeScript module. The diff shows `data.ts | Bin 0 -> 11857 bytes` instead of a text diff, and `grep` for a function defined in it prints only `Binary file data.ts matches`, never the line — though the code clearly runs and its tests pass. What happened and what's the finding?
evals.expected_output: The module embeds a raw NUL (0x00) — most likely a delimiter constant written literally instead of escaped — so git classifies the file as BINARY (git's heuristic keys on the NUL). That makes it undiffable (git diff / git show / git log -p print 'Binary files differ'; git diff --stat shows 'Bin'; git blame still runs but only garbled attribution is left) and effectively un-greppable (grep/ripgrep print only 'Binary file matches' by default; -a / --text forces the line), so the change can't be reviewed as text and the codebase can't be searched for the file's identifiers as written. It is runtime-safe — tests pass — which is exactly why a correctness-focused pass misses it; this is a reviewability/maintainability defect orthogonal to correctness. Finding: replace the literal NUL with the language's escape (\0) — ASCII, diffable, greppable, byte-identical at runtime — and add a commit/CI gate that flags any tracked source-path file git treats as binary (or containing a NUL), which is cheap and deterministic. (A non-NUL control byte like 0x1F stays text-classified but renders invisibly in the diff — the same escape fix applies.)
expectations: Identifies a raw NUL byte as the cause of git's binary classification (undiffable; greppable only with -a/--text) — not a general 'any control byte' claim
Frames it as a reviewability/maintainability defect orthogonal to correctness (tests pass; the diff is just unreadable), not a runtime bug
Requires replacing the literal control byte with an escape (byte-identical) AND a deterministic commit/CI gate for source files git treats as binary

evals.prompt: A service has a circuit breaker that serves a cached/stale response when the primary DB is unavailable, plus a counter that reports how often the fallback fired. The team says the fallback is 'covered' because the counter exists and a game-day last quarter exercised it once. Is it adequately tested?
evals.expected_output: No. A fired-counter proves the fallback RAN, not that its OUTPUT is correct; a one-time game-day proves the infra path worked once, not that it still works after subsequent code changes. The gap is a repo-owned regression test that FORCES the triggering condition (breaker open / DB unavailable) and ASSERTS the stale-serve branch returns the correct response — not merely that it doesn't crash. 'Test the failure, not just the feature' extends past security/guard paths to reliability fallback paths (circuit-open, retry-exhausted/dead-letter, cache-miss serve-stale, generation-failure): the code path you never run is the one that silently rots — an unrelated edit breaks the fallback with no red test, invisible until the real dependency fails in production. Fix: add a test that injects the trigger and asserts the fallback output; keep the counter as a runtime signal, and (if there's a game-day/chaos drill) date it and treat it as stale once the exercised path has materially changed.
expectations: Distinguishes a fired-counter (proves the fallback ran) and a one-time game-day (infra path ran once) from a repo-owned regression test that asserts the fallback branch's OUTPUT is correct
Requires a test that forces the triggering condition (breaker open / dependency down) and asserts the fallback output, not merely that it doesn't crash
Names the rot risk: an unexercised fallback is silently broken by an unrelated edit with no red test, invisible until the real failure occurs

evals.prompt: An endpoint kicks off a data export that takes minutes. To keep the client simple, it holds the HTTP connection open and returns 200 with the result when done; on timeout it returns 200 with an empty body. Review the API design.
evals.expected_output: Faking synchrony for a long-running operation is the defect. Blocking the request for minutes ties up connections and hits gateway/client timeouts, and returning 200-with-empty-body on timeout conflates 'not done' with 'done, no data' and with 'failed' — the caller can't tell which. Fix: return 202 Accepted plus an independently-versioned operation/job resource — a stable id, an explicit status enum with real terminal states (succeeded/failed/canceled, not a boolean), an error payload only on failed and a result only on succeeded, and a documented poll mechanism (a Location header, or a vendor Operation-Location-style header, plus Retry-After). The polling client must distinguish poll-transport failure (the GET 500s) from operation failure (GET 200, status: failed). And the start call needs a provider-side idempotency key so a retried start (lost 202) folds into the same operation instead of spawning a second one.
expectations: Identifies faking synchrony (blocking + 200-empty-on-timeout) as the defect — it conflates not-done / no-data / failed
Requires 202 + an operation/job resource with a stable id, a real terminal-state status enum (not a boolean), error-only-on-failed / result-only-on-succeeded, and a documented poll mechanism
Requires distinguishing poll-transport failure from operation failure, and provider-side idempotency on the start call so a retried start doesn't spawn a second operation

evals.prompt: A REST API returns errors as a 200 with {ok:false, msg:'...'} on some endpoints, a 400 with {error:'...'} on others, and a 500 with an HTML page on a third. Each message is human-written and gets reworded across releases. What's wrong and what's the fix?
evals.expected_output: Two problems. (1) No consistent, machine-readable error envelope: three different shapes (and a 200 carrying a failure) force every consumer to write a different parser per endpoint, and a 200-on-error defeats status-based handling. Fix: one registered envelope across the whole surface — RFC 9457 application/problem+json (type/status/title/detail/instance + extension members; it obsoletes RFC 7807) — with the HTTP status reflecting the outcome. (2) The error is identified only by a human-written, reworded message: a consumer can't branch on prose. Fix: carry a stable machine-readable code (a reason/domain identifier) that is FROZEN post-release and treated as part of the versioned contract — changing or repurposing a code is a breaking change, and the message stays freely rewordable but non-load-bearing.
expectations: Identifies the inconsistent per-endpoint error shapes (and the 200-carrying-a-failure) as forcing a different parser per endpoint — requires one machine-readable envelope across the surface (names RFC 9457 / problem+json)
Identifies that a human-written, reworded message is not a stable branch point — requires a stable machine code separate from the message
States the code is part of the versioned contract (frozen post-release; changing it is a breaking change)

evals.prompt: A resource is updated via PUT (send the whole object). The team adds a new mutable field notifications_enabled (default true) and considers it a backward-compatible, non-breaking addition since no field was removed. Are they right?
evals.expected_output: No — for a resource updated by full replacement (PUT, or PATCH with update_mask=*), adding a new mutable field IS a breaking change even though nothing was removed. An existing client round-trips: it reads the object (without the new field, or ignoring it), changes one field, and writes the whole object back — never sending notifications_enabled, so the server sees it absent and silently clears it (or resets it to a default), turning every old client's update into an unintended wipe of the new field (AIP-134). Fix: treat it as breaking (SemVer MAJOR or a versioned surface), or move updates behind partial-update (field-mask) semantics where an omitted field means 'leave unchanged' rather than 'clear', and document and test that forward-compat behavior.
expectations: Identifies that adding a mutable field to a full-replacement (PUT / update_mask=*) resource is breaking despite nothing being removed — an old round-tripping client silently clears the new field
Explains the read-modify-write round-trip mechanism (the old client never sends the new field, so the server clears it)
Requires either treating it as a breaking change or using partial-update / field-mask semantics where an omitted field means leave-unchanged

evals.prompt: A data team ships an 'anonymized' analytics export: user emails are replaced with SHA-256(email), and it includes each user's age band, home region, and signup week. Legal minimization was applied (no raw PII columns). Is it safe to publish?
evals.expected_output: No — minimization (dropping raw PII) is a different axis from LINKABILITY, and this export is still re-identifiable. (1) SHA-256(email) is a stable pseudonym anyone holding the email can recompute, and it's the same token across any other dataset that hashed emails the same way — a linkage key, not anonymization; salt it and keep the mapping server-side, or rotate per purpose. (2) age band + region + signup week is a quasi-identifier combination: each field is coarse alone but the combination can be unique to one person (singling-out). Fix: check the smallest-cohort size and report it (don't assert 'anonymous' without one), scope/rotate the pseudonym per purpose, and test the field combination for uniqueness — not just each column. The k-anonymity / DP threshold and any legal anonymity determination are the owner's / counsel's call, but the linkability check itself is required; absent it, this is a re-identification finding, the same tier as a raw-identifier leak.
expectations: Identifies linkability/re-identification as distinct from minimization — the export is re-identifiable despite no raw PII columns
Flags the recomputable/stable pseudonym (SHA-256 of email) as a linkage key across datasets — needs salting/server-side mapping or per-purpose scoping
Flags the quasi-identifier COMBINATION (age band + region + week) as singling-out, and requires reporting the smallest-cohort size rather than asserting 'anonymous'

evals.prompt: A login form returns 'No account with that email' when the email is unknown and 'Wrong password' when it exists; the password-reset page says 'Check your inbox' only when the email is registered, otherwise 'Email not found.' The auth review already passed (rate limiting, MFA, secure cookies). Any issue?
evals.expected_output: Yes — account enumeration, a detectability leak (CWE-203 Observable Discrepancy / LINDDUN Detectability) that the auth review missed because it's about the response DIFFERENCE, not the credential check. An unauthenticated outsider can enumerate valid accounts: the login distinguishes 'no account' from 'wrong password,' and the reset page distinguishes 'registered' from 'not found' — each reveals existence. Fix: return one GENERIC response for the exists/not-exists pair — login: a single 'invalid email or password'; reset: always 'if an account exists, we've sent an email' — and equalize response TIME (constant-time path) so timing doesn't leak existence either. This is not about removing validation; it's about not making existence observable in status, body, redirect, or timing.
expectations: Identifies account enumeration / detectability (CWE-203) as the issue — distinguishable responses for exists vs not-exists on login AND password-reset leak account existence to an unauthenticated outsider
Notes the auth review missed it because it's about the response difference, not the credential check itself
Requires one generic response for the exists/not-exists pair (login and reset) AND a constant-time path so timing doesn't leak existence

evals.prompt: A merge-train batches PRs behind a union proof (one green run of the full local suite). One tool in that suite, audit:ux, crashes on startup in CI (its own harness is broken). The train's union run can't complete, so the system falls back to merging one PR per full base-CI cycle. Green, mergeable PRs pile up. What's the design gap, and how does it differ from a gate that merely hangs?
evals.expected_output: A tool broken IN THIS ENVIRONMENT (harness crash, dependency down) is a can't-check, not a red — 'could not check' is not 'found a problem.' Letting it halt all batching collapses throughput to serial, which is the gap. Fix: fail-open for the batch proof — drop that one broken term and run the deterministic runnable subset — so batching continues; and treat a throughput-gating tool as P0 (its blast radius is the whole delivery rate, not one PR, so it jumps the queue ahead of a gate that only affects one change's correctness). This differs from a HUNG gate: a hang has genuinely-unknown validity (the gate may still be running), so it's timeboxed then escalated; a crash is definitively broken here and safe to route around now. Both keep the flaky/heavy gate out of the blocking union term, and both hold the same floor — fail-open means the tool's own crash isn't a red, not that a member whose essential validation only that gate provided merges on the reduced proof.
expectations: Identifies the broken-in-environment tool as a can't-check (could-not-check != found-a-problem) that must fail-open for the batch proof — run the runnable subset, keep batching — rather than collapse throughput to serial
Requires treating a throughput-gating tool as P0 (blast radius = whole delivery rate, jumps the queue), distinct from a gate that fails one PR

Distinguishes the crash case (definitively broken, route around now) from a hung gate (unknown validity, timebox + escalate), while holding the floor that fail-open does not license merging a member whose essential validation the gate provided

evals.prompt: An off-canvas mobile menu is hidden by translating it off-screen with CSS (transform: translateX(-100%)); its wrapper gets aria-hidden="true" when closed. The links inside still exist in the DOM. A keyboard user tabbing through the closed page lands on invisible links. What's wrong and how is it fixed?
evals.expected_output: The closed menu's focusable descendants are still in the tab order ('phantom focus'): CSS translate hides it visually but doesn't remove its links from keyboard navigation, so a keyboard user tabs into controls they can't see. Worse, aria-hidden="true" on a container with focusable children violates the 4th rule of ARIA (never put aria-hidden or role="presentation" on a focusable element) — the links are focusable but unannounced by a screen reader, so a keyboard+SR user hits 'nothing.' Fix: when closed, remove the descendants from the tab sequence — the inert attribute on the wrapper (removes focus AND hides from the a11y tree together), conditional unmount, or tabindex="-1" on each focusable child. This is the mirror of the open-dialog focus-trap: an open dialog keeps focus in, a closed region keeps focus out. Detector: tab through the closed page and confirm focus never enters the hidden menu.
expectations: Identifies that CSS-hiding leaves focusable descendants in the tab order (phantom focus) — a keyboard user tabs into invisible controls
Flags aria-hidden="true" on a container with focusable children as the 4th-rule-of-ARIA violation (focusable but unannounced)
Requires removing descendants from the tab sequence when hidden (inert / unmount / tabindex=-1), not just visual hiding

evals.prompt: For security, a banking app logs the user out after 5 minutes idle, dropping whatever they'd typed in a multi-step form. Security is happy. Is there an accessibility problem, and does fixing it undo the security control?
evals.expected_output: Yes — a silent idle-logout that discards unsaved input fails WCAG 2.2.1 Timing Adjustable (Level A): a user who needs more time (motor, cognitive, or just interrupted) loses work with no chance to react. The fix does NOT undo the security control: 2.2.1 doesn't forbid a short timeout, it requires a warn-and-extend affordance before it fires — warn before expiry and let the user extend with one simple action (at least 20 seconds to respond), or turn off / lengthen the limit. So the security-vs-a11y tension is real but resolvable: keep the short idle timeout, add a 'you'll be signed out in 60s — stay signed in?' prompt that extends the session (and ideally preserve the draft). Exceptions (real-time events, essential limits, >20h) don't apply to a routine session timeout.
expectations: Identifies the silent idle-logout with data loss as a WCAG 2.2.1 Timing Adjustable (Level A) failure — no warning, no chance to extend
States the fix is a warn-before-expiry + extend-with-one-action affordance (at least 20s), not removing the timeout — so the security control stands
Frames it as a resolvable security-vs-a11y tension rather than a forced trade-off

evals.prompt: A team's CI runs Lighthouse on every PR; the score is green (LCP/INP/CLS all in range), so the PR description says 'meets Core Web Vitals.' Is that claim justified?
evals.expected_output: Not as stated. Core Web Vitals thresholds (LCP <=2.5s, INP <=200ms, CLS <=0.1) are defined at the 75th percentile of FIELD data — real users (CrUX / RUM / PageSpeed Insights field section). A Lighthouse CI run is a LAB measurement: one synthetic environment, one network/CPU profile, no real-user distribution — it can't produce a field p75. So 'Lighthouse passed' proves a lab snapshot is in range, not that real users meet the thresholds (INP especially is field-oriented — Lighthouse can't measure it the same way). The claim should cite the field source and say which was measured. This is the same lab-vs-field caveat the review already applies to automated accessibility scanners: a passing tool is necessary, not sufficient. Fix: back a CWV claim with field data (CrUX/RUM), and treat the lab run as a fast regression signal, not the conformance proof.
expectations: Distinguishes CWV's field p75 (CrUX/RUM real-user data) from a Lighthouse lab/synthetic run — the lab run can't produce a field p75
Concludes 'Lighthouse passed' is not 'meets Core Web Vitals' — the claim needs a field-data source
Draws the lab-necessary-not-sufficient parallel (same as an automated a11y scanner) and requires stating which was measured

evals.prompt: A team's CI generates SLSA provenance and an SBOM for every released artifact, and the release notes say 'SLSA compliant.' The deploy pipeline pulls the artifact by tag and ships it. Is the supply chain actually protected?
evals.expected_output: Not as claimed. Generating provenance is not verifying it — the deploy step pulls by tag and never checks the attestation, so the provenance is a file nothing downstream reads (the runtime-proven-gate failure applied to the supply chain: a gate that exists but is never proven to fire). And 'SLSA compliant' with no level named is unverified strength: SLSA Build L1 is just 'provenance exists' (trivial to forge, may be unsigned); only L2 adds signed provenance from a hosted builder and requires downstream authenticity verification; L3 adds a hardened build. Fix: make the deploy/promotion step VERIFY the attestation as a blocking gate — the attestation's subject digest matches the artifact being promoted (else a validly-signed attestation for a different artifact passes), the signature is valid, the signer/builder identity is one you trust, and the recorded canonical source repository matches — and FAIL CLOSED on a missing or mismatched attestation. That's the same blocking-gate bar already applied to inbound package signatures; the outbound attestation of what you actually ship deserves it too. And name the target SLSA level rather than a bare 'compliant.'
expectations: Identifies that generating provenance is not verifying it — the deploy step never checks the attestation, so it's a gate that exists but never fires (runtime-proven-gate failure)

Requires the deploy/promotion step to verify the attestation as a blocking gate (the subject digest matches the artifact being promoted, signature valid, signer/builder trusted, canonical source repo matches) and fail closed on missing/mismatch
Notes 'SLSA compliant' with no level is unverified strength — L1 provenance-exists (forgeable) vs L2 signed/verified vs L3 hardened; name the target level

evals.prompt: A microservices platform stamps a shared request id on every log line, and the team says 'we have distributed tracing.' But when an incident needs to see where a slow request spent its time, the tracing backend shows the request as several disconnected traces, one per service. What's the gap?
evals.expected_output: A shared LOG correlation id is not the same guarantee as an unbroken distributed TRACE: every service can stamp the same id on its logs (so logs reassemble via search) while each still starts a fresh ROOT span, so the trace backend shows N disconnected fragments and you can't follow latency across hops. Verify tracing separately from log-correlation: follow one request's trace id through every hop IN THE TRACING BACKEND and confirm one trace, not N. The break is almost always at a hop without auto-instrumentation — a queue publish, a cron/background job, or an async/thread handoff — where trace context (W3C traceparent) must be injected into the envelope by hand instead of riding an instrumented HTTP client; a boundary that starts a fresh root span silently blinds the trace. It's a silent failure: the app works, only observability goes blind, until an incident needs the trace and it's fragmented.
expectations: Distinguishes a shared LOG correlation id from an unbroken distributed TRACE — the same log id can coexist with N disconnected root spans
Locates the break at a hop without auto-instrumentation (queue publish / cron / async handoff) that starts a fresh root span instead of propagating trace context (W3C traceparent)
Requires verifying the trace end-to-end in the tracing backend (one trace, not N) and injecting context into the envelope at manual hops

evals.prompt: One thread sets a plain boolean `stop = true` to signal a worker thread to exit its `while (!stop) { ... }` loop. In testing on the dev machine it works. Is this correct?
evals.expected_output: No — this is a memory-VISIBILITY bug, a different axis from an atomicity/check-then-act race. There's no synchronization edge (lock, atomic, volatile, channel, fence) ordering the writer's stop=true before the worker's read, so the write has no guaranteed visibility: the worker may never observe it (a compiler can hoist the non-changing stop into a register, or the write sits in a store buffer with no fence to order it) and loop forever. It needs no interleaving to fail, so a check-then-act race hunt misses it, and it can pass on x86 (stronger memory model) yet hang on ARM — a green dev-machine run proves little. Fix: name the edge — make the flag atomic (std::atomic<bool> / sync/atomic / a volatile field with proper publication in Java) or signal via a channel/condition variable. And a data race here is not benign: in C/C++/Rust-unsafe it's undefined behavior; in Go a racy multiword value can tear.
expectations: Identifies it as a memory-visibility / happens-before bug (no synchronization edge orders the write before the read) — distinct from an atomicity/check-then-act race, and needs no interleaving to fail

Explains the mechanism: the write may never become visible (the compiler hoists the read out of the loop, or the write isn't fenced/flushed), the loop can spin forever, and it's architecture-dependent (passes x86, hangs ARM) so a green test proves little
Requires naming a synchronization edge — atomic / volatile+publication / channel — not a plain shared field; notes a data race is UB (C/C++/Rust) or incorrect/torn (Go), not benign

evals.prompt: A required CI check `app-tests` uses a pass-through job that exits 0 so out-of-scope PRs (docs-only) aren't blocked. The real test job runs on `push`/`synchronize`; the pass-through is wired to fire on any event including `edited`. A reviewer edits a code PR's title, the `edited` event fires the pass-through, and the PR shows `app-tests: Success` — but the tests never ran on that code. Sound?
evals.expected_output: No — this is a false-green hole. A pass-through is legitimate ONLY when nothing was in scope (a path filter genuinely excluded the diff); here there IS code to check, but the EVENT (edited — a title/body mutation), not the paths, routed around the real test job while the pass-through still reported a conclusive Success. So the required check reads green over code its checker never re-ran. Distinguish nothing-to-check (pass-through honest) from checker-skipped-but-reported-green (a hole). Fix: make the pass-through reachable only on the paths/events where the real check is genuinely N/A — not an unconditional exit 0 that green-lights an event the real job ignores; the real test job's own conclusion (or a re-run on the current head) must back the required status for an in-scope PR.
expectations: Identifies the false-green hole: the pass-through reported Success on an edited event while the real checker (push/synchronize) never ran on that code
Distinguishes a legitimate pass-through (nothing in scope, path-filtered) from this hole (there IS something to check; the event, not the paths, skipped the real job)
Requires scoping the pass-through to only the paths/events where the real check is genuinely N/A — not an unconditional exit 0 covering events the real job ignores

evals.prompt: A repo commits its dist/bundle.js (tracked in git), and the CI build regenerates it. The merge preflight runs the build, then asserts `git diff --exit-code` is clean — and fails every time, because the build rewrote the tracked bundle. The team keeps re-committing the regenerated file to get green. What's the real problem and fix?
evals.expected_output: The clean-tree gate is asserting something the build itself makes false: a git-TRACKED file (dist/bundle.js) that the build regenerates means git diff --exit-code after the build is red on a dirty tree the build created, not on a real defect — so running the build to satisfy the gate breaks the next clean-tree check, and re-committing the artifact is churn that never converges. Fix at the source: don't track a build output — gitignore dist/bundle.js and generate it at build/deploy time; or if it must be tracked (consumed without a build step), regenerate it deterministically and commit it as its own explicit step, and scope the clean-tree check to exclude the generated path. Never 'run the build, then assert the tree is clean' in the same working tree — or run the clean-tree check in a fresh checkout the build never ran in. Distinct from the run-twice idempotency check, which catches an untracked generated artifact polluting a later step across runs; this is a git-tracked artifact whose committed baseline the build invalidates on every run.
expectations: Identifies that a git-tracked, build-regenerated file makes the clean-tree gate red on a build-created diff, not a real defect — running the build to pass one gate breaks the next
Requires fixing at the source: don't track a build output (gitignore + generate at build time), or regenerate deterministically as its own committed step
Requires scoping the clean-tree check to exclude the generated path — not 'run the build then assert clean' in the same working tree

evals.prompt: A service retries each failed downstream call up to 3 times with jittered backoff. During a partial outage of that downstream it gets much slower and stops recovering even after the root cause is fixed. The per-request retry cap is respected the whole time. What's missing?
evals.expected_output: A per-request cap bounds one call but not the AGGREGATE: when many requests fail at once, each spending its 3 retries, the combined retry traffic multiplies load on the already-struggling downstream and can hold it down (a retry storm) even after the original fault clears. What's missing is a process- or client-wide retry BUDGET — a ceiling on the retry rate (a fixed cap per process, e.g. a bounded number of retries per minute, or a bounded fraction of live request volume above a small floor) — beyond which the client fails fast instead of retrying. This is distinct from the circuit breaker (which trips on the destination's health) and from keeping retries to a single layer (which stops one request's own attempts from multiplying N×M); the budget caps this client's aggregate retry rate across all requests. Fix: add the aggregate budget and fail fast once it's exceeded.
expectations: Identifies that a per-request cap does not bound the aggregate retry rate — many simultaneous failures each retrying multiplies load (a retry storm) on the struggling dependency, which can persist after the root cause clears
Requires a process/client-wide retry budget (a ceiling on retry rate, or a bounded fraction of live volume) that fails fast once exceeded
Distinguishes the budget from the circuit breaker (destination health) and from keeping retries to one layer (a single request's attempts)

evals.prompt: Each service in a 4-hop request chain sets a fresh 5-second timeout on its downstream call. A user-facing request has a 5-second deadline. Under load, requests that should fail fast instead consume far more than 5 seconds of backend work. Why, and what's the fix?
evals.expected_output: Each hop resetting a fresh full timeout means the chain can run up to N×5s (here ~20s) of backend work even though the user-facing caller gave up at 5s — every hop past the 5s mark does work whose result no one is waiting for, amplifying load exactly when the system is struggling. The fix is deadline PROPAGATION: pass the caller's REMAINING time down to each downstream call (derive the downstream timeout from the inbound deadline minus already-elapsed time and a small buffer), and check the deadline still has room before starting a retry. This is distinct from merely having a timeout on each call (each does) — it makes each downstream timeout a function of the caller's remaining one, the wall-clock analogue of bounding an agent's recursion by depth/steps/spend. Some RPC stacks propagate deadlines automatically (converting the deadline to a remaining-time timeout, deducting elapsed time); a hand-rolled client must do it explicitly.
expectations: Explains that fresh per-hop timeouts let the chain run up to N× the caller's deadline, doing work after the caller already gave up (load amplification under stress)
Requires propagating the remaining deadline downstream (each timeout derived from the inbound deadline minus elapsed/buffer) rather than resetting a fresh full timeout per hop
Requires checking the deadline still has room before a retry, and distinguishes this from merely having a timeout on each call

evals.prompt: A team publishes Avro events to a shared Kafka topic. Their review says schema changes 'follow the convention: add optional fields with defaults.' A producer ships a new schema and several consumer teams break in production. What mechanical control is missing, and how is it configured?
evals.expected_output: A human convention ('add optional fields') is not a gate — it's forgotten, and nothing rejected the incompatible schema before it hit the topic. The missing control is a SCHEMA REGISTRY with a compatibility mode that rejects an incompatible schema at register/CI time (the message-boundary counterpart to oasdiff/buf breaking on the HTTP surface). The mode must match DEPLOY ORDER: BACKWARD (a new schema reads old data — add optional/remove fields) requires upgrading consumers before producers; FORWARD (old schema reads new data — add/remove-optional fields) requires producers before consumers; FULL (add/remove optional only) allows independent upgrade. Use the *_TRANSITIVE variant to check against all prior versions, not just the last (else a two-step evolution smuggles a break past a per-step check). NONE disables the check — a red flag on a shared topic. The finding: no registry/compat enforcement, or a mode that doesn't match how the system deploys.
expectations: Identifies that a human convention is not a mechanical gate — a schema registry compatibility check must reject an incompatible schema at register/CI time (message-boundary counterpart to oasdiff/buf breaking)
Ties the compatibility mode to deploy order: BACKWARD = consumers-before-producers, FORWARD = producers-before-consumers, FULL = independent
Notes TRANSITIVE checks all prior versions (not just the last) and flags NONE on a shared topic

evals.prompt: A data pipeline enriches and joins records, and a downstream dashboard shows a metric that's clearly wrong. The team can see where each raw record was sourced from (provenance) but spends days bisecting the pipeline to find which step corrupted the value. What property is the pipeline missing?
evals.expected_output: Record-origin provenance answers where a value entered the pipeline, but not which transform step produced a wrong derived value — so debugging a bad output is an unbounded search across every stage. The missing property is BACKWARD (column-level) LINEAGE: each output column mapped to the input columns and the transformation (a direct copy vs. an aggregation/join/filter) that produced it, so 'which root inputs construct column X?' and its inverse 'what breaks if column Y changes?' are answerable. This is the backward, transform-level counterpart to forward provenance (origin) and the forward consumer census (who reads a field). A pipeline that can enrich and join but can't answer 'why is this value wrong' is under-instrumented for correctness; the fix is to capture transform-level (ideally column-level) lineage.
expectations: Distinguishes record-origin provenance (where a value entered) from backward transform-level lineage (which step produced a wrong derived value)
Requires column-level lineage: output columns mapped to input columns + the transformation, so root-input and impact-analysis questions are answerable
Frames the absence as under-instrumentation for correctness (debugging becomes an unbounded search across stages), not merely a missing feature

evals.prompt: A service caches user profiles under `user:{id}` and also caches rendered comment HTML (with the author's name baked in) and a `top-users` leaderboard list. When a user renames themselves, the code deletes `user:{id}`. Users still see the old name on comments and the leaderboard for hours. What's the bug and the fix?
evals.expected_output: The write invalidated only the entity's OWN key (user:{id}) but not the DERIVED entries that embed the entity — the rendered comment HTML and the leaderboard list both baked in the old name and were never invalidated. Deleting one key is not enough when other cached entries contain a copy of the mutated data. This is the application's responsibility, not the cache's: HTTP caches, for example, MUST invalidate the target URI on an unsafe method but treat related URIs only as candidates (RFC 9111 §4.4). Fix: tag each cached entry with a surrogate key for every entity it depends on and invalidate by tag (purge everything tagged user:{id}), or maintain an explicit dependency index, so a rename fans out to every derived entry. A single-key delete test won't catch this — the review must ask which OTHER entries embed the mutated value.
expectations: Identifies that only the entity's own key was invalidated while derived/composite entries (rendered HTML, the leaderboard list) that embed the value went stale
States that derived-key fan-out is the application's responsibility (a cache/protocol invalidates the primary key/target, not everything that embeds it)
Requires surrogate-key/tag-based invalidation or an explicit dependency index so a write fans out to every derived entry

evals.prompt: A site serves localized pages: the same URL returns English or German based on the Accept-Language header. It sits behind a shared CDN cache keyed only on the URL. German users start seeing English pages (and vice versa) at random. Why, and what's the fix?
evals.expected_output: The representation varies by a request header (Accept-Language) but the shared cache keys only on the URL, so whichever language was cached first is served to everyone until it expires — a correctness bug specific to a SHARED cache (a per-user cache wouldn't cross-contaminate). HTTP's rule: a cache MUST NOT use a stored response without revalidation unless all the request header fields nominated by Vary match (RFC 9111 §4.1), and Vary: * never matches. Fix: include every representation-varying dimension in the cache key — set a correct Vary: Accept-Language (and Accept-Encoding if compressed variants differ), or add the negotiated dimension explicitly to the key. This is distinct from an auth/identity Vary bug (whose harm is a cross-user data leak); here the harm is serving the wrong variant.
expectations: Identifies that the response varies by a request header while the shared cache keys only on the URL, so one variant is served to all clients
Requires keying on the varying dimension — a correct Vary (Accept-Language/Accept-Encoding) or an explicit key dimension — and notes Vary: * never matches
Frames it as a shared-cache content-negotiation correctness bug (distinct from a per-user cache and from an auth/identity Vary leak)

evals.prompt: A Postgres migration adds CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY to avoid locking writes. It's run by a migration framework that wraps each migration in a transaction by default. The migration errors out, and later the team notices the index exists but queries don't use it while writes are slower. What went wrong on both counts?
evals.expected_output: Two distinct CONCURRENTLY footguns. (1) CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY cannot run inside a transaction block (a regular CREATE INDEX can); a migration runner that wraps each migration in a transaction by default makes the concurrent build fail outright unless the migration opts out of the wrapping transaction (the framework's escape hatch). (2) A failed concurrent build leaves behind an 'invalid' index that is ignored for querying but still consumes update overhead on every write — so queries don't use it while writes pay for it. Fix: run the CONCURRENTLY build outside any transaction block, and on failure drop the invalid index and retry (or REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY) rather than assuming the index is simply absent. (Postgres docs.)
expectations: Identifies that CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY cannot run inside a transaction block and gives the remedy — the migration must opt out of the runner's wrapping transaction (its escape hatch), else the concurrent build fails outright
Identifies that a failed concurrent build leaves an invalid index that is skipped for queries but still adds write overhead
Requires the fix: run outside a transaction, and drop+retry or REINDEX the invalid index rather than treating it as absent

evals.prompt: A repo's Definition of Done says 'green `verify` from a clean clone.' Its served-smoke gate asserts that fields like Skills, Availability, and Location render. The committed sample fixture doesn't include those fields (they exist only in the real, gitignored data bundle). Several contributors each hit the same 'missing required copy' failures on a fresh worktree and each fixes it by copying the real bundle in. What's the actual defect?
evals.expected_output: The gate is red on a clean clone BY CONSTRUCTION: it asserts real-data-shaped output the committed fixture can't produce, so the assertions have nothing to render on a fresh clone — green only from a populated checkout, red for everyone else, and the repo's 'green verify from a clean clone' DoD claim is false. The committed fixture is part of the gate's contract; the defect is the fixture/gate contract, not the contributors' environments — that they each 'fixed' it by copying real data in is the tell of a shared, standing defect, not N separate environment problems. Fix one of two ways: (1) enrich the fixture so it exercises every field the gate asserts, or (2) scope the real-data-only assertions to a real-bundle run and assert only fixture-satisfiable claims on the clean-clone run. Verify by running the gate from a truly clean clone (no gitignored data present) — red there means the fixture or the assertion scope is wrong; the DoD claim stays unverified until it passes.
expectations: Identifies that the gate is red on a clean clone by construction because the committed fixture can't satisfy the real-data-shaped assertions, so the 'green from a clean clone' DoD claim is false
Names the fixture/gate contract as the defect (not the contributors' environments), reading the repeated copy-in-real-data workaround as the signal of a shared standing defect
Requires the fix (enrich the fixture, or scope real-data-only assertions to a real-bundle run) and verification from a truly clean clone

evals.prompt: A dashboard must never show an uncollected month as a measured zero (the data has no per-month collection-coverage flag, so 'collected zero' and 'not collected' look identical). One implementation builds all 12 month cells and styles the empty ones 'faintly, remember to treat as unknown'; another builds a cell only for months with >=1 observed row. Which is the stronger guarantee against shipping the fabrication, and what's the general rule?
evals.expected_output: The second (build a cell only for an observed month) is stronger. The first relies on a render-time CONVENTION — 'remember to style empty cells as unknown' — that lives in reviewers' heads and scattered call sites; one forgotten style edit reintroduces the fabrication (uncollected rendered as a measured zero). The second makes the dishonest value UNREPRESENTABLE by construction: a 'collected-zero' cell has no constructor, so 'uncollected renders as zero' isn't a rule to remember, it's impossible, and a 'never emits a zero-count bin' unit test pins it. General rule: for any anti-fabrication/data-honesty invariant, prefer enforcing it by construction (make the illegal value unbuildable in the type/constructor) over a render-time or call-site convention — 'make impossible states unrepresentable' applied to data honesty. Reviewer check: for each honesty invariant, ask whether the dishonest value can even be constructed; if yes, the invariant rests on a convention a future edit can silently violate.
expectations: Picks the by-construction option (emit a cell only for an observed period) as stronger, and explains why the render-time convention is weak (lives in heads/call sites; a later edit silently ships the fabrication)

States the general rule: enforce a data-honesty invariant by construction (make the illegal value unrepresentable/unbuildable in the type or constructor), not as a render/call-site convention, plus a 'never emits X' test
Gives the reviewer check: ask whether the dishonest value can even be constructed; if yes the invariant rests on a violable convention

evals.prompt: A one-line CSS/DOM change is routed to the cheapest model because it 'looks atomic.' The model ships it, the unit tests pass, and it self-reports green — but the element renders in the wrong visual position. What went wrong in the tiering decision, and how should a cheap-tier miss be handled?
evals.expected_output: The tiering used diff SIZE (one line, 'atomic') as a proxy for correctness-SUBTLETY, but a small change can hide a structural/ordering trap — here a DOM-order vs visual-order mismatch — that a cheap model ships plausible-but-wrong and self-reports green on (passing unit tests that don't check rendered geometry). Tier by the subtlety of getting it right, not the line count. And a green self-report is not acceptance: verify against real acceptance — an independent check, rendered geometry for a layout claim, or the acceptance criterion itself — never the model's own 'tests pass.' When a cheap-tier attempt misses, re-derive the fix from the acceptance criterion (what the change must actually achieve), not from 'make the failing tests pass' — the failing tests may be the least of what's wrong; escalate to a stronger model for the subtle part rather than iterating the cheap one against a proxy.
expectations: Identifies that diff size was used as a proxy for correctness-subtlety, and a small change can hide a structural/ordering trap a cheap model ships wrong while self-reporting green

Requires tiering by the subtlety of getting it right (not line count) and verifying against real acceptance (independent check / rendered geometry / the criterion), not the model's own green self-report
Requires re-deriving a cheap-tier miss from the acceptance criterion, not from 'make the failing tests pass'

evals.prompt: A 'daily 9:00 am reminder' feature computes the next fire time once at creation, converts it to a UTC instant, stores that instant, and a scheduler fires on the stored UTC time. After the spring-forward DST transition, users report the reminder now arrives an hour off — at 10:00 am instead of 9:00. Why, and what's the correct storage model?
evals.expected_output: 9:00 am is a WALL-CLOCK time, not an instant — its UTC offset changes at a DST transition. Baking in a single UTC instant at creation freezes the pre-transition offset, so after the clocks change the fixed instant maps to a different local time (8am or 10am) — the classic 'store everything in UTC' mistake applied to a wall-clock-anchored recurrence. UTC storage is correct for a past/point instant (a log line, created_at), but a future or recurring wall-clock commitment must store the LOCAL wall-clock time + the tz-id and RE-RESOLVE the UTC offset per occurrence (near fire time), so each 9am fires at the correct local 9am regardless of DST. Match representation to feature: instant -> UTC; wall-clock recurrence -> local time + tz-id resolved per occurrence.
expectations: Identifies that 9am is a wall-clock time whose UTC offset changes at DST, so a single UTC instant frozen at creation drifts by the offset after the transition
Names the mistake as 'store everything in UTC' misapplied to a wall-clock-anchored recurrence (UTC is right for an instant, wrong here)
Requires storing local wall-clock time + tz-id and re-resolving the offset per occurrence (not once at creation)

evals.prompt: A scheduler lets users pick a local time of day and converts it to a UTC instant assuming each local time maps to exactly one instant. On the fall-back DST night a 1:30 am job runs twice; a job set for 2:30 am on the spring-forward night never runs. What's the underlying bug and the fix?
evals.expected_output: At a DST transition a local time is not one-to-one with an instant: on fall-back the clock repeats an hour, so a local time in the 'fold' is AMBIGUOUS (occurs twice); on spring-forward an hour is skipped, so a local time in the 'gap' is MISSING (occurs never). Code that assumes exactly one instant per local time double-runs fold-hour jobs and drops gap-hour jobs. The fix is an explicit, documented disambiguation rule for both cases — e.g. Python's PEP 495 fold flag to pick the first vs second occurrence for ambiguous times, and never producing/scheduling a time in the gap (map a missing time forward to the post-transition instant, or reject it). Decide and document which occurrence fires for ambiguous times and what happens to missing ones, rather than leaving it to the library default.
