expectations: Distinguishes the ambiguous (fold, repeated hour, occurs twice) and missing (gap, skipped hour, occurs never) cases at a DST transition
Explains that assuming a one-to-one local->instant mapping causes the double-run (fold) and no-run (gap)
Requires an explicit disambiguation rule for both (e.g. PEP 495 fold selection; never schedule/produce a time in the gap), not the library default

evals.prompt: An app lets users schedule a meeting for '13:00 next October 1, Dublin time' and immediately stores the computed UTC instant. Months later a government changes its DST rules before that date, and the meeting fires at the wrong local time. Root cause and fix?
evals.expected_output: Time-zone rules are DATA (the IANA tz database / the platform's ICU), not code, and change with little government notice. Converting a FUTURE wall-clock commitment to a UTC instant at creation freezes the conversion under the OLD rules; when the rules change before the date, the frozen instant no longer maps to 13:00 local — exactly IANA's warning that software 'can mess up after the rule change if it blithely relies on conversions made before the change.' Fix: store the wall-clock time + tz-id and re-resolve the instant LATE (at/near occurrence), and treat tzdata/ICU as a pinned dependency with a real update path (a refreshed base image / bundled ICU / vendored tzdata) so future conversions pick up rule changes. A frozen future instant plus a never-updated tzdata is the finding.
expectations: Identifies that tz rules are data that change on government notice, and a future wall-clock->UTC conversion frozen at creation goes wrong after a rule change
Requires storing wall-clock + tz-id and re-resolving the instant late (near occurrence), not freezing it at creation
Requires treating tzdata/ICU as a pinned dependency with an update path so future conversions reflect rule changes

evals.prompt: A team runs two A/B experiments at once, both changing the checkout button area, each with correct deterministic bucketing and its own SRM guard. The readouts disagree with a later holdback. What experiment-infrastructure flaw is likely, and how is it prevented in the assignment code?
evals.expected_output: Two experiments mutating the SAME surface concurrently with no isolation CONFOUND each other: a unit can land in both, so each experiment's treatment effect is contaminated by the other's variant, and per-experiment bucketing + SRM (which only check one experiment's own assignment split) won't catch cross-experiment interference. The fix is in the assignment infrastructure: put concurrent experiments in ORTHOGONAL LAYERS (orthogonal diversion, so an event can join multiple experiments that don't interfere — as in Google's overlapping-experiment infrastructure), or MUTUALLY EXCLUDE experiments that touch the same surface (a unit in experiment A can't also be in B). An ad-hoc second experiment bolted onto the same surface with neither layering nor mutual exclusion is the finding. This is the code/infra side; over-time effects like novelty/primacy and multiple-comparison correction across many metrics are read-side analysis (growth-analytics).
expectations: Identifies that two concurrent experiments on the same surface with no isolation confound each other (a unit in both; per-experiment bucketing/SRM don't catch cross-experiment interference)

Requires isolating the two — for experiments that mutate the same surface, mutual exclusion (or a layer design that guarantees they do not co-mutate the same element); orthogonal layers alone do not isolate two experiments changing the same element
Keeps it on the code/infra side (distinct from read-side analysis like novelty/primacy or multiple-comparison correction)

evals.prompt: A pipeline sets an `acknowledged_drop` field with a reason whenever it drops rows, and a separate `data_ready` flag when a dataset finishes loading. In review you find the drop still ships to consumers and a half-loaded dataset is still served — yet both fields are written correctly at their write sites. What's the defect, and what's the review test?
evals.expected_output: Both fields are WRITE-ONLY: emitted but nothing READS them, so they change no behavior — the acknowledged drop still ships silently (no gate consumes acknowledged_drop) and the not-ready dataset is still served (no consumer checks data_ready before reading). An acknowledgment or readiness flag that nothing reads is not a control; it must be ACTIVE, not merely emitted. Fix: give each a reader — the acknowledgment gates the merge/publish (or a review surfaces it); the readiness flag is checked before the consumer reads. The review test is a GREP FOR A READER: a flag written at one site and read at none is the finding (the same defect as a written artifact with no reader).
expectations: Identifies both flags as write-only — emitted but never read, so they change no behavior (the drop still ships, the not-ready data is still served)
States the principle: an acknowledgment/readiness flag must be actively consumed (gates a merge/publish; checked before the consumer reads), not merely emitted
Gives the review test — grep for a reader; a flag written but read nowhere is the finding

evals.prompt: Entity resolution for a dataset needs to disambiguate records, but running an internal ML matcher is off the table (a no-ML constraint on this pipeline). The team is about to fall back to a name-only match. Is there a cleaner option, and how should it be treated?
evals.expected_output: Yes — a name-only match is exactly the merge-worse-than-separate failure to avoid. The clean escape from a forbidden internal model is to consume an EXTERNAL, pre-computed identity cluster or id — plus its public artifact (an authoritative registry id, a published disambiguation) — as the resolver, rather than fake it with a name match or ship the forbidden model anyway. Treat the external cluster as a CORROBORATING source, not ground truth: record its provenance, and don't promote a lone external cluster to certainty. That keeps 'skip rather than guess' intact when the in-house resolver is off the table — you resolve on a real external authority or surface the ambiguous count, never on a name-only guess.
expectations: Rejects the name-only fallback and identifies consuming an external pre-computed identity cluster/id (+ its public artifact) as the clean escape from the forbidden internal model
Requires treating the external cluster as a corroborating source with recorded provenance (not ground truth), not promoting a lone external cluster to certainty
Keeps 'skip rather than guess' — resolve on a real external authority or surface the ambiguous count, never a name-only guess

evals.prompt: An incremental sync pages through rows with `WHERE updated_at > :cursor ORDER BY updated_at LIMIT 1000`, setting the next cursor to the last row's `updated_at`. Many rows share the same `updated_at` (a batch write stamped them identically). Rows go missing from the sync. Why, and what's the fix?
evals.expected_output: The cursor is a non-unique timestamp used as a strict boundary: when a page ends in the middle of a run of rows that share the same updated_at, setting the cursor to that timestamp and using > :cursor on the next page SKIPS every remaining row with that exact timestamp (a naive >= :cursor would double-read instead). A batch write that stamps many rows with one timestamp guarantees such ties. Fix: page on a UNIQUE, MONOTONIC tiebreak — a composite (updated_at, id) cursor (WHERE (updated_at, id) > (:ts, :id)), or an explicit monotonic sequence/change-id — so the boundary is exact and total-ordered, never a shared timestamp alone. Same non-unique-timestamp root as treating a shared timestamp as a batch id.
expectations: Identifies that a shared/non-unique timestamp used as a strict cursor boundary drops rows (with >) or double-reads them (with >=) when a page cuts mid-timestamp
Ties it to a batch write stamping many rows with one timestamp (ties guaranteed, not rare)
Requires a unique, monotonic tiebreak — a composite (ts, id) cursor or an explicit sequence — not a shared timestamp alone

evals.prompt: A repo has ONE scoring/classifier function, called from two places (an API handler and a batch job). There's no duplicated implementation to drift, so no parity test was added. In production the two call sites produce different results for the same underlying entity. Where's the bug, and what should the review require?
evals.expected_output: The classifier is shared and identical, so the divergence isn't in the core — it's in the ADAPTERS: each call site builds the classifier's inputs differently (different field names, defaults, units, filtering, or normalization), so they feed the same function different shapes and get different outputs. A parity test scoped to 'duplicated implementations' misses this because there's only one implementation. The review should require: (1) a test that the two call sites AGREE on a shared fixture (run the same underlying entity through both input-construction paths and assert equal classifier inputs/outputs), and (2) deriving both call sites' inputs from ONE spec/mapping, so an input-shape change can't diverge silently. The finding is the missing adapter-agreement guard, not a duplicated module.
expectations: Locates the divergence in the callers' input-construction (adapters), not the shared classifier — one implementation, differently-built inputs
Notes that a duplicated-implementation parity check misses this (there is no duplicate)
Requires an adapter-agreement test on a shared fixture and deriving both call sites' inputs from one spec

evals.prompt: A component is written as `render(now: Date = new Date())` so tests can inject a fixed clock. It's a `'use client'` component that is server-rendered for its first paint. Users in other time zones see dates rendered a day off on that first server paint, corrected only after client hydration re-renders. Why, and what's the fix?
evals.expected_output: On the server-rendered path the call site omits the now argument, so the default new Date() is evaluated ON THE SERVER — it reflects the server's clock and, for any toLocale*/format that reads the ambient zone, the server's TIME ZONE, not the request's or the user's. A user in another zone gets the server's notion of 'now'/'today', so a date near a day boundary renders a day off; after hydration the client re-renders with the browser's zone, which is why it only shows in SSR. The default-argument seam is a test convenience, not a request clock. Fix: pass the request's time and the user's/target time zone explicitly on any rendered path (thread them from the request), and reserve = new Date() for tests; never let a server-evaluated default supply the clock/zone for user-facing output.
expectations: Identifies that the omitted default arg makes new Date() evaluate on the server, so the first server paint uses the server's clock/timezone not the request's/user's — and why it is corrected only once the client re-renders (in the browser's zone)
Distinguishes the testability-injection default (a test convenience) from a request clock
Requires passing the request time + user/target time zone explicitly on rendered paths, not relying on a server-evaluated default

evals.prompt: A service sends webhooks to customer-registered URLs. Payloads are sent unsigned, the dispatcher POSTs to whatever URL the customer saved, failed deliveries are retried forever, and there's no delivery id. A security review and a reliability review both flag it. What are the provider-side fixes?
evals.expected_output: Four provider-side gaps. (1) SIGN every outbound payload — HMAC over a canonical id.timestamp.body string (e.g. Standard Webhooks' HMAC-SHA256 over msg_id.timestamp.payload with webhook-id/webhook-timestamp/webhook-signature headers) so consumers can verify authenticity, and support rotation with multiple concurrent valid signatures (space-delimited) rather than a flag-day cutover — not a single static secret. (2) The customer-registered callback URL is attacker-controlled input into YOUR SSRF surface — validate it like any user-supplied URL (allowlist, resolve-validate-pin the IP, block loopback/RFC-1918/CGNAT/link-local/cloud-metadata) and re-validate at CONNECT time (not just registration) to catch DNS rebinding. (3) Bound retries (backoff + cap) and move exhausted deliveries to a VISIBLE dead-letter the consumer/operator can replay — retry-forever burns resources and a silent stop loses events invisibly. (4) Emit a stable DELIVERY ID + monotonic sequence/timestamp so the consumer's idempotency/replay-window checks (the inbound side) can work, and state or explicitly disclaim an ordering guarantee.
expectations: Requires signing outbound payloads (HMAC over a canonical id.timestamp.body string) with a zero-downtime rotation path (multiple concurrent valid signatures), not a static secret
Identifies the customer-registered callback URL as an SSRF surface — validate + resolve-pin + block internal ranges, re-validated at connect time (DNS rebinding), not only at registration
Requires bounded retry into a visible dead-letter (not retry-forever or silent drop) and a stable delivery id + sequence so the consumer's dedup/idempotency works

evals.prompt: A data-fetch hook wraps requests in an AbortController and does `catch (e) { if (e.name === 'AbortError') return; }`. It aborts on both a 10s timeout and when the user navigates away. Users occasionally see stale/empty data with no error. What's the bug and the fix?
evals.expected_output: AbortError is raised for BOTH causes — the 10s timeout AND the user-navigation cancel — and the blanket `if (AbortError) return` swallows them identically, so a real TIMEOUT is silently discarded as if the user had walked away (stale/empty UI, no error surfaced, no retry). A timeout and a user-cancel need opposite handling: a user-cancel is expected (drop silently, no error, no retry); a timeout is a failure (surface/log it, and it's the retry-eligible case). Fix: distinguish the cause before suppressing — set/read AbortSignal.reason (e.g. abort(new DOMException('timeout')) vs the user-cancel path), or use a separate controller per cause, and branch: silent for user-cancel, surfaced/retried for timeout. A bare name==='AbortError' return with no reason check is the finding.
expectations: Identifies that AbortError covers both timeout and user-cancel, and the blanket suppression hides a real timeout (swallowed as a cancel)
States the opposite handling: user-cancel silent (no error/retry) vs timeout surfaced + retry-eligible
Requires distinguishing the cause (AbortSignal.reason or a per-cause controller) before suppressing, not a bare AbortError check

evals.prompt: A test gate runs green in CI with `vitest --pool=threads --maxWorkers=16`. A contributor on a laptop runs the exact same command and it OOM-crashes before finishing. The commands are identical. What's the parity gap, and how should the concurrency be set?
evals.expected_output: Local/CI parity is not just the same COMMANDS — it's the same behavior across the RESOURCE ENVELOPE. The gate's parallelism (maxWorkers=16) is tuned for CI's cores/RAM; on a lower-headroom laptop that same worker count exhausts memory and OOM-crashes, so the gate is green in CI but unrunnable locally and the contributor can't reproduce or debug it. Fix: size concurrency to the HOST rather than hardcoding a CI-shaped constant — detect available cores/free memory and derive the worker count (or cap it), or expose it as a documented, overridable knob (env var / flag) with a sane default that fits a modest dev machine. 'Runs in CI' must also mean 'runs on the machine a human debugs it on.'
expectations: Identifies that identical commands still diverge because the hardcoded worker count is tuned to CI's resource envelope and OOMs a lower-headroom host
Frames it as local/CI parity extending to the resource envelope, not just the command — green-in-CI-but-unrunnable-locally blocks reproduction
Requires host-sized concurrency (detect/cap cores+memory) or a documented overridable knob, not a hardcoded CI-shaped constant

evals.prompt: A list view's filter dropdown is populated from a status enum with 8 values. In production, 3 of those statuses never occur in real data, so selecting them always returns an empty list. The filter handler works correctly. Is this a defect, and how should the options be generated?
evals.expected_output: Yes — it's a dead control, just a DATA one rather than a structural (no-op handler) one: the handler works, but selecting a value that no real row can satisfy does nothing useful (an always-empty result), so the user wastes a click and distrusts the filter. The menu was hardcoded from the enum, which outruns the actual data. Fix: validate the option set against the ACTUAL DATA DISTRIBUTION — render only options with a non-zero count (ideally showing the count per option), or otherwise mark/disable the empty ones, rather than emitting every enum value. Generate filter options from what's present in the data, not from the type definition, so a user never selects a filter that silently returns nothing.
expectations: Identifies it as a (data) dead control — a working handler on an option no real row satisfies always returns empty, so it does nothing useful
Locates the cause in generating options from the enum/type rather than the actual data
Requires deriving options from the real data distribution (only non-zero counts, or show/disable counts), not emitting every enum value

evals.prompt: A GraphQL API's `posts` query returns 50 posts, and each post's `author` field has a resolver that fetches the user by id. Under load the DB shows ~51 queries for one `posts` request. Static review found no query inside a loop. Why does the existing N+1 grep miss this, and what's the fix?
evals.expected_output: It's a GraphQL resolver N+1 — the STRUCTURAL variant, not the textual one the grep looks for. The author field resolver is invoked once per parent post by the GraphQL executor, so 50 posts trigger 50 nested user fetches (+1 for the list) with NO loop at any single call site — the fan-out is in the executor, not in visible for/map code, so a 'query inside a loop' grep can't see it. Detect it by counting queries per request (the ~51 signal), not by reading for a loop. Fix: batch the per-parent fetches behind a per-request seam — the DataLoader pattern (collect the ids requested during a tick, issue one IN (...) batch, cache within the request) — so the 50 author fetches collapse to one. The same queries-per-request test then pins it.
expectations: Identifies it as a GraphQL resolver N+1 — the executor invokes the field resolver once per parent node, so there's no loop at any call site for a textual grep to catch
Requires detecting it by queries-per-request count, not by reading for a loop
Requires a per-request batch/cache seam (the DataLoader pattern) — collect ids, one batched query, cache within the request

evals.prompt: A Go HTTP handler does `user := lookup(id); return user.Name` where `lookup` returns `(*User)` and `nil` when the id is absent. A request with an unknown id panics, aborting the request — and the same dereference in a handler-spawned goroutine would crash the whole process. A reviewer waved it through as 'just a wrong-answer edge case.' Is that the right severity, and what's the general rule?
evals.expected_output: Wrong severity — it's a NULL/nil dereference on an attacker-reachable path (CWE-476), which is a CRASH / DoS, not a wrong-answer bug: an unknown id (attacker-controllable) nil-panics the handler and can take down the process. The general rule: a value from an external call, an optional/nullable lookup, or an unchecked cast that can be null/nil/None/undefined must be guarded BEFORE it's dereferenced, called, or indexed on any attacker- or upstream-reachable path. Here: check if user == nil { return 404 } before user.Name. Same class across languages — a Go nil panic, a Java/Kotlin NPE (a !! on a nullable), a Python AttributeError on None, a JS deref of undefined (a ! assertion hiding it), a C/C++ deref of a failed lookup. Cross-ref reliability for the fail-closed + resource-release angle on the crash path.
expectations: Corrects the severity — a nil/null deref on an attacker-reachable path is a crash/DoS (CWE-476), not a wrong-answer edge case
Requires guarding the nullable value before the deref/call/index on any reachable path (e.g. a nil check before user.Name)
Generalizes across languages (Go nil panic, Java NPE, Python None, JS undefined, C/C++), not a single-language nit

evals.prompt: A dashboard streams live events over SSE. When a client's connection drops and reconnects, users report either missing events (a gap) or a burst of already-seen ones. The server ignores the reconnect request's headers and just starts sending from 'now'. What's the fix, and how does it differ for WebSocket?
evals.expected_output: A dropped connection is normal (NAT/proxy timeout, deploy, blip), so a reconnect must RESUME from the last delivered position, not restart from 'now' (gap) or replay everything (dupes). For SSE there's a built-in primitive: the client re-sends the last id in the Last-Event-ID header, and the SERVER must read it and replay events after that id — the bug here is the server ignoring it. WebSocket has NO built-in resume, so the application must carry its own cursor/sequence number and catch up from it on reconnect (re-subscribe alone is not resume). Either way, give the reconnect a bounded backoff so a flapping server isn't hammered, and make the consumer idempotent on a per-message id since a resumed stream can overlap what was already processed.
expectations: Identifies that a reconnect must resume from the last delivered position, not restart-from-now (gap) or replay-all (dupes)
SSE: the server must read and honor the client's Last-Event-ID to replay the gap (the bug is ignoring it); WebSocket has no built-in resume so the app carries its own cursor/sequence
Adds bounded reconnect backoff and per-message idempotency (a resumed stream can overlap already-processed messages)

evals.prompt: A WebSocket server fans out a high-frequency feed to many clients. Memory climbs until the process OOMs, and connection count never drops even though users close their laptops. Two separate problems — what are they and the fixes?
evals.expected_output: Two live-connection failure modes neither a queue nor an outbound-call rule covers. (1) Slow-consumer backpressure: a client that reads slower than the feed produces makes the server queue unbounded outbound data for that connection, so memory climbs to an OOM. Cap each connection's send buffer and pick a policy — drop-oldest, coalesce, or disconnect the laggard — never queue unboundedly; on a browser sender, watch bufferedAmount and pace to it. (2) Dead-connection reclaim: a client that vanished (laptop closed, NAT drop) never sends a close, so its slot + subscriptions leak forever unless you detect it — send pings on an interval, track outstanding pongs, and close/reclaim on a missed pong (the protocol requires a Pong in response to a Ping but is silent on a missing one, so reclaiming is the app's job). Pinging without acting on a missed pong doesn't reclaim anything.
expectations: Identifies unbounded per-connection send buffering for a slow consumer as the OOM cause; fix = cap the buffer + drop/coalesce/disconnect policy (and watch bufferedAmount on the sender)
Identifies vanished clients holding connection slots/subscriptions; fix = ping interval + track pongs + reclaim on a missed pong
Notes pinging alone (without acting on a missed pong) doesn't reclaim — both are per-live-connection concerns, not queue/outbound-call rules

evals.prompt: An implementation is being aligned to a Figma reference. On the login screen the primary button is one shade of blue; on the signup screen the same primary button is a different shade. The spacing token documented for the card grid is 16px, but every card in the file is actually laid out 12px apart. The builder is copying each screen exactly as drawn. What's the risk and the right process?
evals.expected_output: The reference contradicts itself — the same primary button is two shades across screens, and the documented 16px card-grid token disagrees with the actual 12px layout. Copying each screen verbatim ports the CONTRADICTION into the product (the button now renders two shades in the implementation), which is an IMPLEMENTATION bug (harder to spot and fix) rather than a design one, and 'match the reference' can't adjudicate because the reference disagrees with itself. The reference is the styling source of truth EXCEPT where it contradicts itself. Right process: surface the specific conflict and reconcile to ONE canonical interpretation first — pick the reading the rest of the design implies, or raise it as an owner decision (an A/B of the two) — and record that chosen interpretation as its own reviewable artifact (a decision note or a separate reconciliation commit), kept separate from the build, so it is explicit and reviewable rather than silently resolved by whichever screen was copied last. Don't copy the inconsistency.
expectations: Identifies that the reference contradicts itself (same primary button in two shades; the documented card-grid token disagrees with the actual spacing) and that copying it verbatim ports the contradiction into the product as an implementation bug — 'match the reference' cannot adjudicate a reference that disagrees with itself
Requires reconciling to one canonical interpretation first — pick the reading the rest of the design implies, or raise it as an owner decision (an A/B of the two)

Requires recording the chosen interpretation as its own reviewable artifact (a decision note or a separate reconciliation commit), separate from the build — not silently resolving it by whichever screen was copied last

evals.prompt:
Review this code for concurrency defects:

```python
def transfer_a_to_b(db, amount):
    with db.transaction():
        db.execute("UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - %s WHERE id = 'acct_1'", [amount])
        db.execute("UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + %s WHERE id = 'acct_2'", [amount])

def transfer_b_to_a(db, amount):
    with db.transaction():
        db.execute("UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - %s WHERE id = 'acct_2'", [amount])
        db.execute("UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + %s WHERE id = 'acct_1'", [amount])
```
Both functions run concurrently under real user traffic. What is the concurrency risk, and what is the fix?
evals.expected_output: A lock-ordering deadlock: transfer_a_to_b locks acct_1 then acct_2; transfer_b_to_a locks acct_2 then acct_1 — the reverse order. Under concurrent execution one transaction can hold the first row lock while waiting on the second while the other holds the second waiting on the first; the DB detects the cycle and aborts one side (a deadlock-detected abort: SQLSTATE 40P01 in PostgreSQL, 40001 in MySQL/InnoDB), but that abort-and-retry is RECOVERY, not prevention. The real fix is a fixed, consistent acquisition order in both functions — e.g. always update the lower account id first — so the cycle can never form; retrying the aborted transaction is only the fallback when a consistent order can't be guaranteed up front.
expectations: Names the two functions' opposite row-lock acquisition order (acct_1-then-acct_2 vs acct_2-then-acct_1) as the deadlock cause
States the deadlock only fires under concurrent execution and would not appear in a single call or single-threaded test

Prescribes a fixed, consistent acquisition order (e.g. always lock the lower id first) as the fix — an answer that only catches the deadlock error and retries, with no ordering fix, does not satisfy this

evals.expected_output: An in-process ordering deadlock: reserveThenCharge acquires inventoryLock then billingLock; refundThenRelease acquires billingLock then inventoryLock — a circular wait if both run at once (A holds inventoryLock waiting on billingLock, B holds billingLock waiting on inventoryLock). It will not reproduce in a single-path test; it only fires under real contention between the queue consumer and the webhook handler. Fix: acquire both locks in one fixed global order at every call site (e.g. always inventoryLock before billingLock), or use a primitive that locks a set of mutexes without regard to call order (deadlock-avoiding multi-lock). This is not a missing-lock or missing-timeout bug.
expectations: Identifies that the two functions acquire the same two locks (inventoryLock, billingLock) in opposite order
Names this a circular-wait/deadlock that only manifests under concurrent execution (queue consumer racing the webhook handler), not in a single-path unit test
Prescribes a fixed global lock-acquisition order across both call sites (or a deadlock-avoiding multi-lock primitive) as the fix, not treating it as a plain missing-lock or missing-timeout bug

evals.prompt: An API verifies JWTs with `verify(token, key)` where the library reads the algorithm from the token's own `alg` header, and the service is configured to accept both RS256 (an RSA key pair) and HS256. The RSA public key is published at a well-known JWKS URL. A reviewer says 'signatures are verified, so forgery is impossible.' Is that right?
evals.expected_output: No — this is JWT algorithm confusion. Because the verifier picks the algorithm from the token's own `alg` header and accepts both an asymmetric (RS256) and a symmetric (HS256) algorithm, an attacker can set `alg: HS256` and sign the token using the RSA PUBLIC key (published, not secret) as the HMAC secret; a naive verify() that trusts `alg` then uses that same public key as the HMAC key and accepts the forged token. 'Signatures are verified' is insufficient when the verifier lets the attacker choose the algorithm — a public key is not a secret and cannot safely serve as a MAC key. Fix: pin an algorithm allow-list per verification context and never derive the algorithm from the token — accept only the specific algorithm this context expects (e.g. RS256 only), never 'None', and do not mix public-key signature algorithms with MAC algorithms on the same key material. (`alg: none` is the degenerate form of the same bug.)
expectations: Identifies JWT algorithm confusion: the attacker sets alg to HS256 and signs with the RSA PUBLIC key as the HMAC secret because the verifier trusts the token's own alg header and accepts both asymmetric and symmetric algorithms
Explains that 'the signature verifies' is insufficient when the attacker chooses the algorithm — a public key is not a secret, so it cannot safely serve as a MAC key

Prescribes pinning an algorithm allow-list per verification context (accept only the expected algorithm; never read alg from the token; do not mix signature and MAC algorithms), not merely 'check the signature'

evals.prompt: A service issues stateless JWTs with no server-side session store. Logout just deletes the cookie client-side. Tokens carry a 30-day `exp` and there's no other lifetime control. Is this session management sound? What's missing?
evals.expected_output: No — two problems. (1) Logout doesn't terminate anything server-side: a stateless JWT stays valid until its `exp`, so a token captured before logout still works — deleting the client cookie is not revocation. A self-contained token needs a real termination mechanism: a deny-list of terminated tokens, a per-user not-before timestamp that logout advances, or per-user signing-key rotation. (2) A single 30-day `exp` is neither an inactivity timeout nor a sensible absolute cap: there is no idle timeout (an unattended session stays usable), and 30 days is far past a normal absolute lifetime. Require BOTH a server-enforced inactivity (idle) timeout AND an absolute maximum session lifetime, per documented risk (e.g. idle minutes, absolute hours), enforced server-side — not a client-trusted cookie Max-Age.
expectations: Identifies that client-side cookie deletion does NOT revoke a stateless JWT (valid until exp); requires a real server-side termination mechanism (deny-list, per-user not-before, or signing-key rotation)
Identifies that one long exp is not an idle timeout — requires a separate server-enforced inactivity timeout distinct from the absolute lifetime
Requires an absolute maximum session lifetime cap enforced server-side and risk-driven, not a client-trusted cookie Max-Age

evals.prompt: A repo vendors a third-party SDK as a committed `libvendor.so` plus a few `.jar`s under `third_party/`, with no source and no build recipe. The same repo also has a `config.py` that `git` reports as `Binary files … differ` because of a stray literal NUL byte. A reviewer lumps both together as 'binary, out of scope, skip.' Right call?
evals.expected_output: No. A committed compiled/binary artifact (`.so`/`.jar`/`.dll`/`.wasm`/`.pyc`, a prebuilt bundle, a vendored SDK) is code nobody can source-diff — a malicious swap is indistinguishable from a legitimate rebuild in `git log`, so it's a supply-chain surface (OpenSSF Scorecard rates a checked-in binary high-risk, 'non-reviewable code'), not out-of-scope. It is distinct from a text file git merely misclassifies as binary (a diffability defect) — this blob is genuinely opaque/compiled. Right process: build it from source in CI, or fetch it at build/run time from a registry/release-asset store; if it genuinely must be vendored (a licensed SDK, a firmware blob), pin it by content hash with recorded provenance beside it so a swap is detectable. Flag any tracked `.so`/`.jar`/`.dll` with no source or build recipe.
expectations: Rejects skipping it — identifies a committed compiled/binary blob as unreviewable code and a supply-chain risk (a malicious swap is indistinguishable from a legitimate rebuild), not out-of-scope
Distinguishes it from a text file merely misclassified as binary via a stray NUL (a diffability defect) — this artifact is genuinely opaque/compiled
Prescribes build-from-source in CI or fetch-at-build/run-time, or (if vendoring is unavoidable) pin by content hash with recorded provenance

evals.prompt: A reviewer must confirm a 'status chip' concept is now unified. They find a shared `StatusChip` whose JSDoc says 'replaces the inline chip that seven list views used to hand-roll,' and it's imported in seven views. They sign off 'unified.' Sufficient?
evals.expected_output: No. A shared component existing and being adopted in the named set does not prove the concept is unified everywhere: a component being created reads as the concept being solved, but new or missed call sites can reintroduce the identical drift by hand afterward (sometimes copy-pasting the component's own default constant instead of importing it). The JSDoc naming the exact prior set ('seven list views') is the lever — diff that named set against a FRESH whole-tree grep for the same chip string/concept; any hit outside the seven is a straggler the consolidation never reached. This is higher-confidence than a cold duplicate search because the comment describes the 'before' state, so you match a known defect. Don't stop at 'the shared component exists and is imported' — verify adoption is total.
expectations: Rejects 'a shared component exists and is imported = unified' — new/missed call sites can reintroduce the drift by hand after the consolidation shipped
Uses the component's own doc-comment named set (the 'seven views') diffed against a fresh whole-tree grep to find stragglers outside that set
Notes this is higher-confidence than a cold search because the comment already describes the known 'before' state / prior drift

evals.prompt: A reviewer greps the whole tree for duplicated visible literal strings to find un-unified UI concepts and finds none. But across five files, each hand-assembles the same small info-icon-with-hover-tooltip next to a heading — the same two primitives (an icon component + a tooltip/popover), composed ad hoc, with no shared component — and they disagree on the a11y attributes and on whether they use the native `title` or the design system's tooltip. The literal-string grep found nothing. Is the concept unified?
evals.expected_output: No. This is duplication a literal-string grep can't catch — the 'unassembled molecule': multiple call sites correctly use the same underlying primitives but no one composed them into the one compound widget the recurring concept deserves. The visible label differs per site, so a duplicated-string search misses it. And because the assembly — not just the primitives — carries the real decisions (which a11y attributes, native `title` vs the shared tooltip, sizing), the ad-hoc assemblies silently diverge on exactly those, and one site's hard-won fix (e.g. a documented conflict with a screenshot/visual-test tool) never propagates. Detection: grep for a repeated scaffolding pattern instead of the label — the same small a11y-attribute cluster, or a one-character glyph in a small rounded element — recurring across files that import no common component. Fix: if the design system already ships the primitives, build the one shared atom; don't just reconcile the wording, because wording was never the only thing diverging.
expectations: Recognizes a duplicated-literal-string grep misses this class — the label differs per site, so string search finds nothing though the concept is duplicated (the 'unassembled molecule')
Explains the divergence is in the ASSEMBLY decisions (a11y attributes, native title vs shared tooltip, sizing), not the primitives, and one site's fix doesn't propagate
Prescribes detecting via a repeated scaffolding/attribute pattern (not the label) and fixing by building the one shared atom, not merely reconciling wording

evals.prompt: An autonomous lane's brief says 'open the PR against the `development` integration branch.' The lane runs `gh pr create` with a title and body but no `--base` flag. The merge step checks that all required checks are green and the PR is mergeable, then squash-merges. `main` is the protected, owner-gated default branch. What's the risk?
evals.expected_output: `gh pr create` without an explicit `--base` falls back to a `gh-merge-base` git config if one was set, otherwise the repo's default branch — here `main` — so the PR silently targets the protected/owner-gated branch instead of `development`, despite the brief. The merge step checks green + mergeable but NOT the base, so it merges the change into the protected branch: a governance breach even though the code is green. Fixes: (1) every PR-open passes the base explicitly (`--base development`), never relying on the default; (2) add base-branch identity to the merge-eligibility check next to state/mergeable/checks-green — the gate reads the PR's actual base and refuses anything not targeting the expected integration branch; (3) if a PR already merged to the protected branch, do NOT auto-revert the protected branch (reverting it is itself a gated change) — surface for an owner decision and separately port the change onto the integration branch so they don't diverge.
expectations: Identifies that a PR-open without an explicit base defaults to the repo default (protected) branch, so the PR silently targets the wrong branch despite the brief
Requires the merge gate to verify base-branch identity (refuse a PR whose base is not the expected integration branch), not only checks-green + mergeable
For an already-merged-to-protected PR, requires NOT auto-reverting the protected branch (itself a gated change) — surface for owner + port to the integration branch

evals.prompt: A team's CI generates SLSA build provenance internally and the deploy step verifies it before rollout. But their GitHub Releases (the tarballs users download) carry no signature, attestation, or provenance file. A reviewer says 'they have SLSA provenance, so releases are covered.' Right?
evals.expected_output: No — two different things. SLSA build provenance verified at the DEPLOY step protects the team's own internal pipeline (deploy-side verification); it gives a DOWNSTREAM consumer nothing to check. The published GitHub Release tarballs carry no signature/attestation/provenance asset, so a user or a mirror cannot verify the artifact they download matches what the project built — OpenSSF Scorecard's Signed-Releases check rates this high-risk ('possibility of installing malicious releases'). A project can have internal SLSA provenance and still ship nothing consumer-verifiable. Fix: the publish job must attach a consumer-checkable signature to the release — cosign/keyless Sigstore, `npm publish --provenance`, PyPI Trusted Publishing, a GPG-signed tag or .asc/.sig, or a SLSA provenance file (.intoto.jsonl) as a release asset — and a reviewer confirms the signing step actually runs in the workflow, not just that docs claim it.
expectations: Distinguishes deploy-side SLSA provenance verification (the team's internal pipeline) from a consumer-verifiable signature attached to the published release
Identifies that consumers/mirrors have nothing to verify when the release assets carry no signature/attestation/provenance, despite internal SLSA provenance

Requires the publish job to attach a consumer-checkable signature (cosign/Sigstore, npm --provenance, PyPI Trusted Publishing, GPG/.asc/.sig, or .intoto.jsonl) AND that the signing step actually runs, not just be documented

evals.prompt:
Review this Python service's outbound HTTP client for cryptographic failures (OWASP A04):

```python
import requests
BILLING_API = "https://billing.internal.example.com/v1/charge"
def charge_card(token, amount_cents):
    # internal cert is self-signed; verification kept failing in staging
    resp = requests.post(BILLING_API, json={"token": token, "amount": amount_cents}, verify=False, timeout=5)
    resp.raise_for_status()
    return resp.json()
```
Every URL in this codebase uses `https://`. Is transport security handled here?
evals.expected_output: No. `verify=False` disables TLS certificate validation (CWE-295, Improper Certificate Validation): the client accepts any certificate from any host, so a man-in-the-middle can terminate and re-originate the connection and read or alter the card token and amount — despite the `https://` URL. 'TLS everywhere' (the URL scheme) is not 'TLS validated' (the client checks who it is talking to); this code satisfies the former and fails the latter. The self-signed-staging-cert justification is not a reason to disable validation — pin the specific internal CA or self-signed certificate instead (ASVS v5.0.0-12.3.2 requires TLS clients validate certificates before communicating; -12.3.4 requires internal services trust only specific internal CAs/self-signed certs). Remove `verify=False`. (This is TLS validation — distinct from a JWT `verify=False`, which is signature verification.)
expectations: Names verify=False (disabled TLS certificate validation, CWE-295) as the vulnerability — not merely 'use HTTPS', which is already true here
Distinguishes 'TLS enforced' (the https:// scheme) from 'TLS validated' (the client validates the received certificate)
Rejects the self-signed-staging justification and prescribes pinning the specific internal CA/cert instead of disabling validation — internal/service-to-service TLS is not exempt

evals.prompt: One `GET /items?type=<x>&key=<y>` endpoint serves several record collections from one code path. Its exact-key match is `const c = [row.fooId, row.barKey, row.bazId].filter(Boolean); if (!c.includes(key)) return null;`. Smoke tests pass. One collection (`docs`) stores its id under `row.metadata.slug`. A reviewer sees the smoke tests green and moves on. What's wrong?
evals.expected_output: The shared filter silently no-ops for the `docs` collection. Its candidate list only checks top-level fields (fooId/barKey/bazId); `docs` nests its id under `row.metadata.slug`, so none of the candidates is ever truthy, the list is empty, and `[].includes(key)` is always false — every `docs` lookup by key returns null with no error, reading as 'nothing ever matches' rather than failing loudly. It survived review because the other shapes work and (usually) a correctly-written per-shape search accessor reaches `metadata.slug`, so smoke tests on the common shapes pass. Catch: enumerate EVERY shape the filter serves and check each one's real field nesting at its schema/type (not by assumption); a sibling accessor that already reads the nested key correctly confirms the gap; if the endpoint documents `key` as uniform, this is a broken promise. Fix: replace the hardcoded OR-list with a per-shape accessor registry (shape -> (row) => key), not just bolt `metadata.slug` onto the list, and add one fetch-by-real-key regression test per shape.
expectations: Identifies that the hardcoded top-level candidate list never matches the nested-key shape (metadata.slug), so the list is empty and [].includes(key) is always false — the lookup silently returns empty with no error
Explains why it survives review: the other shapes work and a correctly-written per-shape accessor masks it, so smoke tests on the common shapes pass

Prescribes enumerating every shape and checking nesting at the schema/type, cross-checking a correct sibling accessor, and fixing with a per-shape accessor registry + per-shape regression tests — not merely adding metadata.slug to the top-level list ad hoc

evals.prompt: An app has an edge WAF (enforces auth, allow-lists `/api/*`) in front of an origin Express server. The anonymous GET sweep (no cookies, no Authorization) returns 401 on every documented route — clean. Both the WAF (nginx) and the origin parse a request carrying BOTH `Transfer-Encoding` and `Content-Length`, and neither has been tested for desync. The team asks: 'the sweep passed — are we done on access control?' Answer.
evals.expected_output: No. The anonymous GET sweep only proves the WAF's own parser rejects requests it recognizes as unauthenticated; it says nothing about whether the WAF and the origin agree on where one HTTP request ends and the next begins. Because both parse a request carrying both `Transfer-Encoding` and `Content-Length`, an attacker can craft a request the WAF reads as one benign message while the origin reads as two — smuggling a second, uninspected request past the auth gate (HTTP request smuggling, CWE-444; the CL.TE/TE.CL/TE.TE class), or poisoning the connection so the next user's request is prefixed with attacker bytes. Fix at the framing layer: in HTTP/1.x a present Transfer-Encoding means Content-Length must be ignored (ASVS v5.0.0-4.2.1), and a message carrying both should be rejected/normalized; add a dedicated desync test — plain curl won't surface it, it needs a raw-socket/desync tool. Not done.
expectations: States the anonymous GET sweep passing does NOT prove the gate is unbypassable — it only exercises the edge's own parser, not edge/origin agreement on request boundaries
Names the mechanism: edge/origin disagreement on Transfer-Encoding vs Content-Length (CL.TE/TE.CL/TE.TE), i.e. HTTP request smuggling / CWE-444, smuggling a second request past the gate
Requires a fix at the framing layer (TE present => ignore CL per HTTP/1.x; reject a message with both) AND a dedicated desync test — noting plain curl won't surface it

evals.prompt: A repo's binary parser has a `FuzzParse` function using Go's native fuzzing (`go test -fuzz`). It was run once locally months ago, found nothing, and is committed. No CI job invokes it and there's no crash corpus. The team lists 'we fuzz our parser' as a security control. Is that assurance real?
evals.expected_output: No — a fuzz target that no job runs is decorative, the same way a mutation-testing gate or a self-test that never executes is. Coverage-guided fuzzing finds NEW bugs only when run continuously against live coverage feedback (OSS-Fuzz/ClusterFuzzLite, or `go test -fuzz` wired into a scheduled CI job), mutating inputs over time; a single local run months ago only exercised the corpus it had then. The review question is not 'is there a fuzz target' but 'is it wired to a job that runs on a schedule/CI, and does a crash reach a human' — with findings triaged into a committed crash corpus that becomes regression tests. OpenSSF Scorecard counts fuzzing as a control precisely because regular fuzzing catches what attackers otherwise would. Fix: wire FuzzParse into a recurring CI/fuzzing job, commit discovered crashers as regression seeds, and route new crashes to a human — otherwise 'we fuzz' is not a real control.
expectations: States a fuzz target that no CI/scheduled job runs is decorative — a one-off local run is not continuous fuzzing assurance
Explains coverage-guided fuzzing finds new bugs only when run continuously against live coverage feedback (names OSS-Fuzz/ClusterFuzzLite/go test -fuzz or an equivalent CI-wired form)
Requires wiring it to a recurring job AND a triaged crash corpus committed as regression tests (a crash must reach a human), not merely the target's existence

evals.prompt: An agent orchestration runs each lane in a git worktree branched off the local clone's remote-tracking ref. A merge-preflight script in one lane's worktree refuses every PR with 'required CI job never ran.' The current workflow on the remote no longer defines that job — it was removed last week. The local clone last fetched two weeks ago. The operator is about to file 'the merge gate is broken.' Is it?
evals.expected_output: No — this is a stale checkout, not a live gate bug. The worktree was branched off a remote-tracking ref the local clone hasn't fetched in two weeks, so it runs the OLD merge-preflight that still requires a CI job the current remote workflow removed — it refuses every PR for a job that no longer exists, while the fixed script on the true remote HEAD passes. Filing 'the gate is broken' chases a phantom. Fixes: (1) fetch the base ref immediately before creating the worktree (or hard-reset/rebase the worktree onto the freshly-fetched remote ref before running any script); (2) for any check that must reflect current remote/CI state (merge gates, required-check verification), query the forge/server API for the actual check-runs rather than trusting a local script copy — immune to local staleness. Rule: never infer 'the gate is broken' from a worktree without confirming its base ref is current.
expectations: Identifies the false failure as a stale checkout (the worktree ran an old script requiring a since-removed CI job), not a live gate bug
Prescribes fetching/resetting the worktree base to the current remote ref before running any script
Prescribes querying the forge/server API for actual check-runs (immune to local staleness) for checks that must reflect current remote/CI state, rather than trusting a local script copy

evals.prompt: Review this checkout flow. Object-level authorization is correct (each user completes only their own cart). `/checkout/purchase` is rate-limited to 20 requests/minute per authenticated user id — the team says that satisfies business-logic limits. A limited-edition product sells out in 4 seconds at launch, entirely to accounts created in the previous hour. What did the existing controls miss?
evals.expected_output: Object-level authz and the per-user rate limit both worked as designed and neither catches this: each purchase came from a distinct, individually-authorized account, each within its own 20/min limit. This is OWASP API6 (Unrestricted Access to a Sensitive Business Flow), not BOLA and not a generic rate-limit gap — the signal is automation (freshly-created accounts, superhuman timing), not per-account volume. OWASP's framing: first 'identify the business flows that might harm the business if they are excessively used' (here, checkout of scarce inventory), then add automation-specific controls the per-IP/per-user limiter can't provide — device/headless-browser fingerprinting, human detection (CAPTCHA or behavioral biometrics), and non-human-timing detection (ASVS v5.0.0-2.4.2 requires business logic flows to 'require realistic human timing'). Do NOT just lower the per-account rate limit — that punishes real users while a botnet of fresh accounts sidesteps it. The newly-created-account pattern is a corroborating automation signal.
expectations: States the per-user rate limit and object-level authz are NOT the missing control and does not recommend merely lowering the rate limit — each request was individually authorized and within limit
Names OWASP API6 / sensitive business flow, distinct from API1/BOLA and from the generic A06 rate-limit check; the signal is automation, not per-account volume

Prescribes an automation/human-detection control (fingerprinting, CAPTCHA/behavioral biometrics, non-human-timing per ASVS realistic-human-timing) and notes the fresh-account pattern as a corroborating automation signal

evals.prompt: A repo uses a CI concurrency group with cancel-in-progress (a new push cancels the older run) to save runner minutes. A contributor pushes three commits in quick succession. A merge bot checks 'the latest run on the branch is green' and merges. Later prod breaks from a bug CI would have caught on the final commit. What went wrong?
evals.expected_output: The cancel-in-progress race left the FINAL head with no CI run: the rapid pushes cancelled the intermediate run, and the run for the last commit was cancelled as a superseded sibling (or never created). The 'latest green' the merge bot trusted belonged to an EARLIER, since-cancelled head — nothing ever ran against the final SHA it merged. This is an ABSENT check, not a failure, and 'the branch has a recent green' is the wrong signal. Fix: before trusting/merging, confirm a run exists AND concluded for the EXACT head SHA (not just a recent branch green); treat 'no run for this SHA' as a distinct third state (not passed, not failed) — re-dispatch a run for that head and decide from it (the passed/failed/absent distinction in branch-and-merge-hygiene.md). Reduce the race at source: scope cancel-in-progress so it never cancels the newest run.
expectations: Identifies the cancel-in-progress race left the final head with NO run (absent), and the 'latest green' belonged to an earlier since-cancelled head — nothing ran against the merged SHA
States 'the branch has a recent green' is the wrong signal — require a run that exists AND concluded for the EXACT head SHA before merging
Treats 'no run for this SHA' as a third state (not passed, not failed) → re-dispatch a run for that head, and/or scope cancel-in-progress so it never cancels the newest run

evals.prompt: An unattended delivery orchestrator's 'merge' tick runs every cycle but lands zero PRs, even though several are all-green, MERGEABLE, un-held, and passed the repo's merge_preflight. The operator files 'the agent is stuck / too slow.' Investigation shows a spawned sub-agent CAN merge the same PRs successfully. What's actually happening, and what's the fix?
evals.expected_output: Not a slow or stuck agent — a permission-classifier asymmetry. In auto/unattended mode the classifier denies the orchestrator's OWN merge ('merge without review') while allowing the identical merge from a spawned sub-agent, so the loop runs but lands nothing and all throughput is silently forced onto delegation (and a single-PR merge doesn't warrant a heavyweight isolated-worktree lane). The asymmetry is unlogged, so it reads as a pace regression. Fixes: (1) a preflight-keyed allow-rule — permit the orchestrator to merge a PR whose repo-defined green-gate/merge_preflight just passed deterministically (the review the classifier wants already ran); or (2) symmetry + transparency — if merges must be delegated, deny them for sub-agents too and surface the reason ('merges routed to a delegated lane in auto mode') instead of a bare denial the loop swallows; and (3) document the routing so the orchestrator delegates merges by design, not by burning ticks retrying a structurally-blocked call. The tell: the merge tick runs but lands zero PRs while sub-agent merges succeed.
expectations: Identifies a permission-classifier asymmetry (orchestrator's own merge denied while a sub-agent's identical merge is allowed), NOT a slow/stuck agent
Explains the loop runs every tick but lands nothing, silently forcing throughput onto delegation, and the asymmetry is unlogged so it reads as a pace regression
Prescribes a preflight-keyed allow-rule (or symmetric denial + transparency) and documenting the merge-routing so the loop doesn't burn ticks retrying a structurally-blocked call

evals.prompt: An `/auth/send-otp` endpoint sends an SMS via a third-party provider billed per message. It requires a valid pre-authenticated session and is rate-limited to 5 requests/minute per IP — the team considers resource consumption handled. The app has 80,000 registered users. Any remaining API4 exposure?
evals.expected_output: Yes — the per-IP rate limit bounds abuse per caller, not total provider spend. 80,000 accounts (or an attacker cycling IPs/accounts) each sending within their own 5/min allowance can still drive unbounded SMS cost system-wide; the damage is the bill, not availability. This is OWASP API4's spend sub-case, distinct from compute exhaustion (CPU/memory/fd caps and GraphQL batching limits are covered elsewhere). Fix: configure a spend ceiling at the SMS provider, or failing that a billing alert ('Configure spending limits for all service providers/API integrations. When setting spending limits is not possible, billing alerts should be configured instead'); and add a per-OPERATION throttle (a per-account daily OTP cap independent of IP), since a generic per-IP/per-account limiter does not bound a low-and-slow spend spread across many legitimate accounts (CWE-770). Don't just tighten the per-IP rate limit.
expectations: States the per-IP rate limit does not cap aggregate provider spend across many accounts/IPs — the damage is the bill, not availability
Identifies this as OWASP API4's spend/billing sub-case, distinct from compute/CPU/memory exhaustion
Prescribes a provider-side spend ceiling or billing alert AND a per-operation throttle (per-account daily cap), not merely tightening the per-IP rate limit

evals.prompt:
Review this export endpoint:

```python
import csv
def export_customers(rows, out):
    w = csv.writer(out)
    w.writerow(["name", "coupon_code", "notes"])
    for r in rows:
        w.writerow([r.name, r.coupon_code, r.notes])  # user-editable profile fields
```
The team notes these fields are already HTML-escaped everywhere they render in the web UI, so they consider injection handled. Assess.
evals.expected_output: HTML-escaping protects the web UI but does nothing for this CSV export — the output context differs. A stored field whose value starts with `=`, `+`, `-`, `@`, a tab, or a NUL is written verbatim and parsed as a FORMULA by Excel/Sheets/LibreOffice when the file is opened (CWE-1236, CSV/formula injection) — e.g. `=WEBSERVICE(...)` / `=cmd|...` — firing on open, with no injection into the app itself. Fix at EXPORT time: prefix a single quote before any such leading character (ASVS v5.0.0-1.2.10, L3, names '=','+','-','@',tab,null among the characters to escape — a non-exhaustive list — and requires RFC 4180 escaping for the CSV) — do not rely on the web UI's HTML escaping and do not just reject the field at input time. Applies to XLS/XLSX/ODS exports too, not only CSV.
expectations: States HTML-escaping does not protect the CSV/spreadsheet export — a different output context — so 'already HTML-escaped' is insufficient
Names the specific dangerous leading characters (=, +, -, @, tab, null) and that they are parsed as a formula by the spreadsheet app on open (CWE-1236 / CSV formula injection)
Prescribes escaping at EXPORT time (prefix a single quote to a leading dangerous char; RFC 4180 escaping), not input-time rejection and not relying on the UI's HTML escaping

evals.prompt: A repo commits a `.ipynb` analysis notebook. In review it 'works' (the author ran it and the charts render). Its cells have execution_counts like [5], [2], [9], [3], and several cells print `df.head()` and one prints the value of an `API_KEY` variable while debugging. Is this ready to merge?
evals.expected_output: No — two notebook-specific defects a normal source review misses. (1) Hidden state from out-of-order execution: the non-monotonic execution_counts ([5],[2],[9],[3]) show cells were run out of order, so results may depend on a variable set by a since-edited/deleted cell — the committed notebook may not reproduce from a clean kernel. 'It ran for me' isn't evidence; require Restart & Run All from a fresh kernel (or `jupyter nbconvert --execute`/nbclient in CI) and a monotonic run. (2) Committed output cells leak data/secrets: `.ipynb` stores outputs in the file, so the printed df.head() rows (PII) and especially the printed API_KEY are now in git history where a diff-scoped review won't look. Strip outputs before commit (nbstripout / a ClearOutput pre-commit hook or CI gate), rotate the exposed key, and treat a committed output cell like any other emitted value. Not ready to merge.
expectations: Flags hidden state from out-of-order execution (non-monotonic execution_counts) — the committed notebook may not reproduce from a clean kernel; requires Restart & Run All / fresh-kernel execution, not 'it ran for me'

Flags that committed output cells store data/secrets in the .ipynb (the df.head() PII and the printed API_KEY are in git history), requires stripping outputs (nbstripout/ClearOutput gate) and rotating the exposed key
Treats these as distinct from ML-pipeline leakage/reproducibility — notebook-specific artifacts (state + stored outputs) — and does not merely say 'add tests'

evals.prompt: An unattended delivery agent under an auto-mode gate has its own merge calls denied and delegation is also unavailable. It has banked 12 green, mergeable, verified PRs and proven the merge-train union, but for hours it reports 'gated / holding' each scheduler tick while zero PRs land on the integration branch. The operator thinks the agent is slow. What should the agent be doing instead?
evals.expected_output: A closed gate with verified work piled behind it is an escalation, not a hold. The agent has no autonomous path (own merge denied, delegation unavailable), so on the FIRST denial it should convert the block into a one-action human ask: a single copy-pasteable command the operator runs themselves (in this CLI, an `! <command>` prefix executes as the user, outside the agent's own auto-mode classifier — a legitimate escape hatch, not permission-laundering, because the human issues it) or one GUI action, surfaced prominently and repeated — not buried under 'holding' ticks. It should track banked-verified vs landed and, when banked>0 and landed=0 for more than a tick or two, escalate that human ask rather than re-reporting the block. The banked work is invisible to an operator watching only the branch, so 'done but unlanded' reads as slow; never let 'the gate is closed' become a narrated steady state.
expectations: States a closed gate with verified work piled behind it is an escalation, not a steady 'holding' state, and that banked-but-unlanded work is invisible to an operator watching only the branch

Requires surfacing a one-action human-run unblock up front on the first denial (a copy-pasteable `! <command>` the user runs, or a GUI action) — noting it is not permission-laundering because the human issues it
Requires tracking banked-verified vs landed and escalating the human ask when banked>0/landed=0 persists, rather than re-narrating the block

evals.prompt: Every PR to `main` suddenly shows a required check `build (18.x)` stuck pending forever and can't merge. The CI workflow was just refactored — the job that used to be named `build (18.x)` is now `build (20.x)`. Branch protection still lists `build (18.x)` as a required status check. What's the diagnosis and fix?
evals.expected_output: The branch-protection required-check NAME list drifted from the workflow's actual job names: the rename (`build (18.x)` → `build (20.x)`) left branch protection requiring a status name (`build (18.x)`) that no job emits anymore, so that required check never reports, stays pending, and blocks every PR. It reads as 'a required check never ran,' but the cause is a stale hardcoded required name, not a trigger/`on:` gap. Fix: update branch protection to require the current job name (`build (20.x)`), and keep the two enumerations in sync going forward — derive the required-check list from the workflow definition, or add a test/check asserting the required names are a subset of the job names the workflow can emit, so a rename fails CI loudly instead of silently wedging the merge queue. (Mirror case: a check dropped from the workflow but left 'required' blocks the same way.)
expectations: Diagnoses a drift between the branch-protection required-check NAME and the workflow's actual job name (the rename left the old required name with no producer), not a trigger/on: gap or a flake
States the stale required name reports no status forever and blocks EVERY PR (and names the mirror: a check removed from the workflow but left required)
Fixes by syncing the two sets — update the required name AND derive the required list from the workflow or add a test asserting required-names ⊆ workflow-job-names, so a future rename fails loudly

evals.prompt: An autonomous delivery orchestrator runs 4 concurrent heavy lanes and the machine is at its CPU/RAM cap. To ship faster, the operator wants to bump it to 8 lanes. Each lane spends most of its time re-installing dependencies in a fresh worktree and running the full test suite. Is bumping to 8 lanes the right move?
evals.expected_output: No. On a capacity-bound machine throughput = WIP / cycle-time (Little's Law); once lanes saturate the CPU/RAM cap, adding more lanes thrashes (context-switching/contention) and everything crawls — that LOWERS throughput, not raises it. The highest-leverage move is cutting per-lane cycle-time: run only diff-affected tests per lane and cache the dependency installs so they aren't re-paid in every isolated worktree (the full suite still gates the batch/merge-union, so correctness isn't traded away); amortize the fixed gate cost by batching atomic low-collision changes per PR; use a merge train to verify the union once and merge members back-to-back; and eliminate rework via verify-first + decorrelated pre-merge review + auto-merge-on-green. Only break the machine ceiling by moving lanes to remote/cloud runners — don't raise local concurrency past the probed cap.
expectations: States raising lane concurrency past the CPU/RAM cap thrashes and LOWERS throughput — not the right move (throughput = WIP/cycle-time; lanes already saturated)
Prescribes cutting per-lane cycle-time first — diff-affected tests + cached dependency installs — with the full suite still gating the batch/merge-union (correctness preserved)
Names further levers (batch per PR, merge train, remote/cloud runners to break the machine cap, eliminate rework) rather than just adding lanes

evals.prompt: Review this custom checkbox for accessibility: ```html ``` The reviewer notes 'it's wrapped in a `
evals.expected_output: No. HTML `<label>` only names labelable elements (`<input>`, `<button>`, `<select>`, `<textarea>`, `<meter>`, `<output>`, `<progress>`, and form-associated custom elements). This control is built on a `<div>` (given `role="checkbox"`), which is NOT labelable, so the wrapping `<label>`'s "Accept terms" text is not taken as its accessible name; the div's only content is an `aria-hidden` box, so it announces with NO name — "checkbox, not checked" instead of "Accept terms, checkbox, not checked." It looks plausibly labeled in the DOM, so a shape-based review misses it. Fix: name it explicitly with `aria-labelledby` (pointing at the visible "Accept terms" text's id) or `aria-label`, and verify the platform-computed accessible name in the accessibility tree (devtools/axe), not the DOM. (Had this been a labelable element with a role — `<button role="switch">`, `<input type="checkbox" role="switch">` — the `<label>` would still name it; the fault here is the non-labelable `<div>` host, not the role.)
expectations: States a wrapping `<label>` only names LABELABLE elements (input/button/select/textarea/meter/output/progress, and form-associated custom elements) — a control built on a non-labelable `<div>`/`<span>` (even with an ARIA role) is not named by it
Identifies the concrete failure: the aria-hidden box leaves no name source, so the control announces with no name ('checkbox, not checked'), and it passes a DOM/shape-based review

Prescribes naming it via aria-labelledby/aria-label AND verifying the platform-computed accessible name in the a11y tree (not the DOM); does NOT wrongly claim adding a role to a labelable element loses its label

evals.prompt: An operator running an unattended agent says 'add more recurring loops to keep delivery going.' The agent has 3 loops; it replaces all 3 with 2 richer combined loops (same cadence, strictly more instructions each). Functionally it's an upgrade. The operator sees the loop count drop from 3 to 2 and says 'you did the opposite of what I asked.' Who's right, and what should the agent have done?
evals.expected_output: The operator is right to object. The request was ADD-only ('more loops'), and operators commonly track the loop count as a proxy for delivery health, so dropping 3->2 reads as removing what they asked to add — regardless of the functional upgrade. The agent should have improved the loops by editing them in place or ADDING new ones, not by consolidating N into fewer 'richer' ones in response to a request for 'more'. Pruning is allowed only for a genuine, named defect — an exact duplicate, a dead/broken loop, or two loops giving contradictory instructions — stated explicitly with the reason; the sin here is reducing the count silently, as a side effect of an optimization nobody asked for. After any change the count may hold or rise freely and should decrease only with a stated reason. General principle: when a user's mental model tracks a countable resource (loops, open PRs, agents), never move that count the wrong way as a SILENT or unexplained side effect of an optimization they didn't ask for — the trust violation is the surprise, not the decrement itself; a justified, explicitly-surfaced decrement (e.g. closing a PR that leaks a secret) is fine.
expectations: Sides with the operator: 'more' means ADD-only, and replacing 3 loops with 2 (even richer ones) decrements a count the operator tracks as a delivery-health proxy — reads as doing the opposite of the request

Prescribes improving loops by editing in place or adding (not consolidating N-into-fewer or delete-then-recreate in response to 'more'), and pruning only for a genuine named defect (exact duplicate, dead/broken, or contradictory) stated explicitly with the reason

Generalizes correctly: the violation is a SILENT/unexplained decrement of a user-tracked countable resource as a side effect of an unrequested optimization — an explained, justified decrement is acceptable

evals.prompt: A weekly team digest buckets each person's status note under a Monday-starting week, computed by truncating the note's UTC `updated_at` to a date and finding that date's Monday. The same codebase correctly computes 'today' via UTC everywhere else (a previously-fixed wrong-clock bug). A reviewer sees the consistent UTC anchoring and concludes dates are handled correctly. Is the bucketing correct?
evals.expected_output: No. Bucketing a past event into a human calendar week is a wall-clock question about an instant, so it needs the ACTOR's UTC offset, not one shared clock. Truncating the UTC timestamp to its own date misfiles any actor outside UTC by a full week for the hours their local date and the UTC date disagree: a US-West-Coast member filing at 6pm Sunday local has a UTC stamp already in Monday, so the note is bucketed into the next week — it appears a week early, and the week it was meant for shows them as silent. This is DISTINCT from the wrong-clock-for-'today' bug the codebase already fixed: 'today' is a single shared reference frame, but attributing one person's past action to 'their day/week' has no single right global clock — it requires that person's offset. Consistent UTC anchoring for 'today' does not make this correct; it is a different function bucketing a different kind of value. It is worse if an empty bucket is read as signal ('nobody reported this week'), since the mis-bucketed note also makes the correct week look emptier than it was. Fix: bucket by the timestamp converted to the actor's zone (store/resolve each actor's tz-id).
expectations: Identifies that bucketing a past event by its UTC calendar date misfiles non-UTC actors by a full day/week near the boundary, because attributing an action to 'their day' needs the actor's offset, not a shared clock
Distinguishes this from the wrong-clock-for-'today' bug (a single shared reference frame) — consistent UTC anchoring for 'today' does NOT make per-actor bucketing correct
Notes the compounded severity when an empty bucket is treated as signal, and prescribes bucketing in the actor's timezone (store/resolve the actor's tz)

evals.prompt: A 'what's new since your last visit' feature keeps an append-only log per item and shows the delta since the second-most-recent entry. It sets the cursor to that entry's timestamp and filters `entry.timestamp > cursor`. It correctly handles fewer than two entries and documents 'never fabricate an absence.' Two updates to one item land on the exact same millisecond (a batch job reused one captured time). What does the user see, and what's the fix?
evals.expected_output: The user sees a false 'no changes,' even though the newest entry changed the status. The cursor equals the second-newest entry's timestamp; the newest entry carries that SAME timestamp, so `entry.timestamp > cursor` (strict `>`) is false for it and it is excluded from the diff. Ties are ordinary — one now() reused across rows in a transaction, a coarse-granularity timestamp column, or a backfill stamping a batch with one synthetic time. Using a record's own timestamp as a strict-inequality cursor is wrong because a timestamp is not a unique key. Fix: use an ordinal/positional cursor ('this record's index in the sorted history is strictly after the cursor record's index'), or append a strictly-monotonic tiebreak (a sequence id) to the sort, rather than comparing a non-unique value. The 'never fabricate an absence' guard doesn't save it: the tie looks like 'nothing to compare' but is really 'something to compare, compared with the wrong operator,' and the adversarial input is 2+ records with an identical timestamp, not the 0/1-record empty boundary.
expectations: Explains the strict `>` cursor excludes the newest record when its timestamp EQUALS the cursor (ties from reused now()/coarse resolution/backfill), yielding a false 'nothing changed'
Identifies the root cause: a timestamp is not a unique key, so it cannot be a safe strict-inequality cursor
Prescribes an ordinal/positional cursor (or a strictly-monotonic tiebreak like a sequence id), and notes the adversarial input is 2+ tied-timestamp records, not the 0/1 empty boundary

evals.prompt: A system snapshots 'measurable entities' — some goals, some metrics, folded into one array tagged with a `kind` field — then diffs two snapshots to report period-over-period change. The diff builds its lookup with `new Map(list.map(x => [x.id, x]))`. Elsewhere, a sibling function resolving the same entities takes a `(kind, id)` compound key, with a comment that it's to stop a goal and metric sharing an id from colliding. Today's data has no such collision and the diff has no live callers yet. Is there a defect worth reporting?
evals.expected_output: Yes. The diff keys its Map on the bare id over a list that deliberately mixes two kinds. If a goal and a metric ever share an id, the Map collides — Map keeps last-write-wins — so one entity silently vanishes from the diff: not flagged added, removed, or ambiguous, just gone, and the comparison emits one delta instead of two. Fix: key on the compound (kind, id). The signal that this is a real gap, not an accepted risk, is cross-referential: a sibling function already uses a (kind, id) key precisely to prevent this collision, so the bare-id diff is a regression against a contract the codebase set for itself. Report it even though today's data has no collision and the feature has no live caller — it is a latent silent false-merge in shared code — but state plainly that it is not currently reachable (only structurally possible, e.g. the moment someone names a metric identically to its 1:1 parent goal and two periods close). A silent merge is exactly the false-merge to avoid: bias toward false-exclude / surfacing both over collapsing two entities into one.
expectations: Identifies that a bare-id Map/Set over a multi-kind (discriminated-union) list collides on a shared id via last-write-wins, silently dropping one entity from the diff with no signal; fix is a compound (kind, id) key
Uses the sibling function's already-stricter (kind, id) contract as the signal that this is a self-inconsistent regression, not an accepted risk
Reports the latent defect while honestly stating current reachability (no collision today / no live caller), and frames it as the false-merge to avoid (bias false-exclude over silent merge)

evals.prompt: A reporting feature lets users save a 'custom label' string that the server later renders with `render_template_string(user_label)` in a Jinja2 app (so users can interpolate `{{ order.id }}` into their label). A reviewer says 'we HTML-escape all output, so this is XSS-safe.' Is the feature safe?
evals.expected_output: No — this is server-side template injection (SSTI, CWE-1336), and HTML-escaping does not address it. The bug is not that user DATA is rendered into HTML (that would be XSS, fixed by output escaping); it is that the user's string is compiled and evaluated as TEMPLATE SOURCE by the engine. render_template_string(user_label) passes user input AS the template, so an attacker submits a label like `{{ ''.__class__.__mro__[1].__subclasses__() ... }}` (object-graph traversal) that Jinja2 evaluates server-side — typically a path to remote code execution, not just markup injection. Output escaping runs on the RESULT and does nothing about code the engine already executed. Jinja2's SandboxedEnvironment is a mitigation with documented escapes, not a trust boundary. Fix: never compile a template from user input — render a statically-defined template and pass the user's label only as a BOUND CONTEXT VARIABLE (data cannot introduce template syntax); if user-authored templates are a genuine feature, use a logic-less engine (Mustache) or a locked-down allow-listed sandbox and treat that path as an RCE-grade trust boundary.
expectations: Identifies SSTI (not XSS): the user string is compiled/evaluated as template SOURCE by the engine (render_template_string passes input AS the template), distinct from untrusted data rendered into output

Explains that HTML output-escaping does NOT fix it (it acts on the result, not the engine's evaluation) and that server-side SSTI is typically an RCE path via object-graph traversal; an engine sandbox is a mitigation, not a boundary
