Prescribes never compiling a template from user input — pass the user value only as a bound context variable to a static template; for genuine user-template features use a logic-less engine / locked-down sandbox treated as an RCE-grade boundary

evals.prompt: An accessibility crawler flags a focusable control only when its computed style is identical before and after `.focus()`. It reports 0 failures on a design system where many components override the global focus ring with a light token (meant for dark filled buttons) that measures ~1.8:1 on the light cards they actually sit on. Is the focus indicator accessible? What's wrong with the check?
evals.expected_output: No — the indicators are not accessible, and the check validates the wrong property. 'The style changed on focus' is necessary but not sufficient: a change from transparent to a real-but-too-faint colour is a passing diff and a failing product. A focus indicator must clear a numeric contrast floor — WCAG 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast (Level AA) requires 3:1 for the visual information identifying UI-component states, and 2.4.13 Focus Appearance (Level AAA) requires the indicator area to be >=3:1 between the focused and unfocused states — and ~1.8:1 fails it. The detector must resolve the ACTUAL rendered colours on both sides of the focus boundary and compute the ratio (like a text-contrast checker), not just diff that something changed. The root cause is compounding: a narrow-purpose token (documented for dark filled buttons) was reused as the focus colour on light surfaces, and nothing enforced the doc-comment's intended context — so grep the token's call sites, not its comment. The fix is usually just removing the override so the correct global :focus-visible default wins.
expectations: Identifies the check validates the wrong property: 'style changed' passes a too-faint indicator; it must compute the ACTUAL rendered-colour contrast ratio on both sides of focus
Cites the numeric floor correctly: ~1.8:1 fails 3:1 (WCAG 1.4.11 AA for UI-component states; 2.4.13 Focus Appearance AAA for the indicator area between focused/unfocused states)

Names the compounding root cause (a narrow-purpose token reused beyond its documented, unenforced context) — grep call sites not the comment; fix by removing the override so the correct global default wins

evals.prompt: A codebase has thorough prefers-reduced-motion coverage: a CSS duration belt zeroing all transitions/animations under the media query, a per-component motion-reduce variant, and a shared hook wired into every framer-motion usage. A 'jump to section' button calls `element.scrollIntoView({behavior: 'smooth'})` directly. A reviewer greps for `transition-` and the animation library's import, finds everything gated, and passes it. Correct?
evals.expected_output: No. The reduced-motion program gates one KIND of motion (CSS transitions/animations + one library) exhaustively, but scrollIntoView({behavior: 'smooth'}) is an imperative native browser API — not a CSS transition and not driven by the duration tokens or the library variants — so a search scoped to the gated mechanism (transition-, the library import) walks right past it. Audit reduced-motion by the SYMPTOM (motion-producing APIs), not the mechanism the codebase already gates: grep for scrollIntoView / scrollTo / scrollBy with a behavior option, CSS scroll-behavior: smooth, Element.animate(), requestAnimationFrame loops, and autoplay/carousel/marquee logic. For each hit, confirm it branches on matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)') (or the repo's existing hook) before choosing the animated path. The fix is cheap and should reuse the hook already wired for the other animations, cited as the patch.
expectations: Identifies that an imperative native motion API (scrollIntoView({behavior:'smooth'})) is outside the CSS/library mechanism the reduced-motion program gates, so a mechanism-scoped grep misses it

Prescribes auditing by the symptom set (scrollIntoView/scrollTo/scrollBy with behavior, scroll-behavior:smooth, Element.animate, rAF, autoplay/carousel), each branching on matchMedia / the existing hook
Notes the fix reuses the reduced-motion hook the codebase already has (cited as the patch), not a new pattern

evals.prompt: A merge guard reads the latest check run by creation order for a PR's head and renders its status table. Under rapid pushes, run A (CANCELLED as superseded) and run B (PASS) both exist for the head SHA; the guard picks run A and shows the required check red, blocking a PR whose head actually passed. What's wrong and how should the guard work?
evals.expected_output: The guard fails closed on a green head by conflating CANCELLED with FAILURE and by selecting the run non-deterministically. A CANCELLED run (superseded / concurrency-cancelled) is a transient state, not a verdict; rendering it red blocks a genuinely-mergeable PR. Fixes: (1) select the run deterministically — group runs by check NAME at the exact head SHA and take the latest by completion time, never 'latest by creation order,' which returned the cancelled sibling here instead of run B. (2) Distinguish four states per required check — PASS, FAIL, PENDING/IN-PROGRESS, NO-RUN — and treat CANCELLED as a subset of PENDING (re-dispatch or wait for the live run), never as FAIL. (3) In the status table, PENDING/CANCELLED must be visually distinct from FAIL; a CANCELLED row rendered red is the defect. This is the fail-closed mirror of the fail-open cancel-race (merging an earlier green while the final head has no run for its SHA).
expectations: Identifies the guard conflates CANCELLED (a transient/superseded state) with FAILURE, and that the PR is genuinely mergeable BECAUSE a PASS run exists at the same head SHA — so blocking it is a fail-closed error, not a real gate
Requires deterministic selection: latest run per check NAME at the exact head SHA (not latest-by-creation-order, which returned the cancelled sibling)
Prescribes a 4-state model (PASS/FAIL/PENDING/NO-RUN, CANCELLED as a subset of PENDING) and a status table showing PENDING/CANCELLED distinct from FAIL

evals.prompt: A one-writer-per-file collision check reads an in-flight PR's changed files with `gh pr view <n> --json files` and clears a new lane because none of those files overlap. The PR is a 700-file release. Is the 'no overlap' conclusion safe?
evals.expected_output: No — gh pr view/list --json files silently caps at 100 files per PR, with no error or warning, so on a 700-file PR the check saw at most 100 of them and the lane may collide with any of the other ~600 files the capped list never showed — producing exactly the concurrent-writer conflict the check exists to prevent. Read the file list from the paginated REST endpoint instead: gh api repos/:owner/:repo/pulls/<n>/files --paginate --jq '.[].filename'. This is the same failure class as a bare gh pr/issue list truncating to its default page and a forge-only absence check missing a local worktree: a gh read returns a truncated view without erroring, and a partial read yields a wrong 'safe'/'absent' conclusion. Treat every gh read as paginated-until-proven-complete before basing a collision or absence verdict on it.
expectations: Identifies that gh --json files silently caps at 100 files per PR (no error), so 'no overlap' on a 700-file PR is unsound — the check saw at most 100 files
Prescribes the paginated REST read (gh api .../pulls/<n>/files --paginate) for the file list
Generalizes: a gh read returns a truncated view without erroring; treat every gh read as paginated-until-proven-complete before a collision/absence conclusion

evals.prompt: A model is validated with shuffled 10-fold KFold and reports 0.94 AUC. The data has multiple rows per patient (up to 20 visits each) and is timestamped over 3 years. In production on new patients it scores 0.71. What went wrong and how should cross-validation be set up?
evals.expected_output: The CV split violated the data's structure, so 0.94 was leakage, not skill. Two problems. (1) Grouped leakage: plain KFold scatters a patient's correlated visits across train and test, so the model memorizes patient-specific signal rather than a generalizable pattern — the i.i.d. assumption is broken when the generative process yields groups of dependent samples. Split by the group key with GroupKFold so the same patient is never in both train and test; CV then estimates performance on a genuinely new patient, which is what production faces (~0.71). (2) Temporal leakage: shuffled KFold on 3 years of time-ordered data trains on future rows to predict past ones, which autocorrelation rewards; use a forward-chaining TimeSeriesSplit so each test fold is strictly after its train fold. The tell was the implausibly high CV score that collapsed on new patients/time — a leaked split passes too well, it doesn't error. If both group and time matter, combine (group-aware, time-ordered splitting).
expectations: Identifies grouped leakage: plain KFold scatters a group's (patient's) correlated rows across train/test, inflating the score; fix = GroupKFold so the same group is never in both sets and CV reflects a new group
Identifies temporal leakage: shuffled KFold on time-ordered data trains on the future to predict the past; fix = forward-chaining TimeSeriesSplit
Explains the tell (an implausibly high CV score that collapses in production / on new groups — leakage passes too well, doesn't error), not merely 'tune the model'

evals.prompt: To fix class imbalance a pipeline runs SMOTE on the full dataset, THEN does a train/test split and reports 0.97 F1. Is that F1 trustworthy?
evals.expected_output: No. Resampling the entire dataset before the split has two separable problems. (1) Test-set realism: the test set is made artificially balanced, so the reported metric describes a class distribution that does not exist in production — the model will not be tested on a dataset with class distribution similar to the real use-case; it should be evaluated on the natural, imbalanced distribution. (2) Leakage: synthetic/oversampled points can be generated using information from rows that land in the test set (and duplicates cross the split), inflating the score further. Fix: split first, then resample the TRAINING data only, inside each CV fold (an imblearn Pipeline refits the resampler per fold); keep the test/validation set at the real imbalanced distribution and judge with imbalance-appropriate metrics (PR-AUC / per-class recall, not raw accuracy or a balanced-by-construction F1). The realism failure is separate from and additional to the leakage one — even with zero leakage, a balanced test set reports a number production never sees.
expectations: Identifies that resampling the whole dataset before the split makes the TEST set artificially balanced, so the metric describes a distribution that doesn't exist in production (distinct from leakage)
Identifies the leakage half (synthetic/duplicate samples informed by rows in the test split) as an additional, separate problem
Prescribes split-first-then-resample-train-only (inside the CV fold / imblearn Pipeline) and evaluating on the natural imbalanced distribution with imbalance-appropriate metrics

evals.prompt: A Rust struct wraps a raw FFI pointer: `struct Conn(*mut ffi::Handle);`. It won't compile when moved to another thread ('`Conn` cannot be sent between threads safely'). A dev adds `unsafe impl Send for Conn {}`; it compiles and the tests pass. Is this correct?
evals.expected_output: Not necessarily — and 'compiles + tests pass' is not evidence it is correct. `unsafe impl Send for Conn {}` does not make the type thread-safe; it silences the compiler's Send check and asserts a guarantee the compiler can no longer verify. If the underlying ffi::Handle is not actually safe to move to / use from another thread (thread-affinity, interior aliasing, a non-thread-safe library), this is silent undefined behaviour with no backstop — a normal test run won't exercise the UB. Send/Sync are unsafe to implement precisely because the author takes over a proof the compiler otherwise does. Correct approach: establish and write down the safety argument at the unsafe impl (the pointee is genuinely safe to send: no thread-affinity, no aliasing); if it isn't, don't send it — keep it on its thread or make it genuinely Send (an owned, movable resource). Verify unsafe with cargo miri / sanitizers, or mark it unverified — never trust the green build.
expectations: Identifies that `unsafe impl Send` silences the compiler's check and asserts an unverified guarantee (it does NOT make the type thread-safe); 'compiles + tests pass' is not evidence because a normal run doesn't exercise UB
Explains the consequence: if the pointee has thread-affinity/aliasing/non-thread-safety, this is silent UB with no compiler backstop
Prescribes a written safety argument per unsafe impl (or not sending it) and verification via miri/sanitizers, not trusting the green build

evals.prompt: A Go repo has `for _, task := range tasks { go func() { process(task) }() }`. A reviewer runs `go version` -> go1.23, concludes each goroutine gets its own `task` (Go 1.22+ loop-var semantics), and passes it. The module's go.mod says `go 1.20`. Is the reviewer right?
evals.expected_output: No. The Go 1.22 loop-variable change (each iteration creates a fresh variable, instead of one variable updated per iteration) is gated by the MODULE's declared language version in go.mod, not by the installed toolchain. With `go 1.20` in go.mod, the module keeps the old semantics even when built by a go1.23 compiler — so every goroutine still captures the one shared `task` and most will observe the last element (a classic lost-update/wrong-item bug). Checking `go version` is the wrong signal; check the `go` directive in go.mod. Fixes: bump the module's go version to 1.22+, or capture explicitly (`task := task` inside the loop body, or pass task as a goroutine argument) — the explicit capture is correct under every version and is the safest review recommendation.
expectations: Identifies the loop-var fix is gated by the module's go.mod go-version, not the installed toolchain — so `go version` is the wrong check and a go1.20 module keeps the old shared-variable semantics
Explains the resulting bug: all goroutines capture one shared task, most see the last value
Prescribes checking the go.mod directive and/or an explicit per-iteration capture (task := task or a param), correct under every version

evals.prompt: Java: `Set<Order> s = new HashSet<>(); Order o = new Order("A1", PENDING); s.add(o); o.setStatus(SHIPPED); s.contains(o);` where Order's equals/hashCode cover (id, status). What does contains return, and why?
evals.expected_output: It returns false — even though `o` is the same object that was added. equals/hashCode include status; when o was added, HashSet placed it in the bucket for hashCode(A1, PENDING). setStatus(SHIPPED) mutated a field used in hashCode, but the element stays physically in the old bucket. contains(o) now computes hashCode(A1, SHIPPED), looks in a different bucket, and doesn't find it — no exception, just a silent wrong answer (iteration and remove are corrupted the same way). Root cause: a hash-key must be effectively immutable over its hashCode fields while it is in the collection. Fixes: don't mutate hashCode fields after insertion (remove -> mutate -> re-add if you must), or exclude the mutable field from equals/hashCode (often key on a stable id only). Common real-world trigger: a JPA @Entity or Lombok @EqualsAndHashCode over a mutable id/status. (Also: every field used in hashCode must be in equals — a hashCode field that equals ignores makes two equal objects hash differently, breaking the contract; excluding an equals-only field from hashCode only hurts bucket distribution.)
expectations: States contains returns false because mutating a hashCode field after insertion leaves the object in the old bucket while the new hash looks in a different one — a silent wrong answer, no exception
Identifies the rule: a hash-key must be effectively immutable over its hashCode fields while in the collection (and names the JPA @Entity / Lombok classic trigger)
Prescribes not mutating hashCode fields post-insert (or excluding the mutable field / keying on a stable id), preserving the equal-objects-share-a-hashCode contract

evals.prompt: A payments diff adds a `cvv` column to the transactions table 'for retrying failed captures' and logs the full magnetic-stripe track data on decline 'for debugging.' PANs in the same table are already truncated to last-4. A reviewer says 'card data is encrypted at rest, so this is fine.' Is it?
evals.expected_output: No. Encryption at rest does not make it fine: Sensitive Authentication Data (SAD) — card verification codes (CVV/CVC), full track data, and PINs/PIN blocks — must NEVER be stored after authorization, encrypted or not. It may be used transiently in-flight during the transaction, but persisting it post-auth (a cvv column, track data in logs) is prohibited outright — an absolute rule, stricter than any retention/minimization policy for ordinary PII. Both additions are findings: remove the cvv column and the track-data log line (retry a capture with a token / authorization reference, never the CVV). Separately, masking vs truncation are different controls: truncation protects PAN when stored/processed/transmitted (the last-4 column is truncation — fine), masking conceals PAN when displayed/printed; don't treat them as interchangeable. (Whether this system is PCI-in-scope and the exact DSS requirement numbers route to counsel / a QSA; the code-visible defect — storing SAD post-auth — is the finding.)
expectations: Identifies that SAD (CVV/CVC, full track data, PIN/PIN block) must never be STORED after authorization, and encryption at rest does not make it acceptable (absolute rule, stricter than PII retention)
Flags BOTH the cvv column and the track-data log line, and prescribes removing them (retry via token/authorization reference, not the CVV)
Distinguishes masking (display) from truncation (storage) as non-interchangeable, and routes scope/requirement-numbers to counsel while naming the code-visible defect

evals.prompt: A Terraform PR adds a service-account IAM binding with tightly-scoped least-privilege permissions (no wildcards) for a new integration. It has no expiry, no owner tag, and there is no offboarding/reconciliation process that would ever remove it. A reviewer approves it as 'least-privilege, looks good.' Anything missing?
evals.expected_output: Yes — the grant is correct on the SCOPE axis but has no LIFECYCLE, a separate axis the least-privilege check doesn't cover. A perfectly-scoped binding with no expiry/condition, no owner annotation, and no link to a deprovisioning path (an offboarding hook, or a periodic reconciliation against the IdP roster) becomes standing access nothing ever revisits or revokes — it outlives the integration it was for, the person who added it, and any later role change. NIST SP 800-53 AC-2 requires accounts be reviewed for compliance, disabled/notified when users are terminated or transferred, and account management aligned with personnel termination/transfer processes. Fix: attach an expiry/condition where the platform supports it, an owner tag, and wire the grant into a reconciliation/deprovision process (or document the review cadence). Flag any IaC grant that adds access with no expiry/owner/deprovision linkage. (AC-2 is an org process control; the reviewable diff artifact is the ungoverned grant itself.)
expectations: Identifies that grant-time SCOPE and LIFECYCLE are different axes — a least-privilege grant with no expiry/owner/deprovision path is standing access nothing revisits or revokes
Prescribes the concrete fix: expiry/condition, owner annotation, and linkage to a reconciliation/deprovision process (or a documented review cadence)
Frames it as flaggable in the diff (an IaC grant with no lifecycle metadata) while noting AC-2 itself is an org process control

evals.prompt: A free-tier API enforces '100 calls/day per session' keyed on the session token issued at an unauthenticated `POST /session` (no signup, no verification). Usage is correctly counted per token and blocked at 100. Is the cap effective against a determined abuser?
evals.expected_output: No. The cap is only as strong as the cost of obtaining a fresh key, and here a new session token is free and unauthenticated — an abuser just calls POST /session again to mint a new token, resetting the 100-count, so keying on the session token is no better than keying on IP (the rotating-key-vs-stable-identity confusion). 'Correctly counted per token' is irrelevant when the token itself is cheaply re-mintable. Fixes: key the cap on a SCARCE, verified identity — a verified account, a payment instrument, or a credential that itself costs or is rate-limited to create — not on a free-to-mint session/device/API key; and/or rate-limit the minting path (POST /session) itself, with a global/per-subnet backstop and a verification/proof-of-work step before granting a fresh quota. General rule: a per-key limit assumes the key is scarce; if minting a key is free, the limit is only a suggestion.
expectations: Identifies that a cheaply/freely re-mintable key (an unauthenticated session token) makes the per-key cap bypassable — the abuser re-mints to reset the counter, no better than keying on IP
Explains that 'correctly counted per token' is irrelevant when the token is re-mintable; the cap's strength equals the cost of obtaining a fresh key (rotating-key vs stable-identity)
Prescribes keying on a scarce/verified identity (verified account, payment instrument, cost-to-create credential) and/or rate-limiting the minting path itself

evals.prompt: An SSR React app renders fine locally and in CI, but production users intermittently report a button that does nothing on first click. A component renders `{new Date().toLocaleTimeString()}` and, for signed-in users only, a `Math.random()`-chosen promo variant, both during render. What's likely happening and how do you fix it?
evals.expected_output: A hydration mismatch from nondeterministic render output (distinct from invalid-nesting hydration bugs): the server renders one time/promo variant, the client's first render produces a different one, so server HTML and client tree disagree. The framework won't patch a text/markup mismatch and can reconcile incorrectly — leaving event handlers attached to the wrong elements, which is exactly the 'button does nothing on first click' symptom. It slips past local/CI because it is STATE-DEPENDENT (the promo branch only renders for signed-in users; time/random differ only under real server/client timing), so the author's own run doesn't trip it. Fixes: don't read nondeterministic or browser-only values (Date.now/Math.random/typeof window/matchMedia/localStorage) during render — move them to a post-hydration useEffect and render a stable server placeholder; use useId for generated ids; reserve suppressHydrationWarning for genuinely-expected diffs (a live clock), never to silence a real mismatch. Grep for suppressHydrationWarning as a tell.
expectations: Identifies a hydration mismatch from nondeterministic/browser-only reads during render (Date.now/Math.random/typeof window), distinct from invalid-nesting hydration bugs
Explains the consequence (framework won't patch it -> event handlers on wrong elements -> dead first click) and why state-dependence hides it from local/CI
Prescribes gating those reads to a post-hydration effect (stable server placeholder) + useId, and reserving suppressHydrationWarning for expected diffs (grep it as a tell)

evals.prompt: A page's JS bundle, image, and font budgets are all green and each API call returns in under 100ms, but LCP is 3.5s. The page fetches the user, then (after that resolves) the user's org, then (after that) the org's dashboard data — three sequential awaits before first meaningful paint. What's the problem?
evals.expected_output: A sequential data-fetch waterfall (a critical request chain) on the render-critical path: each request starts only after the previous resolves, so three sub-100ms calls plus their round-trip latencies serialize into a multi-second blocking chain before first paint — LCP suffers even though every individual request is fast and all byte-budgets are green. A green byte-budget is not a green load; here the chain DEPTH, not payload size, is the cost. Fixes: parallelize independent requests with Promise.all (if org and dashboard don't strictly depend on the prior result, fetch them together); collapse the chain server-side (a BFF / single endpoint / GraphQL returning user+org+dashboard in one round trip); prefetch/hoist what a later step needs; colocate data requirements with the route so they fire on navigation, not after render. Measure the network waterfall / critical-request-chain view, not just the bundle budget.
expectations: Identifies a sequential/dependent-request waterfall (critical request chain) on the critical path — chain depth serializes latency even with fast individual calls and green byte-budgets
Explains a green bundle/image/font budget doesn't catch it (payload size vs request-chain depth are different axes)
Prescribes parallelizing independent requests (Promise.all), collapsing the chain server-side (BFF/single endpoint), and prefetch/colocation — measured via the request-waterfall view

evals.prompt: An API paginates with `ORDER BY created_at LIMIT 20 OFFSET ?`. Under normal load it's fine in tests. A reviewer flags only that a large OFFSET is slow. Is slowness the only issue?
evals.expected_output: No — OFFSET pagination is also a CORRECTNESS bug under concurrent writes, not only a scan-cost one. LIMIT/OFFSET is positional: if a row is inserted before the current window between two page fetches, everything shifts down by one, so a row that was the last item of page 1 reappears as the first item of page 2 (a duplicate across pages); symmetrically, a delete before the window skips a row. Tests miss it because they don't insert/delete between page fetches. Fix: keyset/seek pagination — a cursor on a stable, unique, monotonic sort key, e.g. WHERE (created_at, id) > (:last_ts, :last_id) ORDER BY created_at, id LIMIT 20 — which is stable under concurrent inserts/deletes and also avoids the large-OFFSET scan cost. The cursor's sort key must be unique/tie-broken: a non-unique timestamp cursor has its own drop/duplicate trap (time-date-correctness.md).
expectations: Identifies OFFSET pagination as a correctness hazard under concurrent writes (positional shift -> duplicate row across pages on insert, skipped row on delete), not only a scan-cost issue
Explains why tests miss it (no insert/delete between page fetches)
Prescribes keyset/seek pagination on a stable unique (sort_key, id) cursor, and notes the cursor key must be unique/tie-broken (cross-ref the non-unique-timestamp-cursor trap)

evals.prompt: A test suite is green on every CI run and always executes in file/declaration order. A dev asks whether it's safe to parallelize or reorder the tests. What should a reviewer check, and why isn't 'it's always green' sufficient?
evals.expected_output: 'Always green' only proves the suite passes in the ONE order it always runs — it can be hiding inter-test state pollution (a module-level cache, a shared fixture, a leaked singleton, an env var one test sets and another reads) that only manifests under a different order. The check: run the suite with RANDOMIZED test order and a LOGGED seed (pytest-randomly; Jest --randomize with --seed; JUnit MethodOrderer.Random). A failure that appears only under randomization is real order-dependence, and re-running with the same seed reproduces it deterministically for debugging. Until that passes, reordering/parallelizing is unsafe — the green is an artifact of the fixed order, not evidence of test independence. Fix the exposed coupling (isolate/reset shared state per test, remove the cross-test dependency), then keep randomized order on in CI so a regression surfaces immediately. Distinct from environment determinism (no real network/clock) — this is execution-order coupling between tests.
expectations: Explains 'always green' only proves the one fixed order works and can hide inter-test state pollution (shared cache/fixture/singleton/env) that appears under a different order
Prescribes randomized test order with a logged/reproducible seed (pytest-randomly / Jest --randomize --seed / JUnit MethodOrderer.Random) as the detection method
Says reordering/parallelizing is unsafe until that passes; fix the coupling then keep randomized order on in CI (distinct from environment determinism)

evals.prompt: A dashboard computes service error rate and p99 latency from traces collected with a fixed 1% head-based sampler. The numbers look healthy. A reviewer says 'sampling is fine, it's statistically representative.' Is the error rate / p99 trustworthy?
evals.expected_output: Partly — but not for the reason either naive framing implies. For a UNIFORM fixed-rate head sampler the sampled error PROPORTION is an unbiased estimate of the true rate in aggregate, so the headline error rate is not systematically biased ('statistically representative' is right about that much). The real problems are: (a) coverage — head sampling cannot guarantee a SPECIFIC error trace was kept (OpenTelemetry: 'you cannot ensure that all traces with an error within them are sampled with head sampling alone'), so it is unreliable for pulling up a given incident's traces; (b) variance — at 1% the error/slow counts in a short burn-rate window are tiny and noisy, under-reading an incident more often than not; (c) tail estimation — p99/p999 from a thinned tail is unstable and biased. And an adaptive / load-shedding head sampler that drops more under load DOES bias the rate, precisely during incidents. So p99 is not trustworthy, per-incident trace coverage is not guaranteed, and short-window SLIs are noisy — even though the aggregate rate is roughly right. Fix: tail sampling with an always-keep-error/high-latency policy, and compute error-rate & latency SLIs from unsampled counters/histograms, not the sampled trace set.
expectations: Corrects both naive answers: a uniform head sampler's aggregate error RATE is ~unbiased (not 'systematically biased'), but head sampling still fails on coverage (can't guarantee a specific error trace is kept), variance at low counts in short windows, and p99/tail estimation — and an adaptive/load-shedding sampler does bias the rate under load
Notes the practical impact: short-window burn-rate/error-budget SLIs are noisy and under-read incidents, per-incident traces may be missing, and p99/tail is unstable from a thinned sample
Prescribes tail sampling with an always-keep-error/high-latency policy and computing rate/latency SLIs from unsampled counters/histograms, not the sampled trace set

evals.prompt: An API returns `429 Too Many Requests` under load with an empty body and no `Retry-After` header. Clients are told in the docs to 'retry with backoff.' Is the throttling contract complete?
evals.expected_output: No. The provider is throttling but giving clients nothing to act on: with no Retry-After header, every client must GUESS a backoff — typically retrying immediately (hammering the already-overloaded service) or backing off far more than necessary (hurting its own latency). The provider's obligation is to emit Retry-After on its 429/503 responses so clients back off by instruction, not by guess — HTTP's Retry-After tells a client how long to wait before a new request, and in a 429 it is the throttle duration. Better still, emit a machine-readable budget signal (the IETF 'RateLimit header fields for HTTP' draft — cite it by name for the current field set, as the draft is actively revised) so a well-behaved client self-paces BEFORE it trips the limit. 'Docs say retry with backoff' is not a substitute for the on-the-wire signal — docs can't tell a client how long THIS particular throttle lasts. This is the provider's outbound obligation, distinct from a caller honoring Retry-After on its own retries. Fix: set Retry-After (a seconds value or HTTP-date), and ideally RateLimit-*, on every throttled response.
expectations: Identifies that a 429/503 with no Retry-After forces every client to guess backoff (hammer immediately or over-back-off); the provider must emit Retry-After so clients back off by instruction
Adds the machine-readable budget signal (IETF RateLimit-* header fields) so clients self-pace before tripping the limit
Notes docs are not a substitute for the on-the-wire signal, and frames it as the provider's outbound obligation (distinct from a caller honoring Retry-After on its own retries)

evals.prompt: A Dockerfile for a production service starts `FROM node:latest`, installs deps, and ends `CMD ["node","server.js"]` — no `USER` line, no resource limits declared, and the base isn't pinned. It builds and the app runs. A reviewer says the Dockerfile is fine since it works. Any container-hardening findings?
evals.expected_output: Several. (1) Runs as root — no USER directive, so the process runs as root in the container; a container escape or app RCE then has root. Add an explicit non-root USER (and drop Linux capabilities, no-new-privileges, read-only root filesystem where possible). (2) Unpinned base — FROM node:latest is non-reproducible and silently pulls a new base over time; pin by digest (node@sha256:...), prefer minimal/distroless, and multi-stage-build so build tools don't ship. (3) No resource limits — nothing caps memory/CPU, so one container can starve the host; set limits (and at the orchestration layer, per-container requests/limits). Also scan the final image (Trivy/Grype) + emit an SBOM, and confirm no secret is baked into a layer or build arg. 'It builds and runs' is not the bar — none of these surface at runtime until they bite.
expectations: Flags running as root (no USER) and prescribes a non-root USER (+ dropped caps / no-new-privileges / read-only rootfs)
Flags the unpinned `:latest` base and prescribes pinning by digest (+ minimal/distroless, multi-stage build)
Flags the absent memory/CPU resource limits (one container can starve the host)

evals.prompt: A Kubernetes Deployment sets `securityContext: { privileged: true, runAsUser: 0 }`, declares no resource requests/limits, and the namespace has no NetworkPolicy. It passes CI and deploys. What should a review flag?
evals.expected_output: Multiple pod-security and isolation findings. (1) privileged: true + runAsUser: 0 — the pod runs as root with full host capabilities, effectively no container boundary; set runAsNonRoot: true, privileged: false, allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, drop capabilities, add a seccomp profile, and readOnlyRootFilesystem: true. (2) No resource requests/limits — one pod can starve the node; set them on every container and add liveness/readiness probes. (3) No NetworkPolicy — the namespace allows unrestricted pod-to-pod traffic; apply a default-deny NetworkPolicy with explicit allows (especially in a shared/multi-tenant cluster, where it also caps cross-tenant blast radius). Enforce with admission policy (OPA-Gatekeeper/Kyverno) so a future manifest can't reintroduce them. Passing CI and deploying is not the same as hardened.
expectations: Flags privileged/runAsUser:0 and prescribes the pod securityContext (runAsNonRoot, privileged:false, allowPrivilegeEscalation:false, dropped caps, seccomp, readOnlyRootFilesystem)
Flags the missing resource requests/limits (+ liveness/readiness probes)
Flags the absent NetworkPolicy (default-deny + explicit allows), noting the multi-tenant blast-radius angle

evals.prompt: A Terraform diff adds a security-group rule `cidr_blocks = ["0.0.0.0/0"]` on port 22, and an object-storage bucket with no public-access block and no encryption configured. `terraform plan` is clean and the reviewer approves. Sound?
evals.expected_output: No. (1) SSH (port 22) open to 0.0.0.0/0 exposes the host's admin port to the entire internet — a top brute-force/exposure finding; scope ingress to a bastion/VPN CIDR or use a session-manager/IAP, never 0.0.0.0/0 on 22 (same for RDP 3389, DB ports, admin panels). (2) The bucket has no public-access block and no encryption — it risks public-data exposure and stores data unencrypted at rest; enable the account/bucket public-access block, enforce encryption at rest and in transit, and add versioning + access logging for a sensitive store. terraform plan being clean only means the config is syntactically applyable, not safe — run an IaC scanner (tfsec/Checkov/KICS) in CI to catch exactly these. (Least-privilege IAM — no `*` actions/resources — is the sibling check.)
expectations: Flags 0.0.0.0/0 on port 22 (admin port to the whole internet) and prescribes scoping ingress (bastion/VPN/session-manager), not world-open on sensitive ports
Flags the public bucket (no public-access block) and missing encryption at rest/in transit (+ versioning/access-logging)
Notes 'terraform plan clean' does not mean safe — prescribes an IaC scanner (tfsec/Checkov/KICS) in CI

evals.prompt: A SaaS runs all tenants' background jobs through one shared FIFO worker pool and rate-limits the public API with a single global token bucket. One tenant bulk-imports millions of records; other tenants' jobs stop running and their API calls start getting 429s. Authz is correct (no cross-tenant data access). Is this a finding?
evals.expected_output: Yes — a multi-tenancy isolation finding on the FAIRNESS/availability axis, distinct from data isolation (which is correct here). A shared FIFO queue with no per-tenant fairness lets one tenant's backlog monopolize the workers (a noisy-neighbour / head-of-line problem), and a single GLOBAL rate limiter means one tenant's traffic consumes the shared budget and 429s everyone else. Correct authz does not prevent one tenant degrading another's service. Fixes: bound per-tenant work (per-tenant quotas / concurrency caps / weighted-fair or per-tenant queues so no tenant starves the rest), key the rate limiter PER TENANT rather than globally, and cap a bulk operation's blast radius (chunk + backpressure). This is the availability/fairness half of tenant isolation — pair it with the data-isolation checks (RLS / scoped queries).
expectations: Identifies a multi-tenancy FAIRNESS/availability isolation gap (noisy-neighbour), distinct from data isolation, which is correct here
Names both mechanisms: a shared queue with no per-tenant fairness (one tenant starves the pool) and a globally-keyed rate limiter (one tenant 429s everyone)
Prescribes per-tenant quotas/fairness/queues + a per-tenant-keyed limiter + bounding a bulk op's blast radius

evals.prompt: A list renders ~150 rows via `.map()`; the parent holds a 'selected ids' set and a text filter that change on every click/keystroke. The team carefully wrapped all callback props in `useCallback` (with comments explaining they're avoiding prop churn), and each row receives only stable props on a filter-only update — its item data, an `isSelected` boolean derived from the set, and the memoized handlers — and pagination caps the visible rows. Typing in the filter still janks — every row re-renders on each keystroke. Why, given the stable callbacks + pagination, and what's the fix?
evals.expected_output: Because a memoized callback only helps if its RECIPIENT is memoized. The row is a plain function component (not React.memo), so on every parent state change (a keystroke updating the filter, a click updating the selected set) React re-invokes and reconciles every mounted row — even rows whose own props are unchanged — regardless of how stable the callback props are; React still calls the child to produce its new element tree. useCallback/useMemo keeping props referentially stable is necessary but not sufficient. Pagination/windowing bounds how many rows MOUNT, not the re-render cost of the mounted ones, so 150 rows still fully re-render per keystroke. Fix: wrap the row component in React.memo — and note it is low-risk/high-payoff precisely because the props are ALREADY stable (that defeats the 'will memo actually help, or will props churn defeat it?' objection). Acceptance: a render-count check — one row's action should re-render that row only, not the whole visible set. The stable-callback code looking 'already optimized' (with its own comments) is exactly why the missing memo boundary one level up gets overlooked.
expectations: Identifies the missing memo boundary: the row isn't React.memo'd, so parent state changes re-render every mounted row regardless of stable callbacks (stable props are necessary but not sufficient)
Notes pagination/windowing bounds mount count, not re-render cost, so it doesn't solve this
Prescribes React.memo on the row (low-risk BECAUSE props are already stable) with a render-count acceptance check (one row's action re-renders only that row)

evals.prompt: A card component used across three high-traffic list routes (dashboard, inbox, my-items) statically imports a rich-text editor library at module scope. The editor only renders when the user clicks 'edit' (behind an `editing` gate). A reviewer checks 'is the editor gated?', sees yes, and approves. The editor adds ~130KB gzip. Is the bundle cost handled?
evals.expected_output: No. The editor's RENDER is gated, but its IMPORT is not — a static import at module scope means the bundler ships the library in the bundle of every route that transitively imports the card component, so all three high-traffic list routes carry the ~130KB even though most visitors never click 'edit.' The reviewer checked the wrong gate: for bundle weight the gate that matters is the import, not the render. Fix: defer the library behind the same interaction gate the render already uses — next/dynamic / React.lazy / an inline await import(...) triggered on 'edit' — so only users who actually open the editor download it. Detect the class generally by grepping each heavy/optional dependency's importers and flagging any imported statically from a component mounted on a list/index route where the heavy part only renders behind interaction. Strong tell: if the codebase already defers a different heavy dependency correctly (e.g. a doc-export lib via await import() from a click handler), name that precedent — it makes the fix trivially arguable.
expectations: Identifies that a static import ships the heavy lib in every route's bundle regardless of the render gate — the reviewer checked the render gate, but the IMPORT determines bundle weight
Prescribes deferring the import behind the same interaction gate (next/dynamic / React.lazy / inline import()) so only users who trigger it download it
Gives the detection method (grep the heavy dep's importers; flag static import from a list-route-mounted component) and/or the existing-precedent tell
